text:
Before her murder made national headlines, Jacquelyn Smith was a 54-year-old electrical engineer at the U.S. Army’s Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland. She had built a career in a demanding technical field and was living in Baltimore with her husband, Keith Tyrone Smith. On December 1, 2018, her life ended in an attack that Keith initially blamed on a stranger.

That evening, Jacquelyn had been out with Keith and his daughter, Valeria. Keith told police they stopped at an East Baltimore intersection, where Jacquelyn offered money to a woman holding a baby. He claimed a male panhandler approached the passenger window and stabbed her. Jacquelyn was rushed to Johns Hopkins Hospital, where she died from multiple stab wounds.

The story spread nationwide, prompting outrage and warnings about giving money to strangers. But investigators found that surveillance footage showed neither the alleged panhandlers nor the family’s vehicle at the intersection. Cell phone records instead placed the car inside Druid Hill Park during the attack.

In March 2019, Keith and Valeria were arrested in Texas near the Mexican border. Valeria later admitted that her father stabbed Jacquelyn inside the vehicle and invented the panhandler story. She testified that Keith ordered her to discard Jacquelyn’s purse while he disposed of the knife. Prosecutors also presented evidence that Keith hoped to collect an $804,000 life insurance policy.

In December 2021, a jury convicted Keith of first-degree murder and a weapons offense. He received a life sentence in February 2022. Valeria, who pleaded guilty to accessory after the fact and testified against her father, received five years in prison followed by probation.

Before the false robbery story, the investigation, and the courtroom testimony, Jacquelyn was an accomplished engineer with a life and career of her own. Her murder stole that future, while her husband’s fabricated account diverted attention toward innocent strangers.

text:
Colonel Edward M House (right photo) was a Texas kingmaker who got behind Woodrow Wilson (left) in 1911. House’s father was an English immigrant who built a fortune, became mayor of Houston, and then a Confederate blockade runner. House inherited a family fortune, sold the plantations and invested in railroads, banks and newspapers. He worked behind the scenes and got four Texas governors elected including “Big Jim“ Hogg. House’s work in politics was always as an inside adviser.

When House met NJ Gov Woodrow Wilson in 1911, the two immediately became close friends. Wilson described House as “my second personality” and “my independent self.” They had similar philosophies about government. 

But the pedantic Wilson, formerly president of Princeton University, who had been a governor for only two years, was not politically street-smart. House immediately started to coach Wilson prior to the Democratic Party’s convention.

House used his Texas contacts and campaign skill to secure Wlson’s  Democratic nomination and, with a divided Republican Party, easily win the 1912 presidential election. Wilson offered him any cabinet post (except Secretary of State). House declined. He preferred being the ‘Philip Dru’ character in his book, an informal role as confidant and “executive agent.” He was given living quarters in the White House.

Modern Security Relocations

Several senior Trump administration officials—including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and White House aide Stephen Miller—have relocated to secure military installations in the Washington, D.C., area to evade targeted doxxing, intense political harassment, and escalated foreign threats. To ensure the safety of these officials, the administration and federal law enforcement have utilized two primary installations situated within minutes of the White House: Fort Lesley J. McNair in Southwest Washington and Joint Base Myer-Henderson Hall in Arlington, Virginia.

Fort McNair, located at the confluence of the Potomac and Anacostia rivers, is one of the oldest active Army posts in the United States, keeping officials just a few miles south of the executive branch. Across the Potomac, Joint Base Myer-Henderson Hall sits adjacent to Arlington National Cemetery, functioning as a primary administrative and residential hub for military leadership. By absorbing cabinet members into these fortified perimeters, the administration provides immediate physical security and access control that civilian residential neighborhoods simply cannot offer against coordinated protests and sophisticated tracking.

The Masonic Heritage of Capital Defenses

The strategic use of these specific bases inadvertently highlights the deep historical ties between Washington’s military infrastructure and American Freemasonry. While neither base was founded explicitly as a Masonic institution, the fraternity is woven directly into their physical and leadership foundations. Fort McNair occupies a peninsula originally surveyed by Pierre Charles L’Enfant, a prominent Freemason who laid out the federal city. Decades later, on February 21, 1903, the Grand Lodge of the District of Columbia performed a formal Masonic cornerstone-laying ceremony for Roosevelt Hall, the fort's architectural centerpiece. President Theodore Roosevelt, an active Freemason, attended and participated in the dedication wearing full Masonic regalia.

Across the river at Joint Base Myer-Henderson Hall, historic Quarters One has served as the residence for numerous Army Chiefs of Staff who were influential Freemasons, most notably General Douglas MacArthur and General George C. Marshall. This profound overlap between federal military installations and Masonic tradition extends throughout the immediate Capital region, mirroring George Washington's own Masonic dedication of the U.S. Capitol building. Just down the Anacostia River from Fort McNair, the historic Washington Navy Yard was fundamentally shaped by Freemasons; Naval Lodge No. 4 was chartered in 1805 specifically by and for the craftsmen and shipbuilders working in the Navy Yard. Today, these installations reflect a centuries-old tradition where the capital's military defense and Masonic heritage continuously intersect, a legacy that is now serving as a modern, fortified shield for the executive branch.

text:
O'Keefe v. Read et al Wrongful Death Suit

C.F. McCarthy’s has filed a motion seeking to exclude the expert report AND testimony of Dr. Barry Logan, the forensic toxicologist retained by the O’Keefe family, from both the summary judgment proceedings and any eventual trial.

This is significant because Logan's opinions are part of the plaintiffs' effort to establish that Karen Read was visibly intoxicated when C.F. McCarthy’s served her alcohol on January 28, 2022.

🔶 WHO IS DR. BARRY LOGAN?

According to the filing, Dr. Logan is a forensic toxicologist whom the plaintiffs intend to offer as an expert concerning:

🔸 How alcohol is absorbed into the body.

🔸 How alcohol impairment manifests.

🔸 The effects of alcohol on cognitive functioning.

🔸 The effects of alcohol on motor skills and physical coordination.

His testimony is intended to help address the relationship between alcohol consumption, impairment, and observable signs of intoxication.

🔶 WHAT IS C.F. McCARTHY’S ARGUING?

The establishment contends that Logan's report and anticipated testimony are inadmissible under Massachusetts case law.

Its central argument is that the plaintiffs have not presented other admissible, direct evidence establishing that Read displayed visible signs of intoxication while being served at C.F. McCarthy’s.

The defense is challenging whether Logan's expert opinions can be used to support the plaintiffs' claims under those circumstances.

🔶 WHY DOES VISIBLE INTOXICATION MATTER?

The legal dispute is not simply whether Read consumed alcohol or whether she was impaired later that evening.

The central issue for the claims against C.F. McCarthy’s is whether she was visibly intoxicated when the establishment served her alcohol.

That distinction is crucial to the establishment's request for summary judgment.

🔶 WHAT EXACTLY IS THE DEFENSE ASKING THE JUDGE TO DO?

C.F. McCarthy’s wants the court to:

🔸 Exclude Dr. Logan's expert report from consideration when deciding summary judgment.

🔸 Prevent Dr. Logan from testifying as an expert if the case proceeds to trial.

🔸 Consider the additional legal arguments contained in a separate accompanying Memorandum of Law.

🔶 WHY THIS MOTION COULD MATTER

The O’Keefe family has relied on expert toxicology opinions in arguing that Read's alcohol consumption supports an inference of visible intoxication.

If the judge excludes Logan's opinions, the plaintiffs would lose that expert evidence in their case against C.F. McCarthy’s.

However, excluding an expert would not automatically establish that the entire lawsuit must be dismissed. The judge would still need to evaluate the remaining admissible evidence and the applicable legal standards.

If multiple witnesses testified that they did not observe Read displaying visible signs of intoxication, and the plaintiffs' toxicology expert is excluded, what evidence would remain to establish that C.F. McCarthy’s served her while visibly intoxicated?

Anthony and his wife, Eileen, had planned to spend the winter in Fort Myers and return to Massachusetts, as they had in previous years.

Then a lump under his arm in November 2024 turned out to be an aggressive form of non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

When Anthony turned up for his second cancer treatment, he was struggling to breathe.

Doctors found a blockage in his heart, and a five-vessel bypass put his cancer treatment on hold for about six weeks, Eileen recalled.

After surgery, doctors gave him lower doses of chemotherapy, but the lymphoma did not respond and his health ruled out further intensive treatment.

His local oncologist referred him to Moffitt Cancer Center in Tampa, where haematologist Sameh Gaballa offered an immunotherapy that helps immune cells recognise and attack cancer cells.

Anthony received it alongside polatuzumab, another cancer medicine, and the team monitored him closely during his first treatments.

As he responded, Gaballa and Anthony’s local oncologist arranged for him to continue treatment in Fort Myers, saving the couple a two-hour drive each way for every infusion.

In May 2026, his scans showed no sign of lymphoma and his team told him he was in complete remission.

With follow-up scans still planned, Anthony was looking forward to getting back to the Massachusetts home he and Eileen had shared for more than 54 years.

Walter McMillian was put on death row 15 months before his trial. The jury recommended life, but the judge sentenced him to the electric chair. No physical evidence linked him to the murder. The main witness admitted lying under police pressure, and another got $5,000 for false testimony. McMillian watched seven men get executed while awaiting his own death. He was freed after six years.

In the video below 60 Minutes investigates the case that inspired the film Just Mercy.

There were no fingerprints. No ballistics. No physical evidence of any kind. Just the word of two men who were paid or pressured to talk.

Ralph Myers was facing the electric chair himself when an ABI agent offered him a deal. Testify against McMillian and get 30 years with parole instead of death. Before the trial he told four psychiatrists his statements were coerced. The jury never heard it.

He described the victim lying face-up behind the register. The first officer on scene found her face-down in a different part of the building. No drag marks. No blood trail.

Bill Hooks claimed he saw McMillian's lowrider truck at the scene. But the mechanic who built it confirmed the modification was done six months after the murder. Hooks got $5,000 and his charges dropped the same day he gave his statement.

The prosecutor asked a police officer to lie about the position of the body. The officer refused. During the trial the prosecutor reminded the jury that McMillian had been sleeping with a white woman. In Alabama.

When Myers recanted, the DA didn't reopen the case. He moved to indict Myers for perjury - not for lying at trial, but for telling the truth now.

Was Walter McMillian failed by one corrupt investigation, or by a system that would rather execute the wrong man than admit it made a mistake?

Independent drug-pricing and health policy analysts point out that while consumer price indices show dropping drug prices, the underlying causes are more complex. Professors and health economists from institutions like the Vanderbilt University School of Medicine note that a major factor is likely the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), a law passed during the Biden administration that allowed Medicare to negotiate prices directly with drugmakers for the first time. The first 10 negotiated Medicare drug prices went into effect in January 2026, directly impacting aggregate price indices. Experts also credit increased market competition, such as the arrival of new biosimilar alternatives for major autoimmune and inflammatory drugs, for driving down costs. 
Furthermore, experts indicate that it is difficult to accurately measure the standalone impact of the Trump administration's policies. Many of the MFN Medicaid programs and voluntary company details remain under development or have not yet filtered through to affect consumer price index calculations. Analysts also noted that while https://t.co/EIH2wImlMd introduces transparency, many brand-name medications on the platform remain cheaper when purchased through traditional health insurance or as generics elsewhere.
Advocacy and policy groups critical of the administration, such as Protect Our Care, dismiss the initiatives as "smoke and mirrors". They argue that the Medicaid MFN agreements offer minimal benefit to enrolled low-income families who already pay very little out-of-pocket for their medications. These groups allege that the voluntary manufacturer deals are "immaterial" to the bottom lines of big pharmaceutical corporations and were designed primarily to help the industry avoid stricter regulations, such as broad tariffs. Critics also question the White House's reported $700 million savings figure for https://t.co/EIH2wImlMd, noting that the administration's platform vendor, GoodRx, acknowledged its actual business utilization and material impact has been incremental.

text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

The artist-led backlash against AI is well underway. While plenty of people are still enjoying letting their imaginations run wild with popular text-to-image models like DALL-E 2, Midjourney, and Stable Diffusion, artists are increasingly fed up with the new status quo. 

Some have united in protest against the tech sector’s common practice of indiscriminately scraping their visual work off the internet  to train their models. Artists have staged protests on popular art platforms such as DeviantArt and Art Station, or left the platforms entirely. Some have even filed lawsuits over copyright.  

Right now, there is total power asymmetry between rich and influential technology companies and artists, says Ben Zhao, a computer science professor at the University of Chicago. “The training companies can do whatever the heck they want,” Zhao says. 

But a new tool developed by Zhao’s lab might change that power dynamic. It’s called Nightshade, and it works by making subtle changes to the pixels of the image—changes that are invisible to the human eye but trick machine-learning models into thinking the image depicts something different from what it actually does. When artists apply it to their work and those images are then hoovered up as training data, these “poisoned pixels” make their way into the AI model’s data set, and cause the model to malfunction. Images of dogs become cats, hats become toasters, cars become cows. The results are really impressive, and there is currently no known defense. Read more from my story here. 

Some companies, such as OpenAI and Stability AI, have offered to let artists opt out of training sets, or have said they will respect requests not to have their work scraped. However, there’s no mechanism to force companies to stay true to their word right now. Zhao says Nightshade could be that mechanism. It is extremely expensive to build and train generative AI models, and it could be very risky for tech companies to scrape data that could break their crown jewels. 

Autumn Beverly, an artist who intends to use Nightshade, says she found her work had been scraped into the populace LAION-5B data set, and that felt very “violating.” 

“I never would have agreed to that, and [AI companies] just took it without any consent or notification or anything,” she says.

Before tools like Nightshade, Beverly did not feel comfortable sharing her work online. Beverly and other artists are calling for tech companies to shift from opt-out mechanisms to asking for consent first, and to start compensating artists for their contributions. These demands would involve some truly revolutionary changes to how the AI sector usually functions, yet she remains hopeful. 

“I’m hoping that it makes it where things have to be through consent—otherwise, they’re going to just have a broken system,” Beverly says. “That is the entire goal for me.” 

But artists are the canary in the coal mine. Their fight belongs to anyone who has ever posted anything they care about online. Our personal data, social media posts, song lyrics, news articles, fiction, even our faces—anything that is freely available online could end up in an AI model forever without our knowing about it. 

Tools like Nightshade could be a first step in tipping the power balance back to us. 

Deeper Learning

How Meta and AI companies recruited striking actors to train AI

Earlier this year, a company called Realeyes ran an “emotion study.” It recruited actors and then captured audio and video data of their voices, faces, and movements, which it fed into an AI database. That database is being used to help train virtual avatars for Meta. The project coincided with Hollywood’s historic strikes. With the industry at a standstill, the larger-than-usual number of out-of-work actors may have been a boon for Meta and Realeyes: here was a new pool of “trainers”—and data points—perfectly suited to teaching their AI to appear more human. 

Who owns your face: Many actors across the industry worry that AI—much like the models described in the emotion study—could be used to replace them, whether or not their exact faces are copied. Read more from Eileen Guo here.

Bits and Bytes

How China plans to judge generative AI safety
The Chinese government has a new draft document that proposes detailed rules for how to determine whether a generative AI model is problematic. Our China tech writer Zeyi Yang unpacks it for us. (MIT Technology Review) 

AI chatbots can guess your personal information from what you type
New research has found that large language models are excellent at guessing people’s private information from chats. This could be used to supercharge profiling for advertisements, for example. (Wired) 

OpenAI claims its new tool can detect images by DALL-E with 99% accuracy
OpenAI executives say the company is developing the tool after leading AI companies made a voluntary pledge to the White House to develop watermarks and other detection mechanisms for AI-generated content. Google announced its watermarking tool in August. (Bloomberg)

AI models fail miserably in transparency
When Stanford University tested how transparent large language models are, it found that the top-scoring model, Meta’s LLaMA 2, only scored 54 out of 100. Growing opacity is a worrying trend in AI. AI models are going to have huge societal influence, and we need more visibility into them to be able to hold them accountable. (Stanford) 

A college student built an AI system to read 2,000-year-old Roman scrolls
How fun! A 21-year-old computer science major developed an AI program to decipher ancient Roman scrolls that were damaged by a volcanic eruption in the year 79. The program was able to detect about a dozen letters, which experts translated into the word “porphyras”—ancient Greek for purple.  (The Washington Post)

🌍 WORLD NEWS REPORT
November 13, 2026 | A World at a Crossroads
War, Political Change, Economic Pressure, Climate Challenges and Humanity's Future
🇺🇸 1. UNITED STATES: DEMOCRATS RESHAPE CONGRESS
America's November 3 midterm elections produced a sweeping Democratic victory. Democrats secured both the House of Representatives and Senate, dramatically changing the political landscape confronting President Donald Trump.

Voters expressed frustration over living costs, inflation and government policies. Democrats gained more than 40 Republican-held House seats. The new Congress, beginning in January 2027, will have stronger oversight authority, although presidential veto powers remain.
Republicans have largely retained their allegiance to Trump. Jim Jordan was selected as their next House leader, while John Thune retained Senate Republican leadership.

The central question: Can divided government produce meaningful economic reforms, or will confrontation dominate Washington?

🇺🇦 2. UKRAINE: PEACE TALKS CONTINUE AS CIVILIANS DIE

Russian attacks struck Zaporizhzhia and Odesa on November 13, killing at least three people and injuring dozens, according to Ukrainian officials. Residential buildings suffered serious damage.

Ukrainian drones also struck targets inside Russia, including energy infrastructure. Both countries continue attacking despite renewed diplomatic negotiations.
American envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner participated in efforts involving Moscow and Kyiv. Negotiations in Abu Dhabi produced agreement on a prisoner exchange but no settlement of fundamental territorial disagreements.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy demands security guarantees and protection of Ukrainian sovereignty. President Vladimir Putin maintains territorial and military demands Kyiv rejects.

Europe fears any agreement permitting territorial conquest could undermine continental security for generations.

🇵🇸 3. GAZA: A CEASEFIRE WITHOUT LASTING SECURITY

More than a year after the October 2025 ceasefire, Gaza continues experiencing deadly violence and humanitarian suffering.

An Israeli strike on Nasser Hospital's surgical wing killed six people, including a surgeon and a 13-year-old boy, according to Associated Press reporting.
Israel said it targeted a Hamas commander allegedly operating from the facility but did not publicly provide supporting evidence.

Gaza's hospitals face devastating shortages of medical equipment, medicine and functioning infrastructure.

International humanitarian law protects medical facilities, subject to narrowly defined exceptions and strict restrictions on attacks.

The challenge extends beyond ending hostilities: rebuilding healthcare, restoring homes and establishing legitimate, lasting security for Israelis and Palestinians.

🇮🇷 4. IRAN: GULF TENSIONS THREATEN INTERNATIONAL SHIPPING

The United States reported intercepting two Iranian drones approaching Bahrain. Iran claimed an attack against American radar facilities, which Washington disputed.

Military tensions surrounding Iran continue threatening shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a strategically critical international energy passage.
The United Nations maritime agency documented 134 regional maritime incidents by November 11, with deadly consequences for seafarers.

Renewed confrontation could disrupt energy supplies, increase transportation costs and further undermine regional stability.

💰 5. GLOBAL ECONOMY: INFLATION AND INTEREST RATES

American producer prices increased 6.5% over the year ending in October, reinforcing concerns about persistent inflation.

Federal Reserve officials are discussing additional interest-rate increases. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent argues that temporary energy-related price increases should not provoke excessive tightening, while other policymakers warn inflation has spread beyond energy.
Higher interest rates can restrain inflation but also increase borrowing costs for households, businesses and governments.

The consequences extend internationally through exchange rates, investment flows and the cost of financing development.

🤖 6. ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: TECHNOLOGY MARKETS FACE UNCERTAINTY

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's unexpected resignation has unsettled investors in the semiconductor industry.

Technology stocks declined on November 13, with the Nasdaq falling approximately 0.9%. Investors are examining whether massive artificial-intelligence infrastructure spending can generate sustainable profits.
Anthropic's anticipated public offering could become another major test of confidence in the industry.

Beyond financial markets, governments face difficult questions about employment, cybersecurity, surveillance, misinformation and the concentration of technological power.

Innovation offers extraordinary possibilities, but responsible human oversight remains essential.

🌡️ 7. CLIMATE: WORLD LEADERS CONFRONT AN UNEQUAL CRISIS

At COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres called for drastic reductions in greenhouse gas emissions.

Negotiations remain divided over fossil fuels, financial assistance and responsibility for addressing climate damage.
Developing nations argue that wealthy industrialized countries should provide greater assistance because historical emissions helped create the problem.

A climate-finance commitment targets $300 billion annually for developing countries by 2035. Achieving meaningful reductions while protecting vulnerable economies remains a central challenge.

🇸🇩 8. SUDAN: WAR, DISPLACEMENT AND THE TRADE IN GOLD

Sudan's conflict, which began in April 2023, continues devastating communities and forcing millions from their homes.

A new Swissaid investigation alleges that illicit gold from conflict-affected countries continues entering the United Arab Emirates despite tighter regulations.
Researchers estimate that illicit gold imports into the UAE reached $74 billion in 2024, including substantial shipments originating in African countries.

The findings raise difficult questions about international supply chains and whether commercial profits are helping sustain armed conflicts.

🌎 9. THE BIGGER PICTURE: HUMANITY'S SHARED FUTURE

Today's developments reveal interconnected dangers.

War destabilizes trade. Energy disruptions intensify inflation. Climate disasters burden vulnerable societies. Technological advances challenge existing economic structures.
Yet diplomacy, scientific progress, humanitarian assistance and democratic institutions provide opportunities for constructive change.

FINAL ASSESSMENT

November 13, 2026, reveals a world confronting difficult choices rather than inevitable catastrophe.

The most important unresolved questions concern whether Ukraine's sovereignty can be protected through diplomacy, whether civilians in Gaza and Sudan can receive lasting protection, whether inflation can be contained without serious economic damage, and whether governments can cooperate on climate change.

The coming months will test not only international leadership, but humanity's willingness to place human dignity, justice and peaceful coexistence above narrow political and economic interests.

Sources: Reuters and Associated Press reporting, November 10–13, 2026; CBS News and ABC News election coverage; United Nations climate and humanitarian reporting; Swissaid investigation as reported by AP.

Reporting reflects information available November 13, 2026. Casualty figures and contested military claims may change as independent verification continues.

China seeks advanced American technology while Russia continues its war against Ukraine. Millions of Americans also have retirement savings exposed to technology companies through their 401(k)s.

Who knew what, when, and why? Are our institutions adequately protecting American interests?

These incidents have different causes, and no evidence establishes that they are part of one coordinated attack. But they raise important questions about foreign influence, national security, corporate responsibility and government accountability.

NOW CONSIDER GEORGE WASHINGTON'S WARNING.

In 1796, Washington opened his Farewell Address:

"Friends and Fellow-Citizens"

He explained that his concerns came from:

"a solicitude for your welfare which cannot end but with my life"

He warned about replacing the people's interests with:

"the will of a party, often a small but artful and enterprising minority"

He described the dangers of political passions creating:

"ill-founded jealousies and false alarms"

And he warned:

"It opens the door to foreign influence and corruption"

Washington also cautioned Americans:

"to guard against the impostures of pretended patriotism"

He believed:

"it is essential that public opinion should be enlightened."

Think about those words. Not through a Democrat's lens. Not through a Republican's lens. Through your own independent American lens.

How many warnings can you recognize in today's headlines?

Washington offered these warnings to protect our union, our liberties and future generations. He did not want Americans divided into enemies by political factions.

Our mission at The Higher Desires includes encouraging independent thought, peace, compassion and helping our fellow citizens.

text:
Sommer lied to her mom that she was "modeling" in Miami while she was stripping and shooting porn, and her family found out when a guy they knew walked up and asked if that was her in the videos.

Her mom had already worked it out: "Is that what you were doing in Miami when you told me you were modeling?" Sommer says she'd leave the house at 7am and come back at 10pm wrecked, makeup gone and hair ruined. At 18 she moved out of her mom's house three days after her birthday and spent the next three years with a boyfriend, stripping on the side whenever they broke up. Around 21 she left him for good and got into porn. As the new girl she had plenty of offers and turned a lot down, trying to keep it secret from her parents and her ex. It didn't stay secret, and when the guy recognized her, her reaction was: why is he watching me, and why is that what we're talking about?

On a good day she makes a thousand dollars, which no normal job pays, and she says that's exactly why she can't go back to one. Her scenes get leaked, though, and people screen-record them all over the internet, which is why she says nobody lives off porn alone anymore. So she sells her own content on premium Snapchat and OnlyFans. OnlyFans fans paid $7.2 billion in fiscal 2024, and the platform says creators keep 80% of it.

When the bookings dried up, she kept asking why other girls got work and she didn't, and changed her hair, her makeup, everything. She ended up smoking weed and drinking wine every day in a toxic relationship in Vegas. Moving to LA and going back to stripping is what pulled her out.

She also says it's rare for Black women in porn to book six to eight scenes a month, even though pop culture copies their look everywhere. Colorlines reported that women of color in porn are paid half to three quarters of what white actresses make. Rolling Stone described studios letting white A-list women charge above their rate to shoot with Black performers, a racial pay ladder that agents profit from through their commissions. Performer Daisy Ducati wrote that directors aren't afraid to tell a Black performer she's being paid less than a white one.

Given the choice between stripping and porn, she picks porn because it's less work. Stripping means hustling men at the ATM all night, while porn is "set rate, come in, get paid", then home.

Smart hustle or a game rigged against her from day one?

text:
Megan Thee Stallion was 25 when she says rapper Tory Lanez shot her in both feet as she left a pool party at Kylie Jenner's house. She says he then offered her $1 million to stay quiet. Then the internet called her a liar. Then a jury convicted him on 3 felonies:

It was July 12, 2020, in the Hollywood Hills. She says there was an argument in an SUV, she got out, and Lanez fired at her. She walked away bleeding. She first told police she had cut her foot on glass. At trial she said she lied because she was afraid of police, weeks after George Floyd was killed.

She testified that Lanez offered her $1 million to say nothing. His lawyers disputed her account and told the jury someone else fired the gun. He pleaded not guilty.

In April 2022 she told the story on TV for the first time. Half the internet believed her. The other half joked that she was lying. In November 2022 Drake and 21 Savage released an album with a line many listeners took as calling her a liar. It debuted at No. 1 with about 400,000 units.

On December 23, 2022 a Los Angeles jury convicted Lanez of assault with a semiautomatic firearm, carrying a loaded unregistered gun in a car and firing a gun with gross negligence. In August 2023 a judge gave him 10 years. In November 2025 an appeals court upheld the conviction. He says he is innocent.

In December 2025 a Miami jury ruled that a blogger defamed Megan and promoted a sexual deepfake video of her, and awarded her $75,000. Her lawyer called the award small next to the millions she asked for.

He got 10 years. She got years of being called a liar.

Do you believe Megan Thee Stallion, or do you think the jury got it wrong?

🎄👑❤️ IT’S OFFICIAL! PRINCESS CATHERINE’S BELOVED TOGETHER AT CHRISTMAS CAROL SERVICE RETURNS FOR 2026! ✨🎶

A beautiful Christmas tradition is returning, and what wonderful news to welcome as we approach the festive season! ❤️🥹

The Princess of Wales and The Royal Foundation have officially announced that Her Royal Highness will host her sixth annual Together at Christmas Carol Service at Westminster Abbey on Friday, December 11, 2026! 👑🎄

Since launching this special tradition in 2021, Catherine has helped make Together at Christmas an occasion that celebrates not only the joy of the festive season but also the extraordinary kindness of ordinary people.

❤️ THIS YEAR’S BEAUTIFUL MESSAGE

The 2026 service will celebrate the importance of love, kindness and caring for one another.

It will recognise the many ways families, friends, neighbours and communities create environments where people feel safe, supported, valued and connected.

At the heart of this year’s celebration is a particularly touching message: sometimes, the greatest gift we can offer another person is the reassurance that they are not alone.

Whether through a comforting conversation, an act of generosity, a listening ear or simply being present during someone’s difficult moments, even the smallest gestures can make an extraordinary difference. ❤️

⛪ MORE THAN 1,600 SPECIAL GUESTS

Westminster Abbey, where Prince William and Catherine married in April 2011, will once again welcome more than 1,600 guests.

Among them will be remarkable individuals recognised for the kindness, compassion and dedication they have shown to others throughout the year.

Many have worked quietly behind the scenes, supporting vulnerable people, strengthening their communities and helping others find hope during challenging times.

What a wonderful way to honour people whose contributions may not always make headlines but whose kindness changes lives every day! 🥹❤️

🎶 A MAGICAL EVENING OF CHRISTMAS MUSIC

The service will feature traditional and contemporary Christmas music, alongside special readings and performances.

And the celebrations will extend far beyond London!

Fifteen additional Together at Christmas community carol services will take place across all four nations of the United Kingdom, from the Shetland Isles to Devon.

These gatherings will recognise local people who have gone above and beyond to bring their communities together and create a sense of belonging. 🎄

📺 WHEN CAN WE WATCH?

The Westminster Abbey service will be recorded for a special Christmas Eve broadcast on ITV1 and ITVX, allowing families across the United Kingdom to share in this beautiful tradition from home.

👑❤️ A TRADITION THAT HAS BECOME SO SPECIAL

Over the years, we have watched Catherine welcome guests to Westminster Abbey, surrounded by Christmas trees, candlelight, beautiful music and the warmth of the festive season.

We have also treasured those precious family moments when Prince William, Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis have joined her for this meaningful occasion.

Those memories make the return of Together at Christmas all the more special.

But beyond the beautiful decorations, music and royal appearances, it is the message behind Catherine’s initiative that makes this tradition so meaningful.

Christmas is not simply about what we receive. It is also about the love, compassion and kindness we give to others. ❤️

What a lovely reminder from our Princess of Wales as another Christmas approaches.

🎄 December 11, 2026 — mark your calendars!

Are you looking forward to Catherine’s Together at Christmas Carol Service this year? And what has been your favourite moment from previous services? 👑❤️

💥 A fifth person has been hauled to court over the Nvidia chips case in Singapore. 🇨🇳 national Shi Bingzhe was handed 41 charges on Nov 13, all for acquiring the benefits of criminal conduct.

Charge sheets state that Shi, who was the director of Superphi and COO of NJ Global Financial, allowed the companies to acquire 917 servers from Aperia International across 41 transactions between May 2024 and Feb 2025.

Shi and the companies had reasonable grounds to believe that those servers represented benefits from Aperia International’s criminal conduct.

Aperia International was among four companies charged in July with false representation in the same case.

Superphi faces six charges, while NJ Global Financial faces 35 charges for acquiring another person’s benefits from criminal conduct.

Both companies were charged alongside Shi. Lawyers for the 34-year-old and the two companies sought an adjournment to take further instructions.

The prosecutor offered Shi bail of S$300,000 and called for him to be electronically tagged, citing the seriousness of his offences.

The judge granted the prosecution’s request for Shi to be electronically tagged.

Police said that five individuals and six companies have been charged in this case, which involves fraud by false representation in the purchase of servers.

They said they would not hesitate to take firm action against businesses and individuals who engage in dishonest and criminal practices.

The other individuals charged are Aaron Woon Guo Jie, Alan Wei Zhaolun, 🇨🇳 national Li Ming, and Jenny Lim.

Wei, Lim and Woon were handed charges for fraud and money laundering, while Li was charged with fraud and fraudulent trading.

Four firms allegedly linked to exporting computer servers that might contain Nvidia chips to Malaysia were charged in July with false representation.

The companies are Aperia International, A-Speed Infotech and Aperia Cloud Services (II) —
collectively known as the Aperia Group — and Luxuriate Your Life.

Wei was Aperia Group’s chief executive, Lim was its CFO and Woon was head of sales.

Li worked at Luxuriate Your Life as the company’s controller.

In the wake of the investigation, the police issued a prohibition of disposal order against a good class bungalow valued at about S$55 million in relation to this case. They also seized about S$1 million in funds from bank accounts linked to the probe.

The case came to light after a US investigation into whether 🇨🇳 DeepSeek had circumvented US restrictions on advanced Nvidia chips by buying them from third parties in other countries, including Singapore.

The scrutiny heightened after Nvidia’s latest financial results showed that 22% of its third-quarter billings were to firms in Singapore, making the country the biggest buyer of its chips after the US.

On Feb 18, 2025, then Second Minister for Trade and Industry Tan See Leng told Parliament that products sold by Nvidia to Singapore that were physically delivered here represent less than 1% of the chipmaker’s overall revenue.

Dr Tan also said that the remainder of Nvidia’s revenue billed to business entities in Singapore did not involve physical shipments into the country.

If convicted, Shi could be jailed for up to 10 years, fined up to S$500,000, or both, for each charge.

Superphi and NJ Global Financial face a fine of up to S$1 million or twice the value of the benefits from criminal conduct, whichever is higher, for each charge.

Their cases will be heard again in court on Jan 4, 2027.

text:
WHO HAS THE RIGHT TO DESTROY WHAT SOMEONE ELSE HAS SPENT A LIFETIME BUILDING?

There is one question I simply cannot ignore.

How many of the people involved in deciding Jensen Huang’s future have ever built a company the size of NVIDIA?

How many have achieved technological breakthroughs of comparable magnitude?

How many have possessed the vision, determination, courage, and perseverance to invest decades of their lives in technologies that others could barely comprehend?

How many have even dared to dream of building something so extraordinary?

Perhaps some of them have achieved remarkable things in their respective fields. I would never deny that.

But there is a fundamental difference we must remember.

Investing money in a technological revolution is not the same as imagining it, designing it, building it, and turning it into reality.

Capital matters. Good governance matters. Boards of directors have legitimate responsibilities and must fulfill them.

But money does not automatically confer wisdom, human sensitivity, or an understanding of what it truly means to be a creator.

A company like NVIDIA was not born simply because someone signed a check.

It was born from a vision. From thousands of difficult decisions, extraordinary risks, sleepless nights, and the relentless dedication of people who dared to imagine a future that did not yet exist.

And now I ask:

What sense of security can any founder or executive have if their private life can become a weapon against them before any relevant wrongdoing has been proven?

Are we seriously suggesting that our greatest innovators should retreat into monasteries?

That they should never fall in love?

That they should never make mistakes in their personal relationships?

That they should give up their private lives out of fear that someone might use their feelings, relationships, or vulnerabilities to destroy their reputation?

For heaven’s sake, wake up!

Corporate security should protect industrial secrets, prevent conflicts of interest, and safeguard people against abuses of power.

It should not become a permanent system of moral surveillance over human intimacy.

Of course, extraordinary positions carry extraordinary responsibilities.

But they should also demand extraordinarily fair, rigorous, and proportionate procedures.

And if sufficient evidence does not exist to justify a decision of such magnitude, reconsidering that decision would not be a defeat.

It would be an act of intelligence, justice, courage, and respect.

Because there is something no stock market valuation can ever fully measure:

The decades of life, imagination, sacrifice, hope, and talent that a human being devotes to creating something that changes the world.

We can replace a position.

We can appoint another CEO.

We can restructure a board of directors.

But we cannot buy, with all the money in the world, the lifetime someone devoted to imagining the impossible and making it real.

And perhaps it is time we remembered that.

There is also another dimension that deserves far greater respect: human relationships.

Behind every public figure stands a private human being.

There may be a wife, a family, children, loved ones, personal commitments, difficult conversations, and emotions that outsiders cannot possibly understand in their entirety.

Those relationships belong first and foremost to the people directly involved.

Not to the media.

Not to strangers seeking entertainment.

Not to a public spectacle in which everyone suddenly believes they have the right to judge another person's most intimate decisions.

Love is not a crime. Human complexity is not evidence of guilt. And personal relationships should not automatically become matters of public prosecution.

If there is coercion, abuse of power, espionage, deliberate disclosure of confidential information, or another demonstrable violation, then investigate it and establish responsibility.

Absolutely.

But let us stop confusing suspicion with proof, personal morality with universal justice, and public curiosity with the right to invade someone's private life.

And let us ask another uncomfortable question.

If someone occupying a position of such strategic importance were unknowingly exposed to a genuine foreign intelligence threat, where would the preventive security and counterintelligence mechanisms be?

Would their responsibility not include identifying risks, issuing appropriate warnings, and protecting individuals and national interests before damage occurs?

Security should mean prevention and protection, not merely finding someone to blame after a controversy explodes.

If serious wrongdoing is not established, there are two paths worth considering.

The first is the path of institutional wisdom: reconsider the decision, offer a return where appropriate, reform the procedures that failed, and acknowledge any injustice.

And if an injustice has truly occurred, there is something remarkably simple that powerful institutions should never be too proud to do.

Apologize.

Yes. Apologize.

Not as a sign of weakness, but as a demonstration of greatness.

The second path is that Jensen Huang may decide to build something entirely new.

And imagine what could happen then.

Elon Musk, what if extraordinary minds joined forces to create a fundamentally new generation of computing?

Ternary architectures. Multi-valued transistors. Revolutionary memory systems. New approaches to energy efficiency and computational performance.

I have personally developed functional ternary implementations using CUDA. Moving those concepts into physical hardware and independently demonstrating measurable advantages would be the next great challenge.

The goal would not be to reproduce NVIDIA.

It would be to imagine what comes after NVIDIA.

But before we talk about processors, artificial intelligence, corporate valuations, or technological revolutions, we must remember something infinitely more important.

Jensen Huang is a human being.

Not merely a corporate asset.

Not a stock price.

Not a headline.

Not a disposable piece on someone else's chessboard.

A human being with a history, a family, relationships, responsibilities, hopes, and the same fundamental right to dignity and fairness as anyone else.

We can admire extraordinary achievements without placing anyone above accountability.

We can demand transparency without destroying reputations through speculation.

And we can protect national security without turning private human relationships into a public circus.

A civilization that demands its greatest creators behave like flawless machines, while proudly proclaiming its commitment to individual freedom, needs to confront its own contradictions.

This is not about demanding special privileges for powerful people.

It is about defending principles that belong to everyone, from the humblest worker to the founder of a global technology leader:

The right to dignity. The right to privacy. The right to a fair investigation. And the right not to be condemned by rumors.

Because if we lose those principles, we may succeed in building the most advanced processors in the universe while failing at something infinitely more fundamental.

Our own humanity.

The future does not merely need more powerful machines. It needs wiser minds, greater compassion, and the courage to distinguish justice from prejudice.

And perhaps the greatest revolution of all will begin when we finally learn that technological progress means very little unless human dignity advances alongside it.

With respect for Jensen Huang, his family, everyone involved, and all those who have dedicated their lives to creating a better future.

A heartfelt embrace, from the depths of my soul.

— Atlas Azul

text:
Self improvement without God will eventually turn you into a fitter version of the Pharisee in Luke 18. He stood in the temple and read his disciplines back to God like a training log, reminding Him how often he fasted and how faithfully he tithed. He went home unjustified, and the tax collector beating his chest in the back went home right with God.

St Paul puts it even more bluntly in 1 Corinthians 13. You can give away everything you own and hand your body over to be burned, and without love it gains you nothing. Aquinas picked this up and called charity the form of all the virtues. Discipline is the raw material and love is what gives it shape and direction. Without it, the habit can be real and the man can still be hollow.

The desert fathers warned that vainglory is the vice that grows out of good works. Cassian said it attacks a man from every side, even through his humility. So the more disciplined you get, the more carefully you need to watch where it's pointing. A man can wake at 4:30 every day for a decade and do all of it for the mirror and the applause.

Check your intention before the work starts. Make a morning offering before you train. Before the fast, the cold, the early alarm, tell God plainly who this is for. Offer it for your wife, your kids, and the men who depend on you, and ask Him to purify the motive when you catch it drifting back toward yourself. Do that long enough and the same disciplines start to feel lighter, because you've stopped carrying the weight of having to impress anyone.

text:
Thailand Travel Guide 2026: Best Destinations & Hotels Across Major Cities
Thailand remains one of the world’s most rewarding destinations, mixing vibrant cities, ancient temples, mountains, and outstanding beaches. Hotel quality is exceptionally high, with several properties holding the top Michelin Key distinctions in the 2026 selection.
This guide covers the major places most travelers visit, with standout hotel recommendations based on recent awards and rankings.
Bangkok
Bangkok is the energetic capital—Grand Palace, Wat Pho, street food, markets, and the Chao Phraya River. Most trips begin or end here. The riverside is ideal for atmosphere and views; Sukhumvit and Siam work well for shopping and transport.
Top hotels
•Capella Bangkok — Frequently ranked among the world’s best; design-focused riverside property with Three Michelin Keys
•Mandarin Oriental Bangkok — Iconic heritage hotel on the river since the 1870s; legendary service and Three Michelin Keys
•Four Seasons Hotel Bangkok at Chao Phraya River — Strong urban-resort feel
•Other excellent choices: The Siam, Aman Nai Lert Bangkok, Rosewood Bangkok, Park Hyatt Bangkok, The Peninsula Bangkok, and Dusit Thani Bangkok
Chiang Mai
Northern cultural capital with hundreds of temples in the old city, night markets, cooking classes, and easy access to mountains. The pace is noticeably more relaxed than Bangkok.
Top hotels
•Four Seasons Resort Chiang Mai — The only Three Michelin Keys hotel in the city; set among rice paddies and gardens in the Mae Rim area
•137 Pillars House — Elegant historic property
•Anantara Chiang Mai Resort — Attractive riverside option
Phuket
Thailand’s largest island offers everything from lively Patong to quieter beaches such as Kata, Karon, and Mai Khao, plus an Old Town and easy island-hopping.
Top hotels
•Amanpuri — The original modern luxury pioneer on Pansea Beach; Three Michelin Keys
•Trisara — Highly regarded clifftop resort with private pool villas
•Rosewood Phuket and Keemala — Strong additional luxury choices
Krabi
Base for Ao Nang and the famous Railay Beach. Dramatic limestone cliffs, island-hopping, and generally better value and a more laid-back feel than Phuket.
Top hotels
•Phulay Bay, A Ritz-Carlton Reserve — Exclusive beachfront setting with Three Michelin Keys
•Rayavadee — Classic Railay Beach resort (boat access only)
•Pimalai Resort & Spa — Reliable high-end alternative
Koh Samui
Gulf of Thailand island known for beaches, wellness, and a more upscale, relaxed atmosphere. Access is mainly by flight or ferry.
Top hotels
•Four Seasons Resort Koh Samui — Hillside pool villas with excellent views
•Six Senses Samui
•Samujana Villas and Banyan Tree Samui
Hua Hin
Quieter Gulf beach town popular with families, golfers, and longer stays. Calmer than Pattaya and an easy trip from Bangkok.
Top hotels
•Chiva-Som — Leading wellness resort
•Anantara Hua Hin Resort & Spa
•Aleenta, Veranda properties, and The Standard Hua Hin
Pattaya
Closest major beach destination to Bangkok. Mix of beaches, nightlife, water parks, and family resorts. Jomtien and Na Jomtien tend to be quieter than the central area.
Top hotels
•Hilton Pattaya
•Centara Grand Mirage (strong for families)
•Andaz Pattaya Jomtien Beach
•Cape Dara Resort and Dusit Thani Pattaya
Chiang Rai & Other Notes
Chiang Rai is known for the White Temple and access to the Golden Triangle. The Anantara Golden Triangle Elephant Camp & Resort is the standout stay.
Ayutthaya (historic ruins), Sukhothai, Pai, and Kanchanaburi work well as shorter add-ons or day trips and have good boutique and mid-range options.
Practical Tips
•Best overall weather: November to February (cool and dry season)
•Classic first itinerary: Bangkok + Chiang Mai + one beach destination (Phuket/Krabi or Koh Samui)

Brian Banks (high school / college football prospect)
In 2002, Banks (then 16–17, a highly recruited linebacker from Long Beach Poly with scholarship offers including to USC) was accused by classmate Wanetta Gibson of kidnapping and raping her on campus. He maintained the encounter was consensual (or that no intercourse occurred). Facing a potential long sentence, he pleaded no contest, served about 5 years and 2 months in prison, spent time on parole, and registered as a sex offender—destroying his athletic prospects.
In 2011 (roughly 9 years later), Gibson contacted him via Facebook. In a recorded meeting with Banks and a private investigator, she recanted, saying there had been no rape or kidnapping. With help from the California Innocence Project, his conviction was vacated in 2012; he was cleared of sex-offender status and later briefly played in the UFL and with the Atlanta Falcons.
Gibson’s family had received a large civil settlement from the school district; she was reluctant to repeat the recantation publicly for fear of having to repay it. A court later ordered her to repay related funds.

text:
MIT Technology Review’s What’s Next series looks across industries, trends, and technologies to give you a first look at the future. You can read the rest of our series here.

This time last year we did something reckless. In an industry where nothing stands still, we had a go at predicting the future. 

How did we do? Our four big bets for 2023 were that the next big thing in chatbots would be multimodal (check: the most powerful large language models out there, OpenAI’s GPT-4 and Google DeepMind’s Gemini, work with text, images and audio); that policymakers would draw up tough new regulations (check: Biden’s executive order came out in October and the European Union’s AI Act was finally agreed in December); Big Tech would feel pressure from open-source startups (half right: the open-source boom continues, but AI companies like OpenAI and Google DeepMind still stole the limelight); and that AI would change big pharma for good (too soon to tell: the AI revolution in drug discovery is in full swing, but the first drugs developed using AI are still some years from market).

Now we’re doing it again.

We decided to ignore the obvious. We know that large language models will continue to dominate. Regulators will grow bolder. AI’s problems—from bias to copyright to doomerism—will shape the agenda for researchers, regulators, and the public, not just in 2024 but for years to come. (Read more about our six big questions for generative AI here.)

Instead, we’ve picked a few more specific trends. Here’s what to watch out for in 2024. (Come back next year and check how we did.)

1

Customized chatbots

You get a chatbot! And you get a chatbot! In 2024, tech companies that invested heavily in generative AI will be under pressure to prove that they can make money off their products. To do this, AI giants Google and OpenAI are betting big on going small: both are developing user-friendly platforms that allow people to customize powerful language models and make their own mini chatbots that cater to their specific needs—no coding skills required. Both have launched web-based tools that allow anyone to become a generative-AI app developer. 

In 2024, generative AI might actually become useful for the regular, non-tech person, and we are going to see more people tinkering with a million little AI models. State-of-the-art AI models, such as GPT-4 and Gemini, are multimodal, meaning they can process not only text but images and even videos. This new capability could unlock a whole bunch of new apps. For example, a real estate agent can upload text from previous listings, fine-tune a powerful model to generate similar text with just a click of a button, upload videos and photos of new listings, and simply ask the customized AI to generate a description of the property. 

But of course, the success of this plan hinges on whether these models work reliably. Language models often make stuff up, and generative models are riddled with biases. They are also easy to hack, especially if they are allowed to browse the web. Tech companies have not solved any of these problems. When the novelty wears off, they’ll have to offer their customers ways to deal with these problems. 

—Melissa Heikkilä

2

Generative AI’s second wave will be video

It’s amazing how fast the fantastic becomes familiar. The first generative models to produce photorealistic images exploded into the mainstream in 2022—and soon became commonplace. Tools like OpenAI’s DALL-E, Stability AI’s Stable Diffusion, and Adobe’s Firefly flooded the internet with jaw-dropping images of everything from the pope in Balenciaga to prize-winning art. But it’s not all good fun: for every pug waving pompoms, there’s another piece of knock-off fantasy art or sexist sexual stereotyping.

The new frontier is text-to-video. Expect it to take everything that was good, bad, or ugly about text-to-image and supersize it.

A year ago we got the first glimpse of what generative models could do when they were trained to stitch together multiple still images into clips a few seconds long. The results were distorted and jerky. But the tech has rapidly improved.

Runway, a startup that makes generative video models (and the company that co-created Stable Diffusion), is dropping new versions of its tools every few months. Its latest model, called Gen-2, still generates video just a few seconds long, but the quality is striking. The best clips aren’t far off what Pixar might put out.

Runway has set up an annual AI film festival that showcases experimental movies made with a range of AI tools. This year’s festival has a $60,000 prize pot, and the 10 best films will be screened in New York and Los Angeles.

It’s no surprise that top studios are taking notice. Movie giants, including Paramount and Disney, are now exploring the use of generative AI throughout their production pipeline. The tech is being used to lip-sync actors’ performances to multiple foreign-language overdubs. And it is reinventing what’s possible with special effects. In 2023, Indiana Jones and the Dial of Destiny starred a de-aged deepfake Harrison Ford. This is just the start.  

Away from the big screen, deepfake tech for marketing or training purposes is taking off too. For example, UK-based Synthesia makes tools that can turn a one-off performance by an actor into an endless stream of deepfake avatars, reciting whatever script you give them at the push of a button. According to the company, its tech is now used by 44% of Fortune 100 companies. 

The ability to do so much with so little raises serious questions for actors. Concerns about studios’ use and misuse of AI were at the heart of the SAG-AFTRA strikes last year. But the true impact of the tech is only just becoming apparent. “The craft of filmmaking is fundamentally changing,” says Souki Mehdaoui, an independent filmmaker and cofounder of Bell & Whistle, a consultancy specializing in creative technologies.

—Will Douglas Heaven

3

AI-generated election disinformation will be everywhere 

If recent elections are anything to go by, AI-generated election disinformation and deepfakes are going to be a huge problem as a record number of people march to the polls in 2024. We’re already seeing politicians weaponizing these tools. In Argentina, two presidential candidates created AI-generated images and videos of their opponents to attack them. In Slovakia, deepfakes of a liberal pro-European party leader threatening to raise the price of beer and making jokes about child pornography spread like wildfire during the country’s elections. And in the US, Donald Trump has cheered on a group that uses AI to generate memes with racist and sexist tropes. 

While it’s hard to say how much these examples have influenced the outcomes of elections, their proliferation is a worrying trend. It will become harder than ever to recognize what is real online. In an already inflamed and polarized political climate, this could have severe consequences.

Just a few years ago creating a deepfake would have required advanced technical skills, but generative AI has made it stupidly easy and accessible, and the outputs are looking increasingly realistic. Even reputable sources might be fooled by AI-generated content. For example, users-submitted AI-generated images purporting to depict the Israel-Gaza crisis have flooded stock image marketplaces like Adobe’s. 

The coming year will be pivotal for those fighting against the proliferation of such content. Techniques to track and mitigate it content are still in early days of development. Watermarks, such as Google DeepMind’s SynthID, are still mostly voluntary and not completely foolproof. And social media platforms are notoriously slow in taking down misinformation. Get ready for a massive real-time experiment in busting AI-generated fake news. 

—Melissa Heikkilä

4

Robots that multitask

Inspired by some of the core techniques behind generative AI’s current boom, roboticists are starting to build more general-purpose robots that can do a wider range of tasks.

The last few years in AI have seen a shift away from using multiple small models, each trained to do different tasks—identifying images, drawing them, captioning them—toward single, monolithic models trained to do all these things and more. By showing OpenAI’s GPT-3 a few additional examples (known as fine-tuning), researchers can train it to solve coding problems, write movie scripts, pass high school biology exams, and so on. Multimodal models, like GPT-4 and Google DeepMind’s Gemini, can solve visual tasks as well as linguistic ones.

The same approach can work for robots, so it wouldn’t be necessary to train one to flip pancakes and another to open doors: a one-size-fits-all model could give robots the ability to multitask. Several examples of work in this area emerged in 2023.

In June, DeepMind released Robocat (an update on last year’s Gato), which generates its own data from trial and error to learn how to control many different robot arms (instead of one specific arm, which is more typical). 

In October, the company put out yet another general-purpose model for robots, called RT-X, and a big new general-purpose training data set, in collaboration with 33 university labs. Other top research teams, such as RAIL (Robotic Artificial Intelligence and Learning) at the University of California, Berkeley, are looking at similar tech.

The problem is a lack of data. Generative AI draws on an internet-size data set of text and images. In comparison, robots have very few good sources of data to help them learn how to do many of the industrial or domestic tasks we want them to.

Lerrel Pinto at New York University leads one team addressing that. He and his colleagues are developing techniques that let robots learn by trial and error, coming up with their own training data as they go. In an even more low-key project, Pinto has recruited volunteers to collect video data from around their homes using an iPhone camera mounted to a trash picker. Big companies have also started to release large data sets for training robots in the last couple of years, such as Meta’s Ego4D.

This approach is already showing promise in driverless cars. Startups such as Wayve, Waabi, and Ghost are pioneering a new wave of self-driving AI that uses a single large model to control a vehicle rather than multiple smaller models to control specific driving tasks. This has let small companies catch up with giants like Cruise and Waymo. Wayve is now testing its driverless cars on the narrow, busy streets of London. Robots everywhere are set to get a similar boost.

—Will Douglas Heaven

text:
The Oregon Trail: Disease, a Lame Cow, and the Real Toll of the Migration

Between the 1840s and the 1860s, hundreds of thousands of emigrants rolled west along the Oregon, California, and Mormon Trails. The popular memory of those journeys is filled with covered wagons, prairie sunsets, and the threat of attack. The written record tells a quieter and more sobering story.

Disease was the great killer. Of the roughly 300,000 to 400,000 people who started the overland journey, historians estimate that 16,000 to 30,000 never arrived. The large majority died of illness rather than violence or accident. Cholera, carried in contaminated water at crowded campsites, was the worst of the killers. It could take a healthy adult in a matter of hours. Diaries from the epidemic years of 1849 to 1855 describe long stretches of trail marked by fresh graves.

Most of those graves were deliberately left unmarked. Families and companies often buried the dead in the middle of the trail itself, then drove the wagons over the site to erase any sign of a burial. The practice was meant to hide the graves from wolves and other scavengers, and also from grave robbers. On a route where thousands of strangers passed in a single season, an obvious grave was a temptation. The result was that the trail became, in the words of later observers, the nation’s longest graveyard, yet almost none of its dead can be located today.

Native communities along the same corridors suffered even more severely. They had little or no prior immunity to the diseases the wagons carried. During the 1849–1852 cholera outbreaks, the Pawnee lost more than a thousand people in a single season; the Southern Cheyenne lost roughly half their number in some accounts. The Kiowa, Comanche, Arapaho, and other Plains groups were likewise devastated. Whole camps were left empty. Survivors sometimes lacked the strength to bury the dead. These losses were not abstract. They broke bands, disrupted seasonal rounds, and left the remaining people less able to hunt, trade, or hold their ground.

In some cases the cultural response to unexplained death was direct. Among the Cayuse and certain other Plateau peoples, a medicine man whose patients died could be held responsible and killed. In November 1847, during a severe measles epidemic at the Whitman Mission near Walla Walla, Dr. Marcus Whitman treated both Cayuse and settlers. Many Cayuse died while most of the white patients recovered. Some Cayuse concluded that Whitman, whom they regarded as a powerful healer, had either failed or deliberately used bad medicine. Acting under their own custom, a group of Cayuse men killed Whitman, his wife Narcissa, and eleven others. The episode, known as the Whitman Massacre, helped trigger the Cayuse War. It was not a general practice applied to every doctor on the trail, but it shows how disease, cultural expectations, and suspicion could collide with lethal results.

Direct violence between emigrants and Native people, by contrast, was limited. Between 1840 and 1860, historian John Unruh counted roughly 362 emigrants killed by Native people and 426 Native people killed by emigrants. Most meetings on the trail were peaceful exchanges of trade or help at river crossings. The popular image of constant warfare does not match the numbers.

One small incident shows how quickly a minor dispute could widen. In August 1854, near Fort Laramie, a lame cow belonging to a Mormon emigrant train strayed into a Lakota camp and was killed by a visiting Miniconjou named High Forehead. The animal was nearly worthless; some accounts describe it as already dying. The owner demanded twenty-five dollars. Brulé chief Conquering Bear offered horses or other cattle in restitution, the customary way such matters were settled under the existing treaty. The local agent was expected to handle the claim, but the military stepped in.

Second Lieutenant John L. Grattan led a detachment of about twenty-nine soldiers and an interpreter into the large Lakota camp to arrest High Forehead. Words failed. Shots were fired. Conquering Bear was mortally wounded. The Lakota then killed Grattan and nearly his entire command. 

The episode is remembered as the Grattan Fight. It helped open the First Sioux War. The following year, troops under General William S. Harney attacked a Lakota village at Blue Water Creek, killing dozens, including women and children. The cycle of retaliation that followed became part of the larger Plains Wars.

The Oregon Trail was more than a migration route. It was a corridor that carried people, livestock, and pathogens across Native lands. Cholera and other diseases took a far heavier toll on tribal populations than settler-Native fighting took on emigrants. Resource competition and poorly handled incidents such as the twenty-five-dollar cow compounded the pressure. The result was demographic loss, displacement, and escalating conflict across the Plains.

These figures come from trail diaries, military reports, agency records, and tribal accounts. The scale of disease deaths among Native peoples is often understated in popular tellings of the trail. The Grattan episode shows how a minor livestock loss, handled without the established channels, could open a wider war. The human cost for the tribes living along the route was severe and lasting.

text:
A former Marc Jacobs model who grew up in Paris now steals wigs from homeless camps on Skid Row and does sex work for smokes. She’s 22. Orphaned, bounced through foster homes that didn’t want a trans kid, on the streets since 16, raped, and when asked about it says “why not, yeah, sure” like someone offered her coffee. “I’m free,” she says. “I’m not suffering the way people want me to suffer.”

Her name is Rebecca. She grew up partly on the Lower East Side, partly in Paris, and spent the rest of her childhood getting shuffled through the foster system. Her parents died before she could know them. She was adopted, but the placements never stuck. “People didn’t really want me because I was trans,” she says. “It was hard to find placement.” At 16 she walked out of the system and never looked back.

She’s been on the streets for six years. New York, Florida, now LA. She came to California because she always wanted to see Big Sur. She ended up on Skid Row instead.

Her daily routine starts with clothes. She goes to Skid Row every morning and picks outfits off the sidewalk. The wig she’s wearing, she grabbed off a pile of trash clothes near a tent. “Intercept the person living in the tent, intercept, they may have a knife, but understand that there is so much stuff here. Grab the wig and run, bitch.” She calls it her J.Lo moment.

She does sex work. She does small modeling gigs when she can get them. She panhandles for cigarettes. She once shot for Marc Jacobs. Now she sits outside McDonald’s asking strangers to buy her something to eat.

In New York she got raped. She doesn’t dwell on it. “I’m not a victim, people get raped, you know. I’m happy I’m in one piece and I didn’t get my legs chopped off after.” She says it the way someone talks about a bad commute.

She has no biological family left. No foster parents who stayed. Her family is a coven of witches she found on the road. “My witches are my family,” she says. “My witches are all the family I would ever need.” When she needs to explain to a cop that she’s on her period and can’t do a blood draw, it’s the coven that shows up.

One morning she ran into supermodel Adwoa Aboah on a beach in LA. It was 7 AM, Aboah was shooting for W Magazine, and Rebecca was coming down hard from a rave. She ran up, got a hug and a cigarette from one of the biggest models in the world. That’s her favorite story.

She sleeps wherever she drops. “If I’m asleep, I’m asleep. If I can find a blanket, I’m out.” She doesn’t eat unless she’s desperate. “It’s LA, no one really eats, right.” Her drug is MDMA when she can afford it. Cigarettes when she can’t.

The interviewer tells her she’s beautiful. She shot for Marc Jacobs but says she doesn’t feel beautiful. “I feel like the weird one, you know what I mean? Like the one with the little f---ing giant forehead.”

In the video below she sits across from Mark Laita on Skid Row with a wig she stole that morning, a cuff she found on the ground, and a full outfit assembled entirely from the street. She talks about sex work, rape, foster homes, and freedom with the same flat calm, like none of it weighs anything anymore.

When asked what she wants to be when she grows up, she says she wants to be an Olsen twin. “I’m obsessed with the Olsen twins. They’re the coolest ever.”

She says she has two good years of fresh young blood left in her, and then she’ll get an office temp job, get fat, and move to the suburbs. She says it like she believes it. She’s been saying things she believes since she was 16 and none of them have come true yet.

Some will say she’s romanticizing a life that’s slowly killing her. Others will say she found a kind of freedom most people never will because they’re too scared to lose everything first.

She’s a former Marc Jacobs model who digs through trash every morning to get dressed. At what point does “I’m free” stop being freedom and start being survival she just learned to smile through?

text:
Robert, let's go through this one step at a time, because you keep declaring victory without establishing a single logical conclusion.

1. Ethnogenesis.

The English emerged as a distinct historical ethnic people through the integration of earlier populations. That's precisely what ethnogenesis means. Nobody is claiming genetic purity.

2. Intermarriage.

English, Scottish, Welsh and Irish populations have intermarried for centuries. Correct. Now explain how that disproves the existence of English ethnicity. By your reasoning, practically every ethnic group on Earth would cease to exist because their ancestors mixed.

3. Your statistics.

You claimed 25% of English people have an Irish great-grandparent. Your evidence doesn't establish that. Now you're arguing that because supposedly 10% have an Irish grandparent, 25% having a great-grandparent is a reasonable assumption.

That's not statistical evidence, Robert. That's you pulling a number out of thin air and calling it logic.

4. Nationality versus ethnicity.

England is a nation containing multiple ethnic populations. The English are also a historical ethnic people. These propositions aren't contradictory.

5. Your logical fallacy.

Your entire argument rests on the assumption that because populations have mixed historically, distinct ethnic groups cannot exist.

That's a non sequitur. Your conclusion simply doesn't follow from your premise.

6. The question you keep avoiding.

If ancestral mixture invalidates English ethnicity, why doesn't it invalidate Scottish, Welsh, Irish or practically every other historical ethnicity?

You haven't answered that once.

Instead, you've offered unsupported statistics, repeated the same argument and declared yourself victorious.

Now, Robert, stop telling me you've demolished my position and actually demonstrate which of these six points is historically or logically incorrect.

Because so far, you've demonstrated precisely why understanding ethnogenesis matters.

text:
Irish GPs were told to write paper prescriptions this week. Several UK police forces asked people to phone 101 or 999 because online crime reports weren't getting through.

Both were caused by the same thing, a Microsoft system outage.

Microsoft says it began at 11:17am US Eastern on Thursday, just after 4pm in London. It disrupted Outlook, then Teams, Copilot and OneDrive. According to Downdetector, reports hit 19,650 a minute at the peak, while a normal Thursday sees fewer than 15.

According to the BBC, Microsoft admitted its attempts to fix the problem were not going "as expected" in an overnight update. It did not call the underlying fault fixed until 11:40am Friday, about a full day in, and some users were still affected.

Microsoft blames an issue from an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced after a recent network change. No cyberattack, it says.

According to Australia's home affairs minister Tony Burke, Microsoft compared it to the 2024 CrowdStrike meltdown, a faulty update that grounded flights and disrupted hospitals.

The internet is flooded with jokes about the 60,000 figure, which is, in fact, true. In late October, Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, more than a quarter of its staff. Nothing on record ties that offer to this outage.
