BRANIFF HISTORY TODAY - On this day, Thursday, November 13, 1930, Braniff Airways, Incorporated, began its first scheduled service. Two Lockheed Vega aircraft inaugurated the new Airline's first flights between Oklahoma City and Tulsa, a distance of 116 miles, and Oklahoma City and Wichita Falls, Texas. The successor of Paul R. Braniff, Inc., and Braniff Airlines, Inc, Braniff Airways, Incorporated, was incorporated in Oklahoma a few days earlier on November 3.

The new airline was the successor of brothers Thomas Elmer Braniff and Paul Revere Braniff's first airline, which began operations in June 1928, between Oklahoma City and Tulsa, Oklahoma. The carrier was initially named Paul R. Braniff, Inc., d/b/a Tulsa - Oklahoma City Airline, and in April 1929, it was sold to a conglomerate of airlines and railroads called Universal Aviation Corporation, which was headquartered in St. Louis, Missouri. By the Summer of 1930, Universal was sold to AVCO or Aviation Corporation, the predecessor of American Airlines. Paul Braniff left Universal, prior to the AVCO purchase, in November 1929, and promptly went to work for a transport airline in Mexico.

In January 1930, AVCO integrated all of its carriers into the new American Airways. American Airways was renamed American Airlines in 1934, making Braniff Airlines, Inc., one of the predecessors to American Airlines. Paul Braniff returned from Mexico and with his brother formed their second airline venture, Braniff Airways, Incorporated. The new company was formed in Oklahoma, on November 3, 1930, with two Lockheed L-5 Vega single-engine aircraft that cost $10,000 USD each.

Ten days after the new Braniff Airways, Incorporated, was incorporated, the two Lockheed Vegas flew the Airline's first scheduled flights, which carried passengers and express freight, although Braniff would not be awarded an airmail contract until May 1934. The company's routes were between Tulsa and Oklahoma City, as they were for the Braniff brother's first airline, with an extension from Oklahoma City to Wichita Falls, Texas. Braniff quickly expanded its route system to include Kansas City Fairfax Airport on December 5, 1930. The new service operated nonstop between Kansas City and Tulsa and additional new cities were added in early 1931.

Braniff's first pilot was Captain Raymond Carrol Shrader who would remain with the company until the early 1970s. Additional pilots were added by the end of 1930, and during 1931, that included Captain R. V. Carleton, who eventually became Executive Vice President and also remained with the airline until 1970, and Captain Virgil Turnbull, who married Bobby Burton, the first female hired at Braniff Airlines, Inc., in 1929. Captain Frank Hover, Captain Wayne Lansing, Captain Charlie Quinn, and Captain Jack Ayres were also hired during the earliest days of the fledgling airline.

Several accomplishments highlighted Braniff's first two months of operation. By the end of 1930, the airline had added new service to its route map and employed six people and the new service between Tulsa and Kansas City had increased system route mileage to 241 miles. On February 25, 1931, Braniff welcomed in the new year by adding Chicago Midway Airport to its route map. The new service operated nonstop between Kansas City and the Windy City, once each day. The flight originated at Wichita Falls and continued to Midway Airport with intermediate stops at Oklahoma City, Tulsa and Kansas City.

The summer of 1931 welcomed St Louis to the Braniff system on June 15, and nonstop service was provided between St Louis and both Chicago and Tulsa. Additional Lockheed Vegas were added to the fleet during 1931 and 1932, and by 1937, the airline had operated a total of 13 of the pioneering aircraft including one from Bowen Airlines that Braniff would merge with in January 1936. A total of six Vegas were flying the routes of "The World's Fastest Airline" by the Summer of 1932.

Braniff Airways administration offices were initially located at the Braniff Building in downtown Oklahoma City on 324 North Robinson Avenue. However, the offices were moved to Oklahoma City's Curtiss-Wright Airport on September 16, 1932 and the company also moved its Kansas City Maintenance Operation to Oklahoma City Curtiss-Wright Airport during the same period. The Braniff Building was Oklahoma City's first skyscraper, built in 1923, and primarily served as the corporate offices for Tom Braniff's burgeoning insurance empire. In 2013, the building was completely restored to its former beauty becoming the first Braniff structure to be fully preserved under the guidelines set forth in the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966. The building is primarily occupied by the Crowe & Dunlevy, Attorneys and Counselor at Law, which was Braniff's first general counsel. The firm today, continues to serve as chief counsel for today's Braniff companies, which include the following:

Braniff Air Lines, Inc. - Oklahoma Incorporation - for historical purposes

Paul R. Braniff, Inc. - Oklahoma Incorporation with original entity reinstated - for historical purposes

Braniff Airways, Incorporated - Oklahoma Incorporation - operates and supports Braniff Boutique, https://t.co/lVzNS0ytDU and Braniff International Historic Airliner Tours and administers all Braniff Airways intellectual property including trademarks and copyrights

Braniff International Corporation - Oklahoma Incorporation - parent company for all Braniff entities, operates licensing and branding

Braniff International Hotels, Inc. - Oklahoma Incorporation - operates hotels and  licensing

Braniff Boutique - division of Braniff Airways, Incorporated, online retailer of Braniff branded products

Braniff Airways Foundation - Texas Incorporation, IRS registered 501C3 Non-Profit Organization that administers Braniff International Heritage Archives, the official Archives of Braniff Airways, Incorporated, its associated companies and merged companies

The addition of new aircraft and combining of its operations at Oklahoma City Airport during 1932 created a busy year for Braniff. New service was also added and by December 31, 1932, Braniff had grown during one year from operating 241 route miles to an impressive 1420 miles. Additional service that was added by the end of the year included Springfield, Missouri; Parsons/Independence/Coffeyville, Kansas; Bartlesville, Oklahoma and Chanute, Kansas. Braniff was also offering service from Chicago to San Antonio with a change of plane at Oklahoma City to a Bowen Airlines aircraft that flew passengers on to Dallas, Ft Worth, Houston, Austin, and finally San Antonio.

In spite of Braniff's initial growth, the company was completely dependent on passenger fares and express cargo shipments for its revenues. Airline flight was still considered a luxury item and passengers, at times, could be few with the same being true for customers needing expensive cargo carriage. By 1933, Braniff was beginning to experience substantial losses and by the end of the year they were asked to come to Tom Braniff's home in Oklahoma City for a meeting with both brothers. Tom Braniff outlined the dire straits that the company was experiencing and that its future was in question.

Accounts of what transpired at the meeting were varied with one stating that the employees ( approximately 33 in attendance) offered to work without pay until air mail contracts could be procured. Another version recounted that the Braniff brothers asked that employees work for a bare minimum wage to sustain living until the air mail contracts could be awarded. Still another version indicated that employees were told to sell tickets and keep the money as payment. Regardless of the outcome, Braniff was in serious trouble and something drastic was required to keep the airline operating.

Something drastic was done and on March 16, 1932, it was announced that Braniff Airways, Incorporated, would cease all operations, for the first time, two days later on March 18. Braniff's only source of revenue, now that scheduled passenger operations were discontinued, was selling aircraft fuel and oil products and providing aircraft maintenance services and pilot training. The future looked bleak for the small Oklahoma airline that had only begun operations less than two years earlier.

However, in Washington, DC, events were transpiring that would not only rescue Braniff Airways but many of the nation's other small independent airlines that were in desperate need of air mail contracts. The Air Mail Act of 1930, had given Postmaster Walter Folger Brown, at his request, a number of new powers in reference to awarding air mail contracts to the nation's airlines. As a result of this power that many felt was overreaching, deals were made between the Postmaster and the larger carriers, which basically blocked out the smaller airlines.

It was this alleged abuse of power that changed the future for Braniff, because, in September 1933, a Senate Investigating Committee was formed to look into a complaint by a radio journalist about fraud and collusion between the Hoover Administration and the nation's big airlines. The complaint stated that awards had been made to airlines that had not submitted the lowest bids as required by law. However, at the Spoils Conference, two weeks after the Air Mail Act of 1930 was enacted, Postmaster Brown had decided that he had the authority to award all air mail contracts to the three largest airlines, TWA, American and United.

Brown's Administration had indeed increased the operating efficiency of the air mail system and even lowered per-mile cost significantly. Postmaster Brown was replaced by James A. Farley when President Franklin Delano Roosevelt assumed office in the spring of 1933. Postmaster Farley and the President concluded that their duty was to protect the public's interest in response to the air mail contract revelations and as a result, President Roosevelt canceled all domestic air mail contracts on February 7, 1934. However, Postmaster Farley had asked that the bids remain in place until June 1, while new bids were being solicited.

The U. S. Army Air Corps assured the President that they could safely and efficiently operate the domestic air mail contracts. President Roosevelt authorized Executive Order 6591, which gave the Air Corps the authority to operate the routes on February 9, 1934, with the Air Corps assuming operations on February 20. The plan was a disaster because of a huge number of crashes and resulting pilot deaths, which created an outcry from the public for change. On June 12, 1934, the Air Mail Act was signed that returned the air mail contracts to the commercial airlines but with strict regulations to ensure that contracts were awarded in a fair manner.

The founders of Braniff Airways were watching with interest the developments in Washington DC. All new air mail contracts awarded in 1934, were generally given to the lowest bidder as required by law, which opened the doors to smaller carriers like Braniff and Delta. Braniff General Manager Paul Braniff traveled to Washington to testify before Congress about the possibility of his airline obtaining air mail contracts between Texas and Chicago. It paid off, Braniff was awarded its first Air Mail Contract, AM-9, between Chicago and Dallas on May 7, 1934. The new route stopped at Kansas City, Wichita, Ponca City, and Oklahoma City and was quickly accompanied by reinstating passenger and express cargo service over the new air mail route. Braniff was saved and the company began a strong and steady growth over the next several years.

IMAGINE A REPUBLICAN DOING THIS: A Democratic Colorado state senator is advertising a TAXPAYER-FUNDED CAPITOL INTERNSHIP that lists being MUSLIM or identifying with certain ethnic groups as its FIRST QUALIFICATION.

State Sen. Iman Jodeh's $1,000 paid internship explicitly prioritizes religious and ethnic identity in its eligibility criteria, raising serious questions about discrimination and whether applicants from other backgrounds are being excluded from an opportunity to work in state government.

The position is being offered through the MENASA & Muslim Joint Legislative Caucus, which Jodeh co-founded with Democratic state Rep. Yara Zokaie.

The internship involves part-time, in-person work in the lawmakers' offices during Colorado's 2027 legislative session.

But before the flyer mentions academic qualifications or an interest in government, it lists this requirement:

"Identify as a Muslim and/or as Middle Eastern, North African, or South Asian."

Applicants must also be current undergraduate students with a minimum 3.5 GPA and demonstrate an interest in public policy, social change, social justice, and the legislative process.

Applications are due November 30, 2026, and must be submitted to an official Colorado General Assembly email address.

The advertisement has drawn criticism because federal and state employment laws generally prohibit discrimination based on religion and national origin.

Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 protects workers and job applicants from discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, and national origin.

Colorado law also prohibits employment discrimination based on protected characteristics, although whether these provisions apply to this particular legislative internship would depend on its legal classification and other circumstances.

And this isn't the first time Jodeh has promoted an internship with religious or ethnic identity requirements.

In 2023, she advertised a similar opportunity specifying that applicants should identify as "Muslim or Arab."

Jodeh, who became Colorado's first Muslim state legislator in 2020, was born in Denver to Palestinian parents. She co-founded the caucus with Zokaie, a first-generation Iranian American, to represent Muslim and Middle Eastern, North African, and South Asian communities.

Following criticism of the latest posting, the advertisement was reportedly removed from at least one of Jodeh's Instagram accounts while remaining visible elsewhere.

The controversy raises a fundamental question about equal opportunity in government: Should religion or ethnic identity be listed as a qualification for a paid position inside a state Capitol?

text:
$APP AppLovin // AppLovin Shareholders Approve the Move From Delaware to Nevada

AppLovin is leaving Delaware. Stockholders holding at least a majority of the voting power approved reincorporating the company in Nevada by written consent on October 29, and the preliminary information statement laying out the move reached EDGAR on November 12. No public vote took place.

• The consent: Chief Executive Officer and co founder Adam Foroughi, Herald Chen and The Foroughi 2015 Irrevocable Trust were among the consenting holders, and the board approved the move unanimously the same day

• The board case: Nevada offers a more predictable, statute based legal environment with less reliance on judicial interpretation, and relief from the cost of defending less meritorious litigation in Delaware

• The savings: about $250,000 a year in Delaware franchise tax goes away, headquarters stays in Palo Alto, and the business itself does not change

• The tape: $APP AppLovin closed up 3.92% Friday to $409.10, riding the third quarter print and the buyback envelope the board lifted to $3.6B at the end of October

▬▬▬

THE CATCH: The tax saving is a rounding error against $2.185B of quarterly revenue. The filing's own logic is legal, not financial. Nevada narrows the room for stockholder litigation against directors and officers, and the decision was made by founder controlled voting power without a public vote. The live legal date for public holders is Monday November 16, the lead plaintiff deadline in the securities class action over the company's AI claims.

THE TAKEAWAY: A domicile change moves no revenue and no cash flow. It does move the goalposts for anyone who later wants to sue the board.

Does a Nevada charter change how you value the stock, or is it housekeeping?

Brazilian coffee, beef and tropical fruit will still be tariffed 40%, says Brazil’s vice president

RIO DE JANEIRO — Brazilian Vice President Geraldo Alckmin said Saturday that Brazilian exported goods to the U.S. including coffee, beef and tropical fruits would still be tariffed 40%, despite President Donald Trump’s decision to remove some import taxes.

In a dramatic move on Friday, Trump scrapped levies announced in April on what he called ‘Liberation Day’ in hopes of encouraging domestic production and lifting the U.S. economy. Brazil at the time was hit with a 10% tariff.

But in July, Trump imposed a further 40% tariff, citing — among other reasons — the trial of his ally, former President Jair Bolsonaro, which he called a “witch hunt.” Proceedings went ahead regardless and in September Bolsonaro was sentenced to 27 years and three months in prison for attempting a coup.

Alckmin said some products, such as orange juice, would now have a zero tariff as they were not targeted by the additional 40%. But that extra tariff remains in place on products including coffee, beef and tropical fruits, such as mangos and pineapples.

While Brazil’s vice president welcomed Trump’s latest decision, which he called “positive” and a “step in the right direction,” he said there remained a “distortion that needs to be corrected.”

“Everyone got 10% less, but in Brazil’s case, which had 50%, we ended up with 40%, which is very high,” Alckmin told journalists in the capital Brasilia.

Alckmin said that Friday's decision means that 26% of Brazilian goods are now entering the U.S. without additional tariffs. That's up from 23%.

Trump’s July decision, which was overtly political as Brazil has a trade deficit with the United States, led to the worst U.S.-Brazil relations in history.

Those relations have since improved, and in October Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Trump met in Malaysia.

“President Lula’s conversation with President Donald Trump was important in terms of dialogue and negotiation,” Alckmin said on Saturday.

After that encounter, Lula said he was confident the two countries would soon reach a trade deal.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Brazil’s Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira met for 50 minutes this week to further the conversation.

The Trump administration has insisted that its tariffs helped fill government coffers and weren’t a major factor in higher prices at grocery stores around the country. But Democrats were quick to paint Friday’s move as an acknowledgment that Trump’s policies were hurting American pocketbooks.

Record-high beef prices have been a particular concern, and Trump had said he intended to take action to try and lower them. Trump’s tariffs on Brazil, a major beef exporter, had been a factor.

Back in Brazil, the Brazilian Association of the Coffee Industry said it would continue to monitor the situation.

“(We) will keep working to ensure legal certainty, competitiveness, and predictability for the Brazilian coffee industry,” the group’s president, Pavel Cardoso, said in a statement. (Wires, A.I News)

Brazilian coffee, beef and tropical fruit will still be tariffed 40%, says Brazil’s vice president

RIO DE JANEIRO — Brazilian Vice President Geraldo Alckmin said Saturday that Brazilian exported goods to the U.S. including coffee, beef and tropical fruits would still be tariffed 40%, despite President Donald Trump’s decision to remove some import taxes.

In a dramatic move on Friday, Trump scrapped levies announced in April on what he called ‘Liberation Day’ in hopes of encouraging domestic production and lifting the U.S. economy. Brazil at the time was hit with a 10% tariff.

But in July, Trump imposed a further 40% tariff, citing — among other reasons — the trial of his ally, former President Jair Bolsonaro, which he called a “witch hunt.” Proceedings went ahead regardless and in September Bolsonaro was sentenced to 27 years and three months in prison for attempting a coup.

Alckmin said some products, such as orange juice, would now have a zero tariff as they were not targeted by the additional 40%. But that extra tariff remains in place on products including coffee, beef and tropical fruits, such as mangos and pineapples.

While Brazil’s vice president welcomed Trump’s latest decision, which he called “positive” and a “step in the right direction,” he said there remained a “distortion that needs to be corrected.”

“Everyone got 10% less, but in Brazil’s case, which had 50%, we ended up with 40%, which is very high,” Alckmin told journalists in the capital Brasilia.

Alckmin said that Friday's decision means that 26% of Brazilian goods are now entering the U.S. without additional tariffs. That's up from 23%.

Trump’s July decision, which was overtly political as Brazil has a trade deficit with the United States, led to the worst U.S.-Brazil relations in history.

Those relations have since improved, and in October Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Trump met in Malaysia.

“President Lula’s conversation with President Donald Trump was important in terms of dialogue and negotiation,” Alckmin said on Saturday.

After that encounter, Lula said he was confident the two countries would soon reach a trade deal.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Brazil’s Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira met for 50 minutes this week to further the conversation.

The Trump administration has insisted that its tariffs helped fill government coffers and weren’t a major factor in higher prices at grocery stores around the country. But Democrats were quick to paint Friday’s move as an acknowledgment that Trump’s policies were hurting American pocketbooks.

Record-high beef prices have been a particular concern, and Trump had said he intended to take action to try and lower them. Trump’s tariffs on Brazil, a major beef exporter, had been a factor.

Back in Brazil, the Brazilian Association of the Coffee Industry said it would continue to monitor the situation.

“(We) will keep working to ensure legal certainty, competitiveness, and predictability for the Brazilian coffee industry,” the group’s president, Pavel Cardoso, said in a statement. (Wires, A.I News)

Brazilian coffee, beef and tropical fruit will still be tariffed 40%, says Brazil’s vice president

RIO DE JANEIRO — Brazilian Vice President Geraldo Alckmin said Saturday that Brazilian exported goods to the U.S. including coffee, beef and tropical fruits would still be tariffed 40%, despite President Donald Trump’s decision to remove some import taxes.

In a dramatic move on Friday, Trump scrapped levies announced in April on what he called ‘Liberation Day’ in hopes of encouraging domestic production and lifting the U.S. economy. Brazil at the time was hit with a 10% tariff.

But in July, Trump imposed a further 40% tariff, citing — among other reasons — the trial of his ally, former President Jair Bolsonaro, which he called a “witch hunt.” Proceedings went ahead regardless and in September Bolsonaro was sentenced to 27 years and three months in prison for attempting a coup.

Alckmin said some products, such as orange juice, would now have a zero tariff as they were not targeted by the additional 40%. But that extra tariff remains in place on products including coffee, beef and tropical fruits, such as mangos and pineapples.

While Brazil’s vice president welcomed Trump’s latest decision, which he called “positive” and a “step in the right direction,” he said there remained a “distortion that needs to be corrected.”

“Everyone got 10% less, but in Brazil’s case, which had 50%, we ended up with 40%, which is very high,” Alckmin told journalists in the capital Brasilia.

Alckmin said that Friday's decision means that 26% of Brazilian goods are now entering the U.S. without additional tariffs. That's up from 23%.

Trump’s July decision, which was overtly political as Brazil has a trade deficit with the United States, led to the worst U.S.-Brazil relations in history.

Those relations have since improved, and in October Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Trump met in Malaysia.

“President Lula’s conversation with President Donald Trump was important in terms of dialogue and negotiation,” Alckmin said on Saturday.

After that encounter, Lula said he was confident the two countries would soon reach a trade deal.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Brazil’s Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira met for 50 minutes this week to further the conversation.

The Trump administration has insisted that its tariffs helped fill government coffers and weren’t a major factor in higher prices at grocery stores around the country. But Democrats were quick to paint Friday’s move as an acknowledgment that Trump’s policies were hurting American pocketbooks.

Record-high beef prices have been a particular concern, and Trump had said he intended to take action to try and lower them. Trump’s tariffs on Brazil, a major beef exporter, had been a factor.

Back in Brazil, the Brazilian Association of the Coffee Industry said it would continue to monitor the situation.

“(We) will keep working to ensure legal certainty, competitiveness, and predictability for the Brazilian coffee industry,” the group’s president, Pavel Cardoso, said in a statement. (Wires, A.I News)

text:
Ohio State and @Microsoft Set Five-Year AI and Azure Partnership

Ohio State and Microsoft are embarking on a reported five-year, $250 million AI and cloud partnership, placing one of the largest U.S. universities at the center of a broader shift toward shared, hyperscale computing. The reported valuation has not been independently confirmed by Ohio State or Microsoft, so it remains a figure attributed to reporting rather than an official contract disclosure.

The infrastructure target is substantial. Ohio State plans to migrate approximately 70% to 80% of its storage and computing to Microsoft Azure. That could give researchers, instructors, administrators, and students access to scalable computing resources without requiring the university to build equivalent capacity entirely within its own data centers.

For Microsoft, the relationship creates a prominent higher-education deployment for Azure. For Ohio State, it offers a way to consolidate fragmented technology estates and make advanced AI infrastructure available across more disciplines. The opportunity extends beyond computer science. Medicine, engineering, agriculture, business, and the social sciences can all generate workloads that benefit from elastic computing, large-scale storage, and managed AI services.

The timing is notable. @IDC said global AI infrastructure spending reached $318 billion in 2025, up from $153 billion in 2024, and forecast spending to eclipse $1 trillion by 2029. Cloud and shared deployments represented more than 86% of AI infrastructure spending in Q3 2025. Universities are participating in the same capacity race as businesses, though their procurement rules, research requirements, and academic missions create a different operating environment.

Cloud demand is accelerating, too. CIO Dive’s coverage of @Omdiahq research noted that worldwide cloud infrastructure services spending reached $110.9 billion in Q4 2025, a 29% increase from the prior year. @awscloud, Microsoft Azure, and @googlecloud collectively accounted for 66% of global cloud infrastructure spending in Q3 2025, illustrating how concentrated the market has become.

text:
The uncomfortable truth.

Your ISP has no incentive to optimize your router settings. They have every incentive to leave them on factory default.

When your Wi-Fi is slow, you call and complain. They run a diagnostic on the line  which tests Speed 1 (the connection to your modem), not Speed 2 (the Wi-Fi to your devices). Speed 1 looks fine. So they tell you everything checks out on their end  and offer to upgrade you to a faster plan. More money. Same bottleneck.

When your router firmware is 3 years out of date, they don't push an update. When your channel is congested, they don't suggest switching. When your DNS is slow, they don't mention Cloudflare. When your channel width is halved, they don't widen it. Every free fix that would make your Wi-Fi faster is a fix that prevents them from upselling you a more expensive plan.

And the rental fee  $10-$15/month for hardware worth $60  is pure recurring revenue. They make more money renting you that router for 5 years ($840) than the device cost them to buy, ship, and provision.

Your ISP isn't slow. Your settings are.

"He was paying $90/month for a 500 Mbps plan he was getting 15% of. He downgraded to a $60/month 200 Mbps plan, optimized 9 settings, bought his own router, and got faster internet for $528/year less."

9 settings. 15 minutes. $528/year back. Same apartment. Same wires. Same ISP.

The internet was never slow. The router was just set up by a company that profits when you think it is.

text:
This story first appeared in China Report, MIT Technology Review’s newsletter about technology in China. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Tuesday.

Over the last year, a few Chinese influencers have made millions of dollars peddling short video lessons on AI, profiting off people’s fears about the as-yet-unclear impact of the new technology on their livelihoods. 

But the platforms they thrived on have started to turn against them. Just a few weeks ago, WeChat and Douyin began suspending, removing, or restricting their accounts. While influencers on these platforms have been turning people’s anxiety into traffic and profits for a long time, the latest actions show how Chinese social platforms are trying to contain the damage before it goes too far. 

The backlash started last month, as students angrily complained on social media about the superficiality of the courses, saying that they fell far short of the educational promises made about them. 

“I paid 198 RMB ($27.50), and the first three courses were void of actual content. It’s all about urging people to keep paying 1980 RMB for the next course,” Bessie, a Chinese user of the social media site Xiaohongshu, posted about her experience. The courses were created by Li Yizhou, a serial entrepreneur turned startup mentor who, despite having no background in AI, pivoted to posting about explaining AI and drumming up anxiety after the release of ChatGPT in November 2022.

Li sold his entry-level course package for $27.50, and an advanced one for 10 times that price. The cheaper offering contained 40 lesson videos, most of which were around 10 minutes long. Li’s course consisted of tutorials of specific generative AI tools, talks with Chinese AI company executives, and introductions to unrelated topics like how to manage your time more effectively. 

His lessons were a huge commercial success. According to the social media data analysis site Feigua, they were sold over 250,000 times last year, which could have brought in over $6 million in revenue. 

Li is not the only influencer who, despite having no background in AI, saw a business opportunity to calm people’s AI anxieties with quick fixes. There’s also “Teacher He,” an influencer with over 7 million followers who until recently mostly talked about marketing and personal finance, and Zhang Shitong, also followed by millions, whose usual videos mix basic economics with sensational conspiracies like 9/11 denialism. These creators also offered beginner AI lessons at a similar price to Li’s.

In addition to quality complaints, buyers reported that it was hard to get a refund when they changed their mind. Bessie tells MIT Technology Review that she got a refund since she applied early, but others who applied for a refund more than a week after the purchase were denied. A Beijing-based AI community website has also accused Li of appropriating their free user-contributed templates and selling them for profit as part of his course offering. 

By late February, the platforms that hosted these video lessons began to heed the complaints. All of the classes by Li and other AI gurus have been removed from Chinese social media and e-commerce websites. Li hasn’t posted on any of his social media channels since he was suspended in late February. Other creators like “Teacher He” and Zhang Shitong have also been silent.

Li and “Teacher He” didn’t respond to a media inquiry sent by MIT Technology Review. But a customer representative working for Zhang Shitong said the team processes all refund requests in 12 hours and that it was the team’s own decision to not post anything for the past three weeks.

On Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, Li’s account, which used to have over 3 million followers, is now hidden from search results. WeChat Channels, another popular short-video platform, blocked Li and other similar creators from getting new followers in the last week of February. Other smaller platforms have also taken action. Zhishi Xingqiu, a Patreon-like platform that was used by many influencers to sell access to AI-focused communities, has now blocked the search for keywords like “AI,” “Li Yizhou,” or “Sora.”

But none of the platforms have specified which rules the gurus violated. While they may have overpromised with their marketing, it’s hard to say whether their activities really qualified as “scams.” Douyin and WeChat declined to comment on their decisions.

However, there are signs that the restrictions could be reversed. While Chinese social media platforms often permanently delete the accounts of users they believe are flouting rules, these AI course creators have kept their accounts on all platforms. On WeChat, after around two weeks of being blocked from receiving new followers, the creators quietly regained that ability in mid-March. On Douyin, Li’s account was hidden from in-app search results, but his past videos can still be found by going directly to his profile page. 

So far, the Chinese government has not directly addressed the phenomenon or given its official stance. The government has been reining in the livestreaming industry heavily in recent years to censor how influencers act and post, and Chinese platforms set their own rules accordingly, sometimes ahead of government orders, to show they are doing their parts in content regulation.

Even as the creators and their lessons were removed online, there are still lots of Chinese people keen to access these lessons. On social media, some people are now reselling pirated videos of Li’s courses through file sharing, likely without Li’s permission. Now, instead of $27.50, people can spend a few bucks to access the whole course package.

Do you think these AI gurus have crossed a line? Let me know your thoughts at zeyi@technologyreview.com.

Now read the rest of China Report

Catch up with China

1. The US House of Representatives voted overwhelmingly to pass a bill that would force ByteDance to either sell TikTok or see it banned in the US. Now it’s heading to the Senate, where there’s less urgency to pass it. (Associated Press)

2. While the TSMC chip plant in Arizona is delayed, the company’s other new plant in Japan is set to start mass production on schedule in the fourth quarter of 2024. (Wall Street Journal $)

3. Tesla is talking to countries like Thailand to prepare for a potential production expansion in Southeast Asia. But it will have to compete with Chinese EV companies like BYD, which currently accounts for over a quarter of the EVs sold in the region. (Reuters $)

4. An obscure Chinese e-commerce platform called Pandabuy is recruiting influencers to peddle counterfeit products on TikTok and Facebook. (Wired $)

5. The US and Chinese governments quietly renewed their bilateral deal on science and technology research for another six months. (Wall Street Journal $)

6. Chinese students and academics say they are increasingly being targeted at US airports when they enter the country. (Washington Post $)

7. As the Chinese population ages quickly, a tutoring industry for the elderly is thriving. (Reuters $)

Lost in translation

As the Chinese automobile industry moves fast toward battery-operated cars and electric motors, internal combustion engine technology is increasingly seen as a thing of the past. The Chinese publication Economic Observer talked to students who chose to study combustion engines out of their love for cars. They found it’s a decision some now regret, as they’re finding it hard to land a job after graduation. 

Engineering universities are recruiting experts who can teach students about car batteries, but the pace is not fast enough to catch up with the speed of the Chinese market. From January to July 2023, there was a 6% increase in job postings in the automotive industry in China, but a 18% increase in job postings in the EV industry. As a result, large numbers of combustion engineering students say they are being rejected by the auto industry. They either have to compete for the limited positions still available, or find jobs outside the car industry.

One more thing

Youdao, a Chinese online dictionary app, recently started letting users upload their own pronunciations of English words to appear alongside the standard pronunciations in American or British accents. It soon became a vehicle for fun, with people competing to insert jokes, cultural memes, viral TikTok soundbites, and dramatic acting as pronunciations. In a particularly amusing example, someone pronounces “constipation” as if they are actually experiencing it.

1. Almost every company uses it.

3. It's been around for 50 years.

13. It reads like plain English.
14. Results are exact and repeatable.
15. It processes data where the data lives.
16. Every dashboard runs on it.
17. Data pipelines are built with it.
18. Transactions keep data correct.
19. AI starts with data, and data starts with SQL.
20. AI writes SQL, but you still have to check it.
21. It teaches you to think in sets.
22. One query can find a bug.
23. Good indexes make pages load fast.
24. It makes you better at designing systems.
25. It's a language every team speaks.

Tools change. SQL stays. 💡

text:
Microsoft is spending $175 billion on AI while offering buyouts to 60,000 employees.

17 days later, a routine network update took down Outlook, Teams, and Copilot across 74 countries.

430 million users were locked out for 18 hours while European hospitals went back to paper fax machines.

This is the story of incident EX1550543 and how Wall Street's favorite AI accounting trick broke the internet's backbone.

October 26, 2026

Microsoft Chief People Officer Amy Coleman sends an internal memo across the US, UK, Canada, and India.

The company is rolling out a Voluntary Exit Offer to 60,000 employees, roughly 27% of its global workforce.

The buyouts reach all the way up to Level 70:

- veteran systems engineers
- senior directors and general managers
- institutional memory built over 20 years

Why would a profitable tech giant push 60,000 people toward the door by December 31?

Because of how Wall Street grades AI spending:

- $175B in AI server racks is CapEx, depreciated slowly over years
- 60,000 human salaries are OpEx, deducted 100% from quarterly margins right now

Cut the people, buy the GPUs, and your operating margin looks like a masterpiece.

November 12, 2026

17 days after the buyout memo, at 12:30 PM EST, a network config change hits Exchange Online.

A large batch of core servers suddenly fails Microsoft's automated health checks.

The automated system does what it was programmed to do and pulls every failing server offline at once.

Then the real nightmare starts.

Live traffic from 430 million users dumps onto the few remaining servers in seconds.

The sudden flood crushes the login and routing layer, sending 140,000 outage reports straight up on Downdetector.

Outlook goes down. Teams goes down. SharePoint goes down.

Even Copilot, the flagship AI assistant meant to replace human workflows, goes dark because it runs on the exact same legacy plumbing.

Every time engineers try to restart a dropped server, the wall of waiting traffic immediately freezes it again.

18 hours later

No AI agent could break the loop.

Human engineers had to manually halt deployments, override the health checks, and bleed traffic back in slow stages while extending email timeouts to 48 hours.

To this day, Microsoft incident codes EX1550543 and MO1550821 stand as a live stress test of replacing institutional memory with automation.

You can spend $175 billion on AI clusters and cut 60,000 roles to make a quarterly earnings slide glow for Wall Street.

In enterprise infrastructure, senior engineers aren't bloat on a spreadsheet, they are the only circuit breaker standing between a bad config file and a global blackout.

I’ll offer my two cents here because keyboard warriors really irritate me sometimes, especially when it comes to trying to police BTS and ARMY. It’s so easy to attack people when you don’t know them. 

Attending as many concerts as you can and want is such a joyful thing and no one should make you feel bad about that. Music=Life in my world. And life is way too short to not enjoy every second you can. As a young widow, trust me on this. Also as someone who flew to Paris for 1.5 days just to see a concert (Celine Dion), if you have the means, absolutely use them. 😉

As for the event, I might presume from your statements that you were offered an invitation and one of two things happened: 
1. You accepted mostly based on the fact that BTS members might attend and you would get to see/interact with them-this was your first consideration in attending
2. You accepted because you had personal ties to the charity, cause, attendees, and/or just thought it would be a fun night out, and then BTS happened to show up unexpectedly 

Likely it might have been a combo of these, but if #1 was in there, or people assume it was #1–and I’m not saying I think that would be wrong (I honestly don’t know what I would do in that situation)—maybe that’s why people are being mean. They might see that more like obsessive behavior than if you were completely unaware that they might attend —again, I’m not saying it was obsessive behavior, just that others could see it that way. Does that make sense? 

You don’t need to clarify any more than you have. I just wanted to help you settle your mind about what others might be thinking. At the end of the day, you and the people you know and love (in real life) know what kind of human you are, and if you and they are happy with the answer, no one else matters. 💜

text:
The General’s Dispatch — Friday, November 13

Commanders: The market’s ranks broke in different directions today: the $SPX lost 0.4%, the $IXIC fell 0.9%, and the $DJI edged up 0.1%. Despite Friday’s retreat, the S&P still secured its first winning week since early October—an army can lose a skirmish and still keep the campaign ledger respectable.

The AI battalion remained unsettled after $NVDA’s leadership upheaval. Nvidia fell again, and fellow chipmakers $AVGO and $AMD also retreated as investors weighed whether enormous AI spending will earn its keep. Health care and financial shares advanced, while $MSFT ticked higher despite a global outage affecting its web services. A report of slightly cooler wholesale inflation offered a small comfort; energy costs and expectations of further Fed rate increases kept the market’s brow furrowed.

Across the intermarket battlefield, the formations disagreed:

Treasuries: The 10-year yield rose to about 5.15%, keeping pressure on rate-sensitive shares.
Oil: U.S. crude settled near $95.84 a barrel after a choppy session amid the U.S.–Iran conflict.
Gold: Bullion recovered some ground after Thursday’s sharp selloff, but remained on course for a weekly decline.
Market breadth: The Nasdaq’s 0.9% loss and declines in chipmakers showed the strain in growth stocks, even as health care and financials advanced.
Dollar: The greenback remained firm, part of the broader backdrop of high yields and rate-hike expectations.

The General’s assessment: The day’s retreat had a narrow trouble spot in technology, while higher yields and energy costs supplied a less cheerful soundtrack. The S&P’s weekly gain suggests the broader campaign survived the week’s turbulence, though today’s cross-asset picture still looked cautious—not a clear signal of what comes next.

text:
PMIF26 Concludes with Major Investment Agreements, Pakistan Reaffirms Commitment to Mineral Value Addition

The 2-day forum brought together over 10,000 attendees, 122 exhibitors and participation from more than 60 countries

ISLAMABAD, November 13, 2026: The two-day Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum 2026 (PMIF26) concluded in Islamabad on Friday with Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif inviting international investors to explore Pakistan’s mineral wealth, assuring them of investment protection and government support, while calling for a shift from exporting raw minerals to developing domestic processing and refining facilities.
Addressing the concluding day of the forum, attended by over 10,000 participants from more than 60 countries, the prime minister declared, “Your safety is our safety,” and pledged to address concerns and facilitate investment in the mining and minerals sector. He stressed that Pakistan must move beyond exporting unprocessed resources and establish facilities to convert raw materials into finished and semi-finished products, generating greater economic value, employment, technical expertise and technology transfer. Referring to a Goldman Sachs projection that Pakistan could become the world’s sixth-largest economy by 2075, PM Shehbaz said he hoped the country would achieve the milestone earlier than 2050.

The prime minister, accompanied by Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, also inaugurated the National Minerals Data Centre and the Geological Survey of Pakistan (GSP) GeoPortal. The digital platforms are designed to improve access to geological information, support mineral exploration, reduce uncertainty for investors and facilitate informed investment decisions.

In his address, Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir said Pakistan’s ambition extended beyond exporting raw minerals to developing the complete value chain domestically, including refining and manufacturing. He described turning the country’s mineral wealth into tangible economic gains as a collective national goal and stressed that communities in mineral-rich areas must benefit directly from mining projects. He called for long-term partnerships that generate lasting value for Pakistan and its partners, urging the country to move “from potential to production, from promises to action, and from raw exports to value-added growth”. He said Pakistan’s resources offered opportunities, while its people remained the strength needed to turn them into results.

A major announcement during the forum came from the Frontier Works Organization (FWO), which announced an estimated 350 million tonnes of copper in the Dasht-e-Kain area of Chagai, Balochistan, based on approximately half of its drilling data analysed so far. The announcement highlighted the exploration potential of Pakistan and added to the range of investment opportunities presented during the forum. 

Mari Minerals announced the discovery of its first-ever gold and copper reserves in Chagai. The reserve has a potential of around 1 billion tonnes of copper and gold. The National Resources Limited (NRL) announced a $100 million investment in Pakistan’s mineral sector.

Federal Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik outlined Pakistan's push into critical minerals like copper, gold, lithium, and antimony, emphasizing domestic refining, advanced geological mapping, and infrastructure upgrades like the Rohri-Nokundi railway to link mineral hubs globally.

OGDC President Ahmed Hayat Lak celebrated PMIF26's success in forging international partnerships and launching digital data portals, stressing that execution, technical excellence, and transparent policies are vital to turning mineral wealth into lasting economic progress.

Global mining leaders, including executives from Barrick Mining, Ivanhoe Mines, and Minmetals, shared international insights on policy certainty and regional cooperation during high-level strategic dialogues.

text:
Social media staff for official accounts are typically communications specialists, not operational first responders or senior decision-makers directing emergency responses. Posting about one topic (here, subpoenas) while another unrelated event unfolds does not mean the White House or federal government is ignoring the latter.

The Mississippi River collision near the Port of New Orleans was handled primarily by local and state authorities, the U.S. Coast Guard, New Orleans Harbor Police, fire/EMS, and others. New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno, Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry, and Coast Guard officials led public updates; the river was closed in the area for rescue efforts. All passengers and crew from the American Heritage were accounted for, with no fatalities and 32 people treated for non-critical injuries—outcomes local officials called a “miracle on the Mississippi.”[](<https://t.co/i6xVtKGoyM>)

President Trump addressed the incident directly on Truth Social the same evening, thanking the Coast Guard, law enforcement, and first responders, noting that “incredibly, nobody was killed,” and praising Gov. Landry’s leadership. He had also called the governor to offer federal support. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin noted Coast Guard involvement as well.[](<https://t.co/QQ7sunU8vR>)

Official accounts routinely post on multiple issues in parallel. The subpoena statement and the ship collision were concurrent but distinct matters; the former does not indicate operational neglect of the latter.

text:
For those who do not know FFK, here is why this matters.

Chief Femi Fani-Kayode is Nigeria's High Commissioner to South Africa, appointed by President Bola Ahmed Tinubu. He arrived in Johannesburg on 25 October 2026.

He is not new to public life, and he was not discovered yesterday.

He was born 16 October 1960, the very month Nigeria took her independence. His lineage is history wearing a human face.

His great-grandfather, Rev. Emmanuel Adelabi Kayode, earned an MA in Theology from Fourah Bay / Durham in the 1890s. One of the earliest Nigerians ever educated in England.

His grandfather, Justice Victor Adedapo Kayode, studied Law at Selwyn College, Cambridge, in 1922.

His father, Chief Remilekun Fani-Kayode, studied Law at Downing College, Cambridge, in 1943. Deputy Premier of the West, a father of our nationalism, former Finance Minister.

FFK himself studied Law at Pembroke College, Cambridge, in 1984.

Four generations. Over 100 years of unbroken Cambridge law. Only a few families in the whole world can rival that training.

But the training did not start at Cambridge. It started at age seven.

He has said it himself: I never went to school in Nigeria. From the age of seven, I went to the very best private boarding schools in England. I was at Brighton College, Holmewood House, Harrow School, Kelly College, London University and Cambridge University.

Brighton College. Holmewood House, Kent. Harrow School on the Hill, twin and rival of Eton, school of eight British Prime Ministers including Winston Churchill, school where the British elite learn that a gentleman does not shout, he out-argues you in a whisper. Kelly College, where he finished.

Then SOAS, University of London, LL.B Law, 1983. Then Cambridge, Pembroke College, Law, 1984. Then Nigerian Law School, Called to the Nigerian Bar, 1985. Then Accra, Diploma in Theology, 1995.

Harrow gave him composure. Cambridge gave him precision. Law gave him argument. Theology gave him the grace to bless after being insulted.

His life was not smooth. As a schoolboy in England, he confronted racism. In 1979, he was arrested protesting the South African rugby tour, fighting apartheid when it was not fashionable to do so.

For 35 years after, he survived the trenches of Nigerian politics: Special Assistant to President Obasanjo. Minister of Culture and Tourism. Minister of Aviation. Campaign spokesman. Writer. Lawyer. The most quoted, most attacked, most resilient voice of his generation.

Many called those years his rough patches. They were wrong. Those were his apprenticeship.

On 27 October 2026, I wrote him an open letter. 

I asked for one thing: translation, from words into tangible improvement. Protect Nigerians in South Africa. Restore dignity. Give real consular support. Make the friendship between Nigeria and South Africa mean something in real life.

Yesterday in Pretoria, the world saw what translation looks like.

Nigeria was cut out of the livestream. Our voice was erased from the room. A lesser man would have shouted. 

He did not.

He spoke directly to President Cyril Ramaphosa. Quietly. Firmly. The President intervened. The speech was eventually released. And when SABC News offered him an interview on the same premises, he turned them down and told them to go and listen to the speech they had refused to air.

Protection with dignity. Firmness without shouting. Grace without surrender.

That is why I wrote the letter. That is why I am sharing it again now.

Below is the letter as it was written.

OPEN LETTER TO H.E. AMBASSADOR FEMI FANI-KAYODE

High Commissioner of Nigeria to South Africa (concurrently accredited to Lesotho & Eswatini)

Your Excellency,

I write as a Nigerian who watched your arrival in Johannesburg on 25 October 2026 with measured hope.

You have stated clearly that your primary focus, entrusted by President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, is to rebuild the bridge of friendship and cooperation between Nigeria and South Africa

text:
Seeking Clarity on Recent Removals from Sylent’s Corner, Everglade Grove, and Ritzy’s Server

I am writing this publicly because private channels have closed and I have been left without any explanation. Today, I was removed from Sylent’s Corner and Everglade Grove. In both cases Discord notified me that a server moderator made the decision and that Discord itself did not. No reason was provided in the notification or afterward.

Earlier that day I had replied positively under a post by Ritzy about wanting deeper fellowship beyond streaming. Both @RitzyVT and @SylentBell  later interacted under that same thread. Roughly two hours later I received the removal notices.

Before the removals I reached out privately. On November 11 I sent Ritzy a short message checking in, mentioning that I had seen her in Shiro’s server previously, noting that we had reconciled, and asking if she was okay. I described myself as a faithful person who simply wanted to look after good people and offered to answer any questions. The message was polite and contained no demands.

I also messaged a moderator associated with Sylent’s servers (KN1GHT). I explained that friends had spoken well of him, that I was trying to meet more people in the Christian VTuber space, and that I had heard Zion might have been asked about something (blacktemplar117 was the one who talked him not KN1GHT). I attached a clip and clarified that my main purpose was simply to make acquaintances. When I later asked why I had been removed, the response was limited. Another moderator (blacktemplar117) later told me the removal had nothing to do with Zion, that decisions are made case by case, that he was not the one who removed me but stands by the other moderators’ actions, and that he is “not at liberty to say” more. When I asked whether there was anyone I could speak with or any appeal process, the reply was simply “There is not.”

I offered, if the issue concerned past allegations or rumors, to provide documentation and conversation records that address them. That offer received no substantive reply.

I have stated publicly and privately that I regard both Ritzy and Sylent as faithful Christians who speak well of fellowship and community. My recent messages were written in that spirit: a check in, an attempt to meet people, and ordinary questions. I believed I had been courteous. I still do not understand what rule was broken or what conduct prompted an immediate, unexplained removal with no warning and no path to clarification.

If the decision rests on something I said or did in the servers (Although, I barely interacted in either other than make a religious post in Sylents server about verse of the day), on older public claims about me, or on any other concrete reason, I remain willing to hear it and to respond with evidence where evidence exists. Silence and a closed appeal process leave me unable to correct a misunderstanding if one occurred, or to accept a clear boundary if one was intended.

I am posting the relevant screenshots and this account because the private conversations ended without an explanation. I continue to wish both of them well although I find this current behavior very unchrist like in nature especially because I just wanted to be part of more Christian communities for fellowship. I would still prefer a direct, truthful conversation over continued uncertainty. Until one is offered, this is the record of what took place.

text:
WHAT COULD A 15-YEAR-OLD GIRL POSSIBLY HAVE DONE TO DESERVE THIS?

I’m not entirely sure why, but this incident in Ohio bothers me more than most.

We have all seen the video.

A young girl being savagely beaten on a school bus. Punched, kicked, and placed in a chokehold while other children laugh.

What could she possibly have done to deserve such brutality?

NOTHING. ABSOLUTELY NOTHING.

And perhaps what bothers me most is what this says about the environment in which we are raising our children.

Parents send their children to school every morning trusting that teachers, administrators, and the educational system will protect them.

But what happens when that trust is broken?

We have created a public education system where discipline has become a national controversy, accountability is constantly debated, and parents are left wondering whether their children are safe.

Teachers’ unions, school administrators, and elected school boards all need to answer a fundamental question:

WHO IS PROTECTING THE CHILDREN WHO COME TO SCHOOL TO LEARN?

And what about parents who want to remove their children from an environment of violence and chaos?

Not every family can afford private school. Not every parent can homeschool. And not every community offers a realistic public-school alternative.

I grew up in another America. It wasn’t perfect. We had bullies, fights, and plenty of problems.

But I remember a time when discipline meant something and when serious misconduct brought serious consequences.

We should not have to sacrifice one child’s safety to preserve another child’s place in the classroom.

Every child deserves an education.

But no child should have to endure violence to receive one.

We owe that 15-year-old girl more than an investigation and an apology.

We owe her protection, accountability, and justice.

And we owe every American parent something increasingly precious:

THE CONFIDENCE THAT THEIR CHILD WILL COME HOME SAFE.

text:
Saturday's Free Pick: Tennessee/Texas A&M UNDER 44.5

There will be 15 MPH winds in College Station on Saturday that will aid us in cashing this UNDER 44.5 ticket between Tennessee and Texas A&M.  But there's a lot more reasons to back the UNDER, especially above the key number of 44.

Texas A&M has really been an UNDER team in conference play.  The Aggies have gone 5-1 UNDER in their last six games overall finishing with 41 or fewer combined points in five of those six games.  You could argue the Aggies have the worst offense in the SEC this season as QB Marcel Reed has taken a big step back.  He is averaging just 6.2 yards per pass attempt with a 8-to-8 TD/INT ratio and only 206 rushing yards on 2.6 per carry this season.

The Aggies have been held to just 16.0 points per game in SEC play this season.  But their defense has kept them in games, allowing just 18.7 points per game on the season.  They rank 22nd in scoring defense and 28th in total defense this season.

Tennessee has gone 7-2 UNDER this season as Josh Heupel has really leaned into relying on his defense to win games instead of the high-octane offenses he has been known for in the past.  The Vols rank 10th in scoring defense this season allowing just 15.1 points per game.  They are also 17th in total defense at 296.4 yards per game.  The Vols are only allowing 15.7 points per game in conference play.

This Tennessee offense has been disappointing all season scoring just 24.8 points per game in SEC play.  QB MacIntyre has a 2-to-3 TD/INT ratio on the season and offers nothing in the way of a dual-threat with 15 carries for zero yards.  They are a run-first offense, but they are without 2nd-leading rusher Duane Morris (434 yards, 6.6/carry, 3 TD).

Tennessee has been an up-tempo offense under Heupel up until this season as the Vols rank just 63rd in tempo snapping the ball every 26.2 seconds.  Texas A&M ranks 93rd in tempo snapping the ball every 27.5 seconds.  I expect both defenses to have their way with these two offenses today in another SEC grinder between two teams who are used to playing in defensive battles.  Bet the UNDER in this game Saturday.

FINANCE IDEA | November 14, 2026

THE LEVERAGE MOVED

The Federal Reserve's Financial Stability Report, released Friday, puts hedge fund leverage at its highest since data collection began in 2013. Gross notional leverage hit the record in the first quarter of 2026, the latest quarter with full data, even as basis trade activity fell. The record is broad. Equity, relative value, and macro strategies all sit at record or near-record leverage.

The basis trade was the market's most watched leveraged position. A fund buys cash Treasuries, sells the matching future, and funds the bonds in repo. The gap is small, so the trade only works at scale and on borrowed money. Fed staff research puts it at about $830 billion in September 2025, a third of large funds' long Treasury exposure. Hedge funds held about $2 trillion of cash Treasuries at the end of 2025, a record 7 percent of marketable debt.

That trade is losing its edge. Futures contracts price delivery against a fixed 6 percent reference yield. As yields climbed toward that level, with the 10-year above 5 percent, the delivery option at the heart of the trade lost value. The bonds eligible for delivery now look more similar, so the payoff shrinks, the Dallas Fed notes. Leveraged funds' net short futures positions have plateaued since 2025.

The money changed shape. The Dallas Fed finds front-end swap-spread wideners now offer risk-adjusted returns close to a long basis position. A fund holds the same repo-financed Treasury and pays fixed in a swap instead of selling a future. Fed staff data put swap-spread positions at about $305 billion in September 2025.

A swap-spread position carries considerably more dollar risk per unit of notional than a basis position, the Dallas Fed warns. The basis trade converges at expiry because the future settles into the bond. A swap spread has no delivery date and can stay dislocated. The same leverage now sits in a trade with a longer fuse and a harder exit.

The aggregate confirms it. Hedge fund gross assets reached about $13 trillion in early 2026, triple the 2013 level, the IMF's October report records. Borrowing from US global systemically important banks hit a record $3.63 trillion in the second quarter, per Office of Financial Research data.

The risk the Fed flagged did not shrink. It moved where there is no expiry date to force convergence. The Treasury market's largest leveraged holder is still there, holding a different trade.

News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

text:
You may hear people in Sabinal say or ask… “Mayor, I honestly don’t care, just fix the damn potholes!” Or

“How does this help make my ride home smoother?” Or

“I have to get a new suspension on my car and the Mayor is on vacation” Or

“The Mayor just cares about getting in front of a camera”

Well… everything I do has a point. & the point is simple. Promotion, responsible growth & development of Sabinal, Texas.

For those who may not know, Sabinal is a small rural community of roughly 2,000 people in Uvalde County, Southwest Texas.

This week, I signed the founding documents for the City of Sabinal to join the Hill Country Mayor’s Alliance. An advocacy group whose mission is to serve the people of our communities.

The City of Sabinal gets much of its rules from the Texas Legislature in Austin. They’re the ones who set laws on the Tax System, Laws for General Law cities like ours, procedures and policies regarding state oversight and regulatory agencies, ethics, etc.

When rural cities like Sabinal have a voice at the table in establishing those rules, we can help form them to a point that we can get things like more grants for road and street repairs accomplished, a better tax system so that the city and taxpayer are treated fairly, more funding for water and sewer infrastructure so citizens are getting better quality water at an affordable rate, the list goes on and on.

Promoting- if I can sell to the world, the hidden paradise that is Sabinal… I will! If I can get people to realize the true potential Sabinal has in Uvalde County and Southwest Texas… I will! If I can bring in more customers for our businesses, more investors for our economy, more homebuyers for our housing market, etc. I will!

Sabinal is a hidden paradise filled with untapped potential. As Mayor, I will gladly serve as the Ambassador and try to bring in as much support, resources, investors, shoppers, etc. as I possibly can!

So I kindly ask, before you say or hear anyone say “Erik only wants to get in front of a camera” or “he acts like he does a lot but our roads still suck,” understand that unless there’s a way 18 million dollars can fall from the sky, the team and I are doing our best to try to get our roads repaired. I’m doing my best to promote Sabinal and get people to believe in us.

I have a vision for Sabinal that is much more than a dying town, with ugly roads and falling buildings that people drive through to get to Concan and Garner State Park.

I want people from across Texas and beyond to see the potential in our little community and realize that Sabinal has so much more to offer!

And slowly, we’re getting closer.

Here are just a few things our team has accomplished:

✅ New Playground
🚧 Downtown Beautification- Plaza!
🚧 HUGE Sidewalk for our kids
🚧 Sewer System Upgrade
✅ Functioning Little League Restrooms
✅ Dozens of state violations cleared
✅ AWARD WINNING Animal Shelter
✅ Free Police Vehicles
🚧 New Firetruck
✅ MORE EMS PRESENCE
✅ Improved Electrical Infrastructure
✅ Downtown Improvements
✅ Dozens of Grant Applications
✅ Almost 4 million dollars in Grants!

And many more!!

For a small rural Texas community of roughly 2,000 people, I believe these are accomplishments worth being proud of!

To my friends outside of Sabinal, I hope you’ll come visit our little town, support our local businesses, and see for yourselves why I believe so strongly in its future!

And to the people of Sabinal, please trust the process and try to have confidence in the team and I! Rome was not built in a day but we are certainly trying to speed up those odds!

And if you can’t get behind the process… I encourage you to speak up at a council meeting or better yet, you have a constitutional right to replace me, by voting me out of office- for another person who may deliver results faster for Sabinal.

text:
It's almost comical to see so many people watch Tesla launch a vehicle for sale to customers without a wheel and pedals and their first reaction is to complain about how bad of a deal it is. Let me explain to you why this is painfully shortsighted

Business 101: when you have a lot of demand and limited supply, you charge higher prices to capture the margin from those early adopters that are gladly willing to pay. Plenty of people, especially early on, will happily pay whatever the price is set at to be among the first owners of a fully autonomous vehicle. Tesla has exactly NO incentive to have the monthly subscription underpriced right now. Demand already will far exceed supply

As Tesla learns and adjusts allocations (in house fleet vs. sold to customers), it will be able to track supply and demand as the manufacturing of Cybercab ramps. We have to remember most Cybercabs will still be deployed to Tesla's own fleet, so it's likely going to be a long time before personally owned Cybercabs hit any type of scale where a lower monthly subscription may be needed to move the sales needle

Further, the $299 gets you a lot more than just autonomy:

• Fully Unsupervised driving
• Premium connectivity
• Remote support
• Roadside help with towing up to about 50 miles
• Tire replacement and flats, windshield and wipers, cabin filters, inspections, camera cleaning and washer fluid and more (effectively all regular maintenance)
• The car driving itself to service and back

Comparing this to a regular vehicle or a lease is foolish - no other car exists where you don't have to pay attention to get around that handles the service on its own. And yes, the geofences are limited now, but just think about what they will look like in 2-3 years. I'm expecting nearly all of Texas to be covered in that timeline and likely a few other states as well

Long term, as Tesla scales to hundreds of thousands of Cybercabs deployed, they can always lower the monthly subscription price. Same goes for Unsupervised FSD on other customer cars - Tesla can start that price on the high end, capture early adopter margin, assess demand, and adjust from there

Once Tesla reaches economies of scale, it will have the flexibility to HYPOTHETICALLY offer it at $0/month and still make money hand over fist. They likely will never do this, but the most important point is they would be able to and still remain profitable. No other company has a chance in hell at doing anything similar anytime soon $TSLA

CRYPTO WAS SUPPOSED TO BREAK THE SYSTEM — NOT BECOME PART OF IT

November 13, 2026 | Crypto Market Commentary

Let’s address the elephant in the room. What the hell happened to cryptocurrency?

An industry built on decentralization, financial independence, and freedom from traditional banking has become increasingly dependent on Wall Street, institutional capital, Federal Reserve decisions, and Washington’s regulatory agenda.

The very system cryptocurrency was created to challenge now has enormous influence over its market.

And retail investors are getting absolutely destroyed.

THE WALL STREET TAKEOVER

Bitcoin has fallen below $70,000. Ethereum has slipped beneath $2,000. Solana has taken another beating.

Meanwhile, approximately $1.48 billion flowed out of major U.S. spot cryptocurrency ETFs over five trading days in early November.

Think about that.

We spent years celebrating institutional adoption as cryptocurrency’s ultimate victory. Bitcoin ETFs arrived, major financial institutions entered the market, and everyone cheered.

But there’s another side to that equation.

When institutional money flows in, markets celebrate. When that money starts leaving, the consequences spread across the entire ecosystem.

Retail traders are left fighting volatility, shrinking liquidity, and cascading liquidations.

WASHINGTON WANTS A SEAT AT THE TABLE

The @SECGov and @CFTC are increasingly shaping the rules of the industry, while @federalreserve policy continues influencing investor appetite for risk.

The CLARITY Act stalled in the Senate, leaving major questions about cryptocurrency regulation unresolved.

Regulation itself isn’t necessarily the enemy. Fraud prevention, transparency, and investor protections matter.

But at what point does oversight become another layer of dependence on the institutions cryptocurrency was supposed to make less necessary?

THE MEME COIN MARKET IS PAYING THE PRICE

Look at the Solana ecosystem.

When confidence deteriorates and liquidity disappears, smaller speculative tokens can get absolutely annihilated.

Projects lose momentum. Traders abandon positions. Communities disappear overnight.

And the people who believed crypto offered an alternative to traditional financial markets discover they’re still exposed to many of the same economic forces.

THE BIGGER PROBLEM

Government involvement alone didn’t cause this selloff. Institutional outflows, leverage, inflation concerns, and declining liquidity are all contributing.

But the bigger question deserves an answer:

Are we watching cryptocurrency mature into a legitimate global financial system, or are we watching its original purpose slowly get swallowed by the institutions it was meant to challenge?

Because those are two very different futures.

Crypto promised financial freedom.

It wasn’t supposed to become another market where ordinary investors spend their lives worrying about Washington’s next announcement and Wall Street’s next selloff.

Decentralization was supposed to mean something.

And if this industry forgets that, what the hell was the revolution for?

@SECGov @CFTC @federalreserve @BlackRock @solana

text:
A California man faces three felony counts of human smuggling after investigators say he was transporting three people from California to Colorado through Utah for money.

According to a probable-cause affidavit, Hector Pec Tecum was arrested Nov. 11 and booked into the Washington County Purgatory Correctional Facility. A Washington County sheriff’s detective who also works with Homeland Security Investigations wrote that immigration officers had taken Pec Tecum into custody after interviewing people in the vehicle.

The affidavit says three passengers were interviewed at the jail. One told detectives he paid $500 for transportation to Florida. Another said he was offered a ride to Colorado for $200 and was given a phone number to arrange it. A third said friends had arranged and paid for his travel but could not provide further details.

In his interview with detectives, Pec Tecum said he had left California the previous afternoon and was driving the passengers to Denver. He said he charged each passenger $300, keeping some of the money for fuel and the rest as payment. He also told investigators he planned to meet family members of some passengers along the way to collect payment, according to the affidavit.

The detective’s affidavit says Pec Tecum acknowledged knowing the passengers were not lawfully in the United States. It quotes him telling investigators, “I wouldn’t be transporting them if they weren’t illegal.”

Pec Tecum was charged with three counts of human smuggling, each a second-degree felony under Utah law. The affidavit says investigators filed a separate count for each person allegedly transported.
