text:
AMERICAN HERO OF THE DAY:

KENTUCKY STATE POLICE TROOPER HAYDEN PHILLIPS, 28, SHOT AND KILLED ON A TRAFFIC STOP TWO DAYS BEFORE HIS 29TH BIRTHDAY

Kentucky State Police Trooper Hayden Phillips of Post 3 in Bowling Green was 28. On September 28, 2026, two days before he would have turned 29, he was shot and killed during a traffic stop on northbound Interstate 65 in Warren County, just north of Bowling Green.

He had stopped a gray 2017 Honda Civic near mile marker 39 for an expired temporary tag. His dash camera shows him leaning into the passenger window, then two shots.

The suspect, Emonnie Dion Branch, 51, of Portland, Tennessee, has a long criminal record and was wanted on a parole violation, according to the Associated Press. Louisville Metro Police stopped him with a grappler device on Dixie Highway about three hours later.

A Warren County grand jury indicted him for murder of a first responder, a capital offense in Kentucky, along with being a felon in possession of a handgun and tampering with evidence.

He pleaded not guilty on October 27 and is being held without bail. Prosecutors have not said whether they will seek the death penalty.

He grew up in Russell Springs, Kentucky, and graduated from Russell County High School in 2016.

Before joining the Kentucky State Police, he served with the Glasgow and Russell Springs police departments, including as a K-9 handler, and as a volunteer firefighter and EMT.

He left the Kentucky State Police Academy the first time so he could be by his wife Jordan's side when she had a medical condition. He came back, graduated with Cadet Class 103 in August 2023, and was assigned to Post 3.

The day before he was killed, he installed a flagpole at his home with his sons.

His wife has described him as her best friend, and as someone who could light up a room and make anyone laugh.

He is survived by Jordan and their three sons, Kason, Knox, and Konnor. The youngest is 1.

He is also survived by his mother, Robin, his father, Larry "Homer" Phillips, and his sister, Heather.

Rest in peace, Hayden.

You were the best America has to offer, and you always will be 🇺🇸

Jensen Huang's resignation — what it means for NVDA and the AI industry
The resignation — verified:
Thursday, November 12, around 8:48 AM ET, Nvidia announced Jensen Huang resigned as President, CEO and board member, effective immediately, ending a 33-year tenure. He co-founded the company in 1993.
Interim CEO: CFO Colette Kress (EVP + CFO since September 2013, keeping the CFO role); the permanent search is internal and external. Harvey C. Jones was appointed the company's first-ever Chair of the Board.
The 8-K: the board accepted the resignation on November 11, effective immediately; the company gave no reason. "Firing" is Rep. Moolenaar's word, not the fact — his own statement's title says "Resignation."
Market reaction: Wednesday's close of $173.73 → pre-market $157.54 (-9.32%, about $400 billion of market value erased) → Thursday's close $165.77 → Friday $162.85 (-2.01%). NVDA fell 12.75% on the week.
Analysts: Ives $225 (without Huang) vs $300 (with him); Stifel $315 → $205; BofA $350 → $280; William Blair cut to Market Perform.
Rotation: AMD +18.93% on the week (Friday -8.75% to $534.06), AVGO up about 19% on the week (Friday $347.01, -4.76%). The NVDA–AMD spread is about -$371. Red pen: AMD trades at 38.44x forward earnings vs NVDA at 13.72x; the scale gap is about 11–13x (NVDA's data-center quarter is about $75 billion, AMD's $6.7 billion).
Three structural breaks for the AI industry:
The founder premium is gone: "Jensen is Nvidia" no longer holds, and the market has to re-price succession uncertainty.
A succession vacuum: Kress is an interim CEO from finance, with no product or visionary pull. In your framework: "NVDA doesn't need an operator, it needs a visionary."
The scrutiny continues: the Senate and House will investigate the Trump administration's approval of Nvidia chip exports to China; Huang has agreed to testify before Congress on the Alice Huang matter before Thanksgiving (no date set). The Warren + Coons preservation letter requires confirmation by November 17.
Rumors and investigations (reported, not established):
The NYT reported an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, his direct report; Reuters reported an intimate relationship with a second employee (two sources, unnamed). Both are allegations, not findings.
The Alice Huang spy case: CNN reported that intelligence to date "does not prove" she spied for Beijing (not an exoneration); the FBI probe is ongoing, with no official finding. CNBC reported she owned stakes in Chinese businesses that provided computing power to Huawei (source reporting, not a finding).
Your rule has fired: the November 11 rule — liquidate NVDA holdings once the CEO is replaced — has fired. The $200 calendar spread (long Jun 17, 2027 $200 calls / short Dec 24, 2026 $200 calls, $12.18 debit) is confirmed held, with a maximum loss of $1,218 per spread. The next test: NVDA earnings Tuesday after the close, Kress's first print facing analysts — watch data-center demand, H200 sales to China, and guidance.
Earnings breakdown: CoreWeave (CRWV) — beat-and-raise, sold on leverage
Q3 (Nov 10, after the close): revenue $3.661 billion, +168% YoY, beating consensus of about $3.5 billion and the company's $3.4–$3.6 billion guide; GAAP EPS -$1.27, beating Zacks' -$1.45 (Finnhub shows -$0.95, a different basis); net loss $709 million.
Profits: adjusted operating income $379 million, beating the $200–$260 million guide; GAAP operating income $207 million. The Sankey: revenue $3.7B → gross profit $2.5B (68%) → operating profit $0.2B (6%) → interest $0.8B + tax and other $0.1B → net loss $0.7B.
Red pen: Q3 net interest expense of $846 million is more than 4x operating profit; Q4 interest is guided at $1.05–$1.15 billion; debt is $46.9 billion. R&D of $2.0 billion is 55% of revenue. 98% of revenue comes from committed contracts ($3.6B) — revenue quality is high; the problem is cost and leverage.
Guidance: backlog $132.5 billion (+138% YoY); FY26 revenue guided up to $13.0–$13.3 billion; capex $37–$39 billion; active power over 1.7 GW; operating cash flow $1.975 billion; cash $6.5 billion.
The stock: Nov 11 close $60.77 → Nov 12 $56.60 → Friday intraday $52.27 (-7.66%, low $49.24). A beat-and-raise sold off — that's the leverage story, not the revenue story.
The slide's numbers were checked against the official print; US $3.4B + rest of world $0.2B sums to $3.6B vs the $3.7B total — a $0.1B rounding difference.
Earnings breakdown: Nebius (NBIS) — a big beat, and the stock fell
Q3 (Nov 12, before the open): adjusted EPS $0.31, revenue $980.8 million; revenue +571% YoY (Q3 2025: $146.1 million) and +68% QoQ (Q2 2026: $582.3 million). Adjusted EBITDA $465.8 million.
Slide check: EPS consensus -$0.63 vs actual $0.31 (a 149% beat); revenue consensus $907.17 million vs actual $980.8 million (an 8% beat). The revenue consensus varies by vendor — the slide's $907.17 million matches MarketBeat, Finnhub's $925.68 million is the high outlier; the beat is large either way.
Red pen one: the slide's "EPS +178% YoY / +358% QoQ" uses the absolute-negative-base convention — the reality is a swing from loss to profit (YoY -$0.40 → +$0.31; QoQ -$0.12 → +$0.31). Don't say +178%.
Red pen two: FY26 revenue guidance was cut to the low end of the $3.0–$3.4 billion range (FactSet $3.35 billion); 2026 capex was raised to about $27 billion (from $20–$25 billion); 2027 capex is $40–$45 billion, far above the expected $28.77 billion; $7 billion-plus ARR was pushed from December to February; about $325 million of Q3 revenue was non-recurring.
Prepayments are the bright spot: Q3 new deals had prepayments covering over 100% of related capex (Q2: 50–60%); over 90% of Q3 contract value carries a prepayment (up about 20 points); deferred revenue on the balance sheet is $9.4 billion (from $1.6 billion at end-2025); payback on 1–3 year deals is 19 months (Q2: 22 months); 2027 prepayments are expected at $17–$20 billion (2026: $10 billion). Customers are paying to fund the build-out.
The stock: Nov 11 close $154.69 → Nov 12 $128.64 (-16.84%) → Friday intraday about $117 (-8.92%, low $109), about -24% in two days; one month -37.01%; 52-week high $299.86.
NBIS continued: 2027 revenue guidance is about 4x — but the market is pricing capex
Revenue trajectory: 2024 $92 million → 2025 $530 million → 2026 guide about $3.0 billion (low end of the range; analysts expect $3.37 billion) → 2027 guide $12–$13 billion, about 4x 2026 (analysts expect $11.98 billion). Q3 was $981 million, +571% YoY, beating the expected $908 million.
Quarterly outlook (VJN estimates): Q3 2026 about $0.9B, Q4 about $1.5B; 2027 Q1 about $2.2B, Q2 about $2.7B, Q3 about $3.2B, Q4 about $4.0B; 2028 Q1 about $4.6B, Q2 $5.2B. Everything after Q3 2026 is an estimate (e), not actuals.
Why a big beat still fell: revenue and EPS both beat big, but guidance was cut, capex jumped, ARR was delayed, and $325 million of revenue was non-recurring — the market is pricing the speed of the cash burn, not the speed of revenue. Prepayments covering 100%+ of capex are a guardrail, not a guarantee.
Against CRWV: both are "revenue exploding, interest and capex exploding faster" AI infrastructure stories; CRWV's interest is 4x its operating profit, and NBIS's capex guide is about 50% above expectations. This week the market chose to sell first and ask later.
Anthropic IPO — the price range is out; the seven giants are putting in $26 billion
Price range: $70–$78 (S-1/A No. 2, Nov 10); about 825 million shares offered, raising $57.75–$64.35 billion; on shares outstanding the valuation is about $916 billion–$1.02 trillion, midpoint about $968 billion — about equal to the May Series H mark of $965 billion.
Fully diluted: at $78, up to about $1.404 trillion (TechCrunch) — a different yardstick from the $1.02 trillion on shares outstanding; both numbers are real.
The $26B concurrent placement (Class N non-voting shares, at the IPO price): Alphabet $10 billion, NVIDIA $10 billion, AMD $2.5 billion, Broadcom $1 billion, Micron $1 billion, Microsoft $1 billion, TSMC $0.5 billion — exactly $26.0 billion in total. All seven buyers are also Anthropic's chip and cloud suppliers.
Timing: pricing reportedly Nov 18, first trade Nov 19 — unconfirmed; the filing carries no date. The founders keep 50.1% voting control through a single Class F share; the lock-up releases in stages (some non-founder insiders can sell 10% on day one).
Anthropic results: Q3 revenue $16.96 billion, compute ate 58%
Q3 2026: revenue $16.956 billion, +1,127% YoY, +47% QoQ (Q2 was +144% — growth is slowing); compute and infrastructure cost $9.863 billion, 58% of revenue; GAAP operating loss $567 million; adjusted operating income $2.463 billion, a 15% margin.
The Sankey: revenue $17.0B — consumption-based $13.2B (78%, API and app token usage), subscription $3.7B (22%, Claude fixed-fee plans); customers over $100K: 11,900+ (+1,153% YoY), net revenue retention 900%. Operating expenses $17.5B: compute $9.9B (58%), personnel $1.7B (10%), sales and marketing $2.4B (14%), other $3.6B (21%); operating loss $0.6B (-3% margin).
GAAP net loss of $23.29 billion is mostly a $21.9 billion non-cash note revaluation — not cash burned. Nine-month revenue is $33.24 billion, net loss $104.04 billion. Long-term commitments are about $900.9 billion (about $70.7 billion due within a year); the annualized run-rate at Oct 31 is about $81 billion; net proceeds are $84.6–$93.7 billion (including the placement).

AMTC’s ManuTech Center set to open Dec. 14, 2026, with a 4:30 p.m. ribbon cutting

The Advanced Manufacturing Training Center consortium plans to open the ManuTech Prototyping Center on Dec. 14, 2026, with its ribbon cutting set for 4:30 p.m. The center is intended to give startups and small to medium-sized manufacturers in the Jackson region a route from an idea to a physical prototype in one afternoon. Rather than requiring those users to buy the equipment themselves, the facility is led by Lean Rocket Lab and is primarily aimed at businesses seeking a place to try ideas. Its proposed workflow links digital design and physical production for both products and electronic hardware, including the ability to reproduce an existing part in multiple materials and processes. The opening therefore centers on shared access to prototyping tools, while the planned one-afternoon turnaround describes the intended use for customers rather than a measured production result.

The public program, ManuTech LIVE Innovation Experience 2026, is scheduled to run at the AMTC from 3:30 to 6 p.m. on Monday, Dec. 14. The ribbon cutting falls within that event at 4:30 p.m., so the scheduled program includes the opening ceremony as well as other activities. Those activities are meant for manufacturers, technology companies, students, educators, community leaders and others interested in manufacturing technology and training. The event listing also identifies company demonstrations, while the wider AMTC site is slated to host demonstrations in its manual machining and welding labs and on multiple CNC machines. The program thus places the new center within a broader facility where visitors can see other kinds of manufacturing work, although the listed event hours do not describe how long each demonstration will last.

The center’s named equipment includes a handheld scanner for three-dimensional parts, a resin printer for larger formats, FDM printers and a workstation running SOLIDWORKS computer-aided design software. Together, these tools are presented as parts of a digital-to-physical process, beginning with the capture of an existing component and extending to making versions through different materials and methods. The equipment list describes scanning, design and additive-manufacturing capacity, but it does not specify output volumes or the time required for a particular job. The center also expects to add electronics capabilities in the near future, which means the announced hardware list is not necessarily the final one. No particular equipment or schedule for those additions is identified in the available announcement.

Lean Rocket Lab leads the center, and its Entrepreneur-in-Residence, Steve Tebbetts, is expected to guide users through product development. The announcement says Tebbetts brings experience from running a prototyping lab for a Michigan original-equipment manufacturer. That guidance is paired with access to equipment for startups and small to medium-sized manufacturers that want to test concepts without acquiring the tools themselves. The arrangement gives the center a stated role in both providing machinery and helping users move through product development, rather than describing access to equipment alone.

The AMTC operates through a partnership involving JAMA, the Shop Rat Foundation and Lean Rocket Lab, with the partners bringing apprenticeship training, youth STEM education and startup and small-business support into one facility. JAMA apprentices and Shop Rat Foundation students are expected to gain direct experience with scanning, design and additive-manufacturing tools at the center. The Shop Rat Foundation reaches more than 4,000 young people annually and describes ManuTech as another route toward technical careers. That figure refers to the foundation’s yearly reach, not to a stated number of students who will use the prototyping center or attend the opening. JAMA will provide information on its apprenticeship programs at ManuTech LIVE, and the foundation will present its youth STEM work.

JAMA executive director Olivia Steele said manufacturing workers need chances to learn and adjust as their work changes. Steele also said ManuTech LIVE can introduce people to career options and explain how apprenticeships fit into them. Shop Rat Foundation executive director Kelly Kofflin said bringing students, educators and industry together can help young people connect with advanced manufacturing careers. The two leaders’ comments frame the event’s training activities around both workers’ ability to adapt and young people’s exposure to career pathways.

Among the demonstrations, Detect-It is listed as showing AI-based vision technology used for inspection and defect detection, with a possible example involving CNC-produced parts. Jendamark is set to present its Odin Workstation, an AI-powered manufacturing execution system intended for assembly processes. Machine AI Solutions is expected to show technology connected with machine data and monitoring. These demonstrations cover inspection, assembly processes and machine monitoring, but the announcement does not establish that every demonstration will involve the center’s own equipment.

Other participating companies named for the event include Veriti, Tackboard, Strain Guard and Cerebion. Their listed offerings range from software that turns drawings into quotes and systems for maintenance tickets to protection for RV cables and cybersecurity for industrial settings. This range places the company presentations beyond prototype-making equipment, showing several kinds of products and services connected with manufacturing operations. The announcement names the participating firms and broad areas of their offerings, but it does not provide performance results or comparisons among them.

The center’s stated audience includes businesses that want to test ideas, while the event also extends to learners, educators, technology firms and community representatives. That combination reflects the AMTC partnership’s stated mix of business support, apprenticeships and youth STEM education rather than a facility described for only one group. For prospective users, the central offer is access to a digital-to-physical workflow and product-development guidance without purchasing the equipment independently. For students and apprentices, the announcement identifies hands-on exposure to specific tools and opportunities to learn about programs and careers, without giving a projected participation count. The opening date, event hours and equipment are specified, while the effects on users and the future scale of activity are not quantified in the announcement.

text:
The True History of BP: From Imperial Instrument to "Beyond Petroleum"

Beneath BP’s iconic green-and-yellow sunburst logo and clean "Beyond Petroleum" marketing facade lies a volatile century-long survival story defined by geopolitical coups, massive industrial disasters, and strategic reinvention.

Imperial Beginnings & The Iran Crisis (1914–1953): Originally created to secure fuel for the British Royal Navy under Winston Churchill, the company (then Anglo-Persian) faced an existential crisis when Iranian Prime Minister Mohammed Mosaddeq nationalized the country's oil in 1951. 

To restore Western access, US and UK intelligence orchestrated Operation Ajax, a 1953 coup that overthrew Mosaddeq. Shaken by the single-nation vulnerability, the company rebranded as British Petroleum and began hunting for global reserves.

The Hunt for Arctic & Offshore Reserves: Pushed out of the Middle East, BP pioneered high-risk frontiers—investing in brutal North Sea maritime drilling and partnering to unlock Prudhoe Bay, the largest oil field in North American history, via the Trans-Alaska Pipeline.

Corporate Raiders & Mega-Mergers (1980s–1990s): Threatened by Wall Street corporate raiders and full government privatization, oil giants executed defensive mega-mergers to become "too big to swallow". BP absorbed colossal competitors like Standard Oil of Ohio, Arco, and Amoco, creating a sprawling supermajor.

The Cost of Hyper-Scale (2010): Stretching global operations to the breaking point culminated in the tragic Deepwater Horizon blowout in the Gulf of Mexico, killing 11 workers, sparking the largest marine oil spill in U.S. history, and costing over $61 billion.

The Net-Zero Paradox: Following the 2022 Ukraine invasion, BP took a $24 billion write-off by exiting Russia. While public relations lean heavily into a net-zero transition, capital allocation reveals that traditional oil and gas upstream investments still pull in roughly $10 billion annually, as green alternatives offer lower profit margins.

text:
1/68 🚀 ANDHRA PRADESH CII INVESTMENT DRIVE 2026: ₹9.89 LAKH CRORE IN PROPOSED INVESTMENTS (SUMMIT + REGIONAL MEETS)! What worked, which firms signed, and what Tamil Nadu can pursue next. A 68-part evidence-based thread. 🇮🇳

2/68 📊 CLOSING TALLY: 109 summit MoUs worth ₹9,02,434 Cr; 2,00,358 potential jobs. Add 194 MoUs from October regional conferences (₹86,522 Cr; 1,47,951 jobs): 303 agreements, ₹9,88,957 Cr, 3,48,309 potential jobs. Since Jun 2024: ₹32.49 lakh Cr cumulative intent.

3/68 ⚠️ These are commitments, not capital already spent or jobs already created. Some reports cite ₹9.98 lakh Cr; the CM’s closing 303-MoU breakdown gives ₹9.89 lakh Cr including regional deals. Do NOT add these totals together.

4/68 🏆 WHY AP ATTRACTED INVESTORS — USP 1/6: CM Naidu, Minister Nara Lokesh and state agencies engaged investors directly, including global delegations. Visible senior leadership and follow-up can reduce uncertainty for firms considering long-term projects.

5/68 🧭 USP 2/6: AP’s sector-specific 2024–29 policies cover clean energy, data centres, electronics, semiconductors, drones, aerospace, EVs and more. Investors need predictable incentives, land terms, utilities and a realistic approval calendar.

6/68 🏗️ USP 3/6: LAND READINESS. APIIC publicly maps industrial plots and parks; NICDC highlighted Krishnapatnam, Orvakal and Kopparthy greenfield industrial nodes. Firms can compare sites before making an investment decision.

7/68 🚢 USP 4/6: PORTS + CORRIDORS. AP links a long coastline and maritime industry with road, rail and industrial-corridor plans. The proposed ~190-km Amaravati Outer Ring Road was tendered by NHAI in 4 HAM packages—not yet built.

8/68 🧩 USP 5/6: CLUSTER DESIGN. AP’s 25-sectoral-park vision ties locations to strengths: chips, rockets, drones, medtech, solar, apparel, toys, critical minerals and more. Supplier clustering matters more than scattered announcements.

9/68 ⏱️ USP 6/6: EXECUTION TRACKING. AP reports 526/714 previous projects 'converted' (~74%); 303 worth ₹7.1 lakh Cr grounded/grounding as of Oct 2026. It also proposed real-time clearances and investor-protection legislation. Converted ≠ commissioned.

10/68 📅 DAY 1 | 12 NOV: 73 MoUs + 15 government orders, ₹5,84,355 Cr in proposals and 1,07,693 potential jobs. Below are publicly identified companies and values; a complete, verified 73-MoU company ledger was not available.
11/68 🏭 DAY 1 — MANUFACTURING: Reliance Industries ₹2,73,000 Cr (East Godavari); Rashmi Metallurgical ₹18,500 Cr (Srikakulam); JSW Group ₹15,000 Cr (Kadapa). AP’s manufacturing subtotal: ₹3,57,386 Cr.

12/68 🔎 RELIANCE CAUTION: AP lists a ₹2.73 lakh Cr long-term proposal. Reuters reports ~₹43,000 Cr in initial phases, with the full scale dependent on feasibility, pilot trials and regulatory approvals. Don't treat the entire long-term amount as assured spending.

13/68 ⚡ DAY 1 — CLEAN ENERGY: Greenko Energies ₹45,000 Cr (multiple districts); CleanMax Enviro ₹41,000 Cr (multiple); Megha Engineering & Infrastructures ₹36,000 Cr (Krishna). Sector subtotal ₹1,65,020 Cr.

14/68 🚗 DAY 1 — AUTOS/EVs: Kia India ₹18,878 Cr (Penukonda, Sri Sathya Sai); Hero MotoCorp ₹1,457 Cr (Tirupati); MNL Solutions ₹750 Cr (Prakasam). Kia proposes capacity expansion of ~2 lakh cars/year.

15/68 🧪 DAY 1 — CHEMICALS: GAIL India ₹13,500 Cr (Srikakulam); N.A.N. Magnetech ₹3,000 Cr (Nellore); N.A.N. Silox Greenmet ₹1,800 Cr (Tirupati). Sector subtotal ₹19,995 Cr.

16/68 🌾 DAY 1 — FOOD: SLN Coffee ₹2,500 Cr (Nellore); Hindustan Coca-Cola Beverages ₹1,127 Cr (government order); Sree Vasudha Foods ₹400 Cr (Anantapur). Food-processing agreements/orders: ₹4,770 Cr.

17/68 🔬 DAY 1 — CHIPS: fabrIQ (Analog–MEIL joint venture) ₹4,300 Cr. A major opportunity for materials, electronics packaging, precision parts, cleanrooms, equipment suppliers and engineering graduates.

18/68 🚀 DAY 1 — DEFENCE/SPACE: Astrobase Space Technologies ₹800 Cr (Sri Sathya Sai); Vajrashakti Ventures ₹500 Cr (Nellore); Aditya Precitech ₹500 Cr (GO, missiles/loitering munitions/drones). Sector subtotal ₹3,406 Cr.

19/68 🧵 DAY 1 — OTHER SECTORS: Another ₹8,193 Cr was reported across textiles, pharma, logistics, circular economy, tourism, ports, shipbuilding, footwear and skills. The full company-wise breakdown needs AP’s official MoU register.

20/68 📅 DAY 2 | 13 NOV: Two publicised signing sessions—CM Naidu: ₹1,40,705 Cr in 11 MoUs (+ ₹880 Cr Hindalco expansion GO); Minister Lokesh: ₹1,05,634 Cr across 24 agreements. Avoid adding these to the closing tally twice.

21/68 🏢 DAY 2 — WITH CM NAIDU (1): AirTrunk India–JCK Infra ₹1,03,018 Cr (data centres/telecom capacity); JSW/Jindal manufacturing ₹15,000 Cr; Greenzone Renewable Energy ₹8,000 Cr; Indian Oil (IOCL) ₹6,600 Cr.

22/68 🚢 DAY 2 — WITH CM NAIDU (2): Kakinada Seaports ₹6,452 Cr; Dixon Technologies ₹700 Cr; Agnikul Cosmos ₹510 Cr; Hathor Rockets ₹250 Cr; EIH ₹175 Cr. The ₹880 Cr Hindalco expansion was a separate government order.

23/68 🤝 DAY 2 — SOCIAL PARTNERSHIPS: Hero MotoCorp proposed ₹32.8 Cr in student scholarships; ITC partnered to support 100 villages, including 15 model villages. CSR commitments should be reported separately from industrial capex.

24/68 💻 DAY 2 — WITH MINISTER LOKESH (1/5): Panchshil Realty ₹37,000 Cr (hyperscale data centre); AM AI Factory ₹31,387 Cr (integrated AI data centre); Waaree Energies ₹10,000 Cr; CleanMax Enviro ₹8,000 Cr.

25/68 🛰️ DAY 2 — LOKESH (2/5): Kaynes Technology ₹3,145 Cr; Archean Group ₹2,000 Cr; KIMS Hospitals ₹1,500 Cr; Yodha Healthcare ₹1,359 Cr; Cyient DLM + Hindustan Shipyard ₹1,000 Cr.

26/68 🏟️ DAY 2 — LOKESH (3/5): SMAX Digitech ₹4,270 Cr (AP Sports Village) + ₹1,500 Cr (district sports clubs/arenas) = ₹5,770 Cr; Sub State Manufacturing ₹931 Cr; SALVO Industries ₹800 Cr.

27/68 🚀 DAY 2 — LOKESH (4/5): EPACK Data Centre Solutions ₹570 Cr; Bellatrix Aerospace ₹550 Cr; IG Defence ₹500 Cr; AIL Dixon Technologies ₹450 Cr; PVS Rammohan Healthcare ₹312 Cr.

28/68 🛠️ DAY 2 — LOKESH (5/5): Infinity ₹250 Cr; Samudra Surya LLC ₹100 Cr; Office Space Solutions ₹10 Cr. Also: HORIBA (training), UNEP (climate-responsive urban planning) and Pawan Hans (heliports)—no capex value specified.

29/68 📌 REPORTING NOTE: 'JSW Group ₹15,000 Cr' appears in Day 1 coverage and a ₹15,000 Cr JSW/Jindal item in Day 2 coverage. These announcements need deal-ID reconciliation; do not assume they are two separate ₹15,000 Cr investments.

30/68 🏗️ SEPARATE ANNOUNCEMENT: Saint-Gobain discussed a new float-glass plant at Atchutapuram, Anakapalli. Reports refer to approximately ₹1,750–2,000 Cr. It also has fresh TN plans—proof that multi-state additive expansion is possible.

31/68 🗺️ AP’S 25 SECTORAL PARKS (slide provided): These are sector/location proposals, NOT 25 completed parks. Named areas include the following 11 districts. Tamil Nadu can publish a comparable sector-by-district investment map.

32/68 🔹 Srikakulam: chemicals. Visakhapatnam: MedTech (AMTZ). Anakapalli: steel downstream, organic food, rare earths/critical minerals, AI data centres; Nakkapalli: toys and bulk drugs. Total here: 8 proposed/identified park themes.

33/68 🔹 Kakinada: oil & gas manufacturing. Palnadu: mega textile + quantum computing. Kurnool: Drone City. Prakasam: solar PV manufacturing. These districts combine energy, industrial inputs and next-generation technologies.

34/68 🔹 SPSR Nellore: petrochemicals, ammunition, furniture and sports goods. Tirupati: construction equipment, semiconductors, Space City, electronics manufacturing and Korean-industry cluster. Strong industry diversification.

35/68 🔹 Sri Sathya Sai: robotics/advanced technology and aerospace/defence. Annamayya (Madanapalle): horticulture hub. These complete the 25 thematic park locations shown in the AP summit slide.

36/68 🏛️ AP NOW HAS 28 DISTRICTS (including Markapuram and Polavaram). Here is a broader district-by-district sector snapshot—existing strengths, signed proposals or potential. Not every entry is a formally approved new park.

37/68 1–5: Alluri Sitharama Raju—coffee; Anakapalli—steel/chemicals/medtech supply; Anantapuramu—agro-processing; Annamayya—horticulture/tamarind; Bapatla—chillies, food processing.

39/68 11–15: Kakinada—port/oil & gas/seafood; Krishna—renewables, fish/shrimp; Kurnool—drones/Orvakal/pulses; Markapuram—granite/minerals (potential); Nandyal—millets/mineral processing.

40/68 16–20: NTR—Vijayawada logistics/services; Palnadu—textiles/quantum/pulses; Parvathipuram Manyam—forest produce; Polavaram—forest/agri-value chains (potential); Prakasam—solar PV, engineering.

41/68 21–25: SPSR Nellore—petrochemicals/defence/furniture; Sri Sathya Sai—autos/robotics/aerospace; Srikakulam—chemicals/metals; Tirupati—electronics/chips/space; Visakhapatnam—medtech/data centres/ports.

42/68 26–28: Vizianagaram—millets/food processing; West Godavari—aquaculture/seafood; YSR Kadapa—steel/minerals. Every AP district needs linked suppliers, logistics, skilling and published implementation milestones.

43/68 🧱 AP PIPELINE, NOT COMPLETED WORK: Six BHAVYA park proposals include Kurnool Drone City, Tirupati Space City, Sri Sathya Sai A&D, Anakapalli organic-food, Prakasam renewable manufacturing and Palnadu textiles.

text:
Behind the polished presentation of Google’s new "Intelligent Eyewear," there is a high-stakes corporate drama playing out between engineers, privacy advocates, and market strategists.

The Google Strategists and Product Leads are likely feeling a heavy burden of historical baggage. Having burned significant goodwill with the original Google Glass over a decade ago, they are navigating a narrow corridor of public trust. Behind closed doors, their primary tension is likely a push-pull between wanting the device to be a "must-have" AI assistant and the desperate need to avoid the "Glasshole" label again. They are calculating that they cannot beat Meta by copying them; they must instead position themselves as the "responsible" alternative—hence the hyper-fixation on privacy indicators and strict data-processing limits. They are likely sweating the technical difficulty of keeping the device light while delivering enough compute to make Gemini actually feel useful.

The Engineers and Designers face the brutal reality of physics. Their constraint is the thermal and power envelope of a device that must be light enough to wear all day. They are likely feeling the tension of feature creep—the marketing team wants the glasses to do everything a phone can do, while the engineering reality is that they are essentially an audio-first peripheral that relies heavily on a connected smartphone. Their internal conversations likely revolve around the nightmare of battery management and the struggle to keep Gemini’s response latency low without needing massive onboard power.

The Legal and Privacy Teams are perhaps the most anxious group. They are likely operating under the assumption that every single privacy feature they build—no matter how robust—will be stress-tested by regulators, hackers, and concerned citizens immediately upon launch. Their mandate is likely to bake in "anti-tamper" measures, not just for security, but to show regulators they are proactively preventing the secret recording scandals that have plagued competitors. They are constantly navigating the contradiction of creating a device that observes the world for you while insisting that it isn't "spying" on the world.

The Partners (Warby Parker and Gentle Monster) are likely balancing enthusiasm with extreme caution. They are incentivized by the potential to modernize their retail footprint and offer a "high-tech" accessory, but they have a brand identity to protect. They are likely pushing Google to ensure the hardware doesn't look like a sci-fi prop, worried that if the device is perceived as socially unacceptable, it will hurt their core reputation as fashion-forward eyewear retailers. https://t.co/r5CtwKEQsF

text:
Hype about Gemini, Google DeepMind’s long-rumored response to OpenAI’s GPT-4, has been building for months. Today the company finally revealed what it has been working on in secret all this time. Was the hype justified? Yes—and no. 

Gemini is Google’s biggest AI launch yet—its push to take on competitors OpenAI and Microsoft in the race for AI supremacy. There is no doubt that the model is pitched as best-in-class across a wide range of capabilities—an “everything machine,” as one observer puts it. 

“The model is innately more capable,” Sundar Pichai, the CEO of Google and its parent company Alphabet, told MIT Technology Review. “It’s a platform. AI is a profound platform shift, bigger than web or mobile. And so it represents a big step for us.” 

It’s a big step for Google, but not necessarily a giant leap for the field as a whole. Google DeepMind claims that Gemini outmatches GPT-4 on 30 out of 32 standard measures of performance. And yet the margins between them are thin. What Google DeepMind has done is pull AI’s best current capabilities into one powerful package. To judge from demos, it does many things very well—but few things that we haven’t seen before. For all the buzz about the next big thing, Gemini could be a sign that we’ve reached peak AI hype. At least for now. 

Chirag Shah, a professor at the University of Washington who specializes in online search, compares the launch to Apple’s introduction of a new iPhone every year. “Maybe we just have risen to a different threshold now, where this doesn’t impress us as much because we’ve just seen so much,” he says. 

Like GPT-4, Gemini is multimodal, meaning it is trained to handle multiple kinds of input: text, images, audio. It can combine these different formats to answer questions about everything from household chores to college math to economics. 

In a demo for journalists yesterday, Google showed Gemini’s ability to take an existing screenshot of a chart, analyze hundreds of pages of research with new data, and then update the chart with that new information. In another example, Gemini is shown pictures of an omelet cooking in a pan and asked (using speech, not text) if the omelet is cooked yet. “It’s not ready because the eggs are still runny,” it replies. 

Most people will have to wait for the full experience, however. The version launched today is a back end to Bard, Google’s text-based search chatbot, which the company says will give it more advanced reasoning, planning, and understanding capabilities. Gemini’s full release will be staggered over the coming months. The new Gemini-boosted Bard will initially be available in English in more than 170 countries, not including the EU and the UK. This is to let the company “engage” with local regulators, says Sissie Hsiao, a Google vice president in charge of Bard. 

Gemini also comes in three sizes: Ultra, Pro and Nano. Ultra is the full-powered version; Pro and Nano are tailored to applications that run with more limited computing resources. Nano is designed to run on devices, such as Google’s new Pixel phones. Developers and businesses will be able to access Gemini Pro starting December 13. Gemini Ultra, the most powerful model, will be available “early next year” following “extensive trust and safety checks,” Google executives told reporters on a press call. 

“I think of it as the Gemini era of models,” Pichai told us. “This is how Google DeepMind is going to build and make progress on AI. So it will always represent the frontier of where we are making progress on AI technology.”

Bigger, better, faster, stronger? 

OpenAI’s most powerful model, GPT-4, is seen as the industry’s gold standard. While Google boasted that Gemini outperforms OpenAI’s previous model, GPT 3.5, company executives dodged questions about how far the model exceeds GPT-4. 

But the firm highlights one benchmark in particular, called MMLU (massive multitask language understanding). This is a set of tests designed to measure the performance of models on tasks involving text and images, including reading comprehension, college math, and multiple-choice quizzes in physics, economics, and social sciences. On the text-only questions, Gemini scores 90% and human experts score approximately 89%, says Pichai. GPT-4 scores 86% on these types of questions. On the multimodal questions, Gemini scores 59%, while GPT-4 scores 57%. “It’s the first model to cross that threshold,” Pichai says. 

Gemini’s performance against benchmark data sets is very impressive, says Melanie Mitchell, an artificial-intelligence researcher at the Santa Fe Institute in New Mexico.

“It’s clear that Gemini is a very sophisticated AI system,” says Mitchell. But “it’s not obvious to me that Gemini is actually substantially more capable than GPT-4,” she adds.

While the model has good benchmark scores, it is hard to know how to interpret these numbers given that we don’t know what’s in the training data, says Percy Liang, director of Stanford’s Center for Research on Foundation Models. 

Mitchell also notes that Gemini performs much better on language and code benchmarks than on images and video. “Multimodal foundation models still have a ways to go to be generally and robustly useful for many tasks,” she says. 

Using feedback from human testers, Google DeepMind has trained Gemini to be more factually accurate, to give attribution when asked to, and to hedge rather than spit out nonsense when faced with a question it cannot answer. The company claims that this mitigates the problem of hallucinations. But without a radical overhaul of the base technology, large language models will continue to make things up. 

Experts say it’s unclear whether the benchmarks Google is using to measure Gemini’s performance offer that much insight, and without transparency, it’s hard to check Google’s claims. 

“Google is advertising Gemini as an everything machine—a general-purpose model that can be used in many different ways,” says Emily Bender, a professor of computational linguistics at the University of Washington. But the company is using narrow benchmarks to evaluate models that it expects to be used for these diverse purposes. “This means it effectively can’t be thoroughly evaluated,” she says.  

Ultimately, for the average user, the incremental improvement over competing models might not make much difference, says Shah. “It’s more about convenience, brand recognition, existing integration, than people really thinking ‘Oh, this is better,’” he says. 

A long, slow buildup 

Gemini has been a long time coming. In April 2023, Google announced it was merging its AI research unit Google Brain with DeepMind, Alphabet’s London-based AI research lab. So Google has had all year to develop its answer to OpenAI’s most advanced large language model, GPT-4, which debuted in March and is the backbone of the paid version of ChatGPT.

Google has been under intense pressure to show investors it can match and overtake competitors in AI. Although the company has been developing and using powerful AI models for years, it has been hesitant to launch tools that the public can play with for fears of reputational damage and safety concerns. 

“Google has been very cautious about releasing this stuff to the public,” Geoffrey Hinton told MIT Technology Review in April when he left the company. “There are too many bad things that could happen, and Google didn’t want to ruin its reputation.” Faced with tech that seemed untrustworthy or unmarketable, Google played it safe—until the greater risk became missing out.

Google has learned the hard way how launching flawed products can backfire. When it unveiled its ChatGPT competitor Bard in February, scientists soon noticed a factual error in the company’s own advertisement for the chatbot, an incident that subsequently wiped $100 billion off its share price. 

In May, Google announced it was rolling out generative AI into most of its products, from email to productivity software. But the results failed to impress critics: the chatbot made references to emails that didn’t exist, for example.  

This is a consistent problem with large language models. Although excellent at generating text that sounds like something a human could have written, generative AI systems regularly make things up. And that’s not the only problem with them. They are also easy to hack, and riddled with biases. Using them is also highly polluting. 

Google has solved neither these problems nor the hallucination issue. Its solution to the latter problem is a tool that lets people use Google search to double-check the chatbot’s answers, but that relies on the accuracy of the online search results themselves. 

Gemini may be the pinnacle of this wave of generative AI. But it’s not clear where AI built on large language models goes next. Some researchers believe this could be a plateau rather than the foot of the next peak. 

Pichai is undeterred. “Looking ahead, we do see a lot of headroom,” he says. “I think multimodality will be big. As we teach these models to reason more, there will be bigger and bigger breakthroughs. Deeper breakthroughs are to come yet. 

“When I take in the totality of it, I genuinely feel like we are at the very beginning.”

Mat Honan contributed reporting.

text:
VIRGIN GALACTIC $SPCE — THE SPACE TOURISM OPPORTUNITY IS INTERESTING, BUT THE BIGGEST RISK IS STILL GETTING TO COMMERCIAL SCALE WITHOUT DESTROYING SHAREHOLDER VALUE.
I've been reviewing Virgin Galactic's Q3 earnings call, and what stood out wasn't the earnings beat. It was the tension between management's ambitious commercial flight plans and the additional capital required to deliver them.
The arrival of its first Delta-class spaceship at Spaceport America is an important milestone. But software and hardware integration delays have pushed commercial service into 2027, reminding investors how difficult it is to turn aerospace engineering into a reliable operating business.
I find the long-term economics interesting. Higher flight frequency, premium ticket pricing and a largely fixed operating cost base could create meaningful operating leverage once the fleet reaches scale.
The proposed launch hangar could improve capacity further, while potential government and defence applications offer another avenue for growth.
But these opportunities remain largely unproven commercially.
MY TAKE
I'm interested in the business model, particularly the potential for higher revenue per flight as Virgin Galactic works through older reservations and introduces newer, higher-priced bookings.
However, the newly announced equity offering introduces significant dilution risk, while continued cash burn leaves little room for further execution delays.
Management expects positive free cash flow in 2028, but that depends on successful flight testing, a reliable commercial launch cadence and sufficient customer demand.
For me, this remains a highly speculative investment rather than an established space economy compounder.
WHAT MATTERS NEXT
Can $SPCE turn its Delta-class fleet into a consistently operating, cash-generating business before additional financing and execution risks overwhelm the potential returns for existing shareholders?
That's the real investment question.

text:
ARTICLE: The Making and Unmaking of the Orange Oval One — Random Ruminations on the Highest Office in the Home of the Brave n’ Land of the Free, by @gjmaybury || #PoxAmerikana250 || 1776-2026

'The great of this world are often blamed for not doing what they could have done; they can reply, just think of all the evil we could have done, but did not do.'  — Georg Christoph Lichtenberg.
- - - - - - - - - - - - -

— A MAGA™️ Nod is as Good as a MAGA™️ Wink (To A Blind Republic)

With the dust now settling on last week’s mid-term election train wreck—and after some post poll musing on the main reasons for the result—it perhaps behooves us all to think a bit more broadly about the role of the bloke Gore Vidal referred to (not always affectionately mind you) as the “Oval One”. 

What follows represents FWIW a compilation of sorts of such musings by your humble, some from my personal 'memory hole' but with a few more recent reflections to get the party warmed up (as it were).

Let there be little doubt at the outset that the tenure of the incumbent alone offers rich pickings for exploring this institution, as I believe my article from earlier this year amply attests. (👀🧵👇) For whatever we might say about MAGAMan™️, he's forever changed the way any of us might think about this once purportedly hallowed political office. 

If (as I posit in this article) it’s becoming increasingly clear Donald Trump’s much vaunted MAGA™️ project is collapsing faster than the Twin Towers on 9/11, then so too might we say same about the Republic itself. The only real debate here is to what extent he and his misfit administration—the political analog of the Keystone Kops—will be held accountable for its decline and fall, said descent into the abyss of imperial history being one which now seems all but irreversible. 

It is especially notable—indeed can't be emphasised too much—that all this is taking place in the year of the 250th anniversary of the fabled Republic. The following commemorative commentary should be viewed then in that light. Cue then oodles of irony.
- - - - - - - - - - - - -
Generally at his most mischievous when commenting on the presidency, the aforesaid Gore Vidal once famously quipped that ‘any American who is prepared to run for president should automatically, by definition, be disqualified from ever doing so.’ 

Riffing on a similar theme, author Douglas Adams said, ‘anyone who is capable of getting themselves made President should on no account be allowed to do the job.’ As pithy and droll as these maxims are, even more so now they are a pointer to the reality of the modern presidency, and to be sure anyone who aspires to the role. 

If we allow ourselves to ponder it, they further provide us some insight into how much the institution of the presidency has changed, and (perhaps paradoxically), how much it's remained the same. Let's recall here that age-old adage, ‘The more things change, the more they stay the same’. The election result notwithstanding, methinks we’re about to witness the essence of this adage manifest itself in spades, more so than ever before. 

(As of this writing, said "writing" is already on the wall, with the now still-born impeachment gambit by Rep. Thomas Massie against the US Secretary for War Crimes the estimable Pete Hegseth being but one pointer in this direction.)

Quite apart from the power, authority and prestige—perceived or real—the position nominally bestows upon the incumbent, such is the inflated mystique, aura, and reverence attached to, or invested in, the institution, that few other countries come close to matching it. 

It is sadly though a shadow of its former self, a state of play for which many will blame Mister Trump. However the reality is that the tarnished reputation and sadly diminished prestige of the office has many fathers. In other words it's been a work in progress for some time. 

To underscore this, the following might be worth considering.

Most folks might imagine there's a world of difference between POTUS 44 (Barack Obama aka the "Great Black n' White Hope") and POTUS 45/47. Yet the cause of Mister Trump’s recent thumping in the mid-terms and his now decidedly "lame duck" status can be summed up in a few words: he over promised and under delivered. Sound familiar?

Indeed, with the possible exception of the present "Oval One", few of his predecessors have promised so much and delivered so little. By any measure, a big call to be sure. Put another way: It was Obama's legacy which proved to be Mister Trump's biggest political drawcard. Not unlike George Bush Jr.'s legacy then, one that in turn served Obama's tilt at the office so well back in the day. (To be ‘fair’ to "Dubya", he under promised and over delivered; though suffice to say, not always in a good way!)

All up then, the Grand American Narrative is rarely short on (grand) irony, all too often of the recurring kind. I trust the preceding gives readers something of a flavour of that irony.
- - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
It’s a given then that any one purporting to deliver insights into the "Narrative" cannot do so without recurring reference to the respective tenants of 1600 Pennsylvania Ave. To be sure much ink is spilt, airtime devoted [to], and bandwidth consumed [in] the preoccupation with analysing and assessing the commanders-in-chief during and well after their time in office.

Often accompanying such ‘presidential performance appraisals', are similar musings on and about the institution itself. Perhaps no more so has this reality been apparent than with the incumbent, a man we might dub a “human headline magnet”. Those still unsure of this will I believe have any such doubts dispelled over the remaining two years* of his tenure, the very nature of his time in office thus far providing enough evidence to underscore the above. (*Assuming of course that he lasts the distance.)

Moreover, all this extends also to those aspiring to the office. This last point should not be lost on those who think that out there somewhere in the Home of the Brave is the long awaited, much anticipated political redeemer who will rescue the Republic from rack n’ ruination, and that it’s only a matter of time before that individual appears to declare themselves the one and only person who can, well, dare I say it?, “Make America Great Again”. 

We can actually hear them queueing up 'outside the door' now that The Donald—a man of whom it may now be said exceeded by a country mile (and then some) all the expectations of those of us who didn’t buy any of his MAGA™️🐂💩from the get go—is on his way out the door, perhaps as noted, sooner rather than later than the balance of his tenure suggests. He is as I've earlier hinted at, a l'ame Duck a l’Orange Man POTUS. (Sorry!)

= = = = = = = = = =
— Giving Peace a Fighting Chance – From the Archives

Although it may not have been widely recognised at the time, in June 1963, just a few months shy of his Farewell Tour, president John F Kennedy (JFK) in his American University Commencement Address delivered what is arguably the most significant oration of his short-lived, ill-fated tenure as commander-in-chief. In fact, it may well have been the most pivotal in American foreign policy in that era, and it’s perhaps never been more pertinent to the times. 

Forget the unforgettable ‘[the] torch has been passed to a new generation….ask not what your country can do for you’ schtick; never mind the indelible 'we choose to go to the moon because it is hard’…spiel!

The following gives us an idea of what was on JFK’s mind: ‘I have….chosen this time and place to discuss a topic on which ignorance too often abounds and the truth too rarely perceived. And that’s the most important topic on earth: peace. What kind of peace do I mean and what kind of a peace do we seek? Not a Pax Americana enforced on the world by American weapons of war….Not the peace of the grave or the security of the slave. I am talking about genuine peace, the kind….that enables men and nations to grow, and to hope, and build a better life for their children – not merely peace for Americans but peace for all, not merely peace in our time but….in all time.’

In this address, it seemed Kennedy was attempting to re-define the accepted notion of Pax Americana to articulate a more inclusive, collaborative version, one that would bring folk with them willingly rather than dragging them kicking and screaming to the position. 

In almost all respects this wasn’t just a redefinition; he was attempting to turn the notion on its head. ‘Peaceful co-existence’ was decidedly the sub-text of his message. It appeared the baptism of fire he experienced in his on-the-job training as president thus far had changed him significantly, the disastrous regime change gambit that was the 1961 Bay of Pigs invasion of Cuba being the most notable example.

But as author James Douglass has observed, when Kennedy uttered these words,‘the priests of our national security state saw him as a heretic.’ He’d already pissed quite a few of them off when he baulked at allowing them to requite their apocalyptic urges by nuking Cuba and the Soviet Union (USSR) back into the Neolithic during the high drama of the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, instead stubbornly persevering with back channel diplomacy to firstly defuse then ultimately resolve the crisis.

Put simply, the hawks weren’t happy with this out-of-the-blue ‘DIY’ foreign policy initiative, especially coming from a president many had already decided wasn’t cut out for the Biggest Game in Washingtown. 

From the Brass Asses in the Pentagon bunkers then to the winkle-pickered wolf-pack down on the Langley Farm and on to the pointy-headed foreign policy and national security wonks in the Beltway think-tanks and in the hallowed hallways of Ivy League academe (and perhaps even a few within his own administration), doubtless this speech would have come across as touchy-feely, appeasement-sounding—indeed naïve, unadulterated—nonsense. This was "not in the brochure" as they say, and quite a few would’ve been spitting hollow points at the wall.

For those who were looking then, this ostensibly represented a road to Damascus-like conversion from unreconstructed 1950’s era McCarthyite-Lite Cold Warrior to a self-styled global Grand Pax proselyte. Herein JFK seemed keen to embrace the rather novel notion of a Pax Americana on the premise that—notwithstanding the fact they were Godless, soul deprived Commies bent on oppression, tyranny and world domination—their Cold War adversaries the Soviets comprised folk with the same aspirations and collective desires as Americans. Kind of a "the Russians love their children too" thing.

As such, a ‘pax’—even one comprising the ostensibly universally attractive, noble ideals of freedom, liberty, democracy, rule of law and basic human rights—all predicated by “American weapons of war” was not something as president he saw as desirable, much less one that would or could work in the long run. 

Instinctively, he seemed to realise that a peace imposed from on high was always going to be a phoney peace (a ‘faux pax’ as it were; again, sorry). Certainly not one compatible with what America ostensibly stood for, or that its founders presumably had in mind back in the day. Clearly, JFK's address gives us key—though not necessarily conclusive—insights into where he might have taken the US in its foreign policy in general, and in its fraught relationship with the USSR in particular. 

Of course it was this relationship—defined by the Cold War—whose apocalyptic possibilities during the CMC as noted became uncomfortably probable as far as the president was concerned. The "Cold War" for the record being no less than the dominant geopolitical dynamic for almost half a century, the battle against which consumed a great deal of the Republic’s blood, treasure and international prestige (Vietnam anyone?).

At all events, by most accounts the AU address even made the Soviets (themselves as equally unnerved by the CMC standoff), sit up and take notice—in particular JFK's notional nemesis at the time, USSR General Secretary, Nikita Khrushchev. ‘You have our full and undivided attention Mr President’ appeared to be the general vibe from the then 'gremlins in the Kremlin'. 

Even Cuban president Fidel Castro—whom folks within JFK’s own administration had spent no small amount of time, ingenuity and effort trying to assassinate with all manner of cockamamie CIA-inspired "Spy v Spy" plots and schemes—was reportedly impressed!

In this address, JFK appeared implicitly to refute the conventional notion that leadership greatness is synonymous with being a wartime POTUS, along with seemingly rejecting—at least questioning—the prevailing Manichean (i.e. “we’re the good guys and you’re not”) worldview characteristic of the Cold War mindset.

Throughout his tragically truncated presidency then—if not throughout his pre-White House years, and unlike most post-War presidents before and especially after him—JFK become more and more conflicted about conventional notions of war and peace, America’s place in the world, and in particular, its relationship with its former wartime ally the Soviets, and what implications that relationship might have for both countries and the ROW.

However—and this is a big “however”, possibly the Narrative’s biggest—unbeknown to him and almost all of his most trusted advisors and confidantes at that point, Kennedy’s days were numbered. Certain forces had their own ideas of Pax Americana, and as history tells us were determined for their own reasons to forcefully deny the president the opportunity to put ‘meat on the bone’ of the Grand Pax he envisioned and then articulated at AU. (For the record, none of these disparate forces would be found residing inside the Soviet bloc.)

For the uninitiated, a short detour might be helpful here. The concept of "Pax Americana" is largely derived from similar abstractions integral to the understanding of, and insightful discourse on, the history and psychopathology of empires from Rome (Pax Romana) to the UK (Pax Britannica). 

Pax Americana—or Romana, Britannica et. al.—referenced halcyon-like periods of relative peace achieved by these respective empires as a result of their hegemony throughout their existence. Although clearly derived from these earlier historical versions, for its part, the American iteration is in many ways unique, and it has changed somewhat since the phrase was first used.

In modern parlance then, Pax Americana became a shorthand for the rise of US dominance in global affairs after World War Two—especially that which derived from their geopolitical influence, their economic power, and their military dominion (underscored by their nuclear monopoly at the time, which unbeknown to them, was short-lived).

Thus ‘pax’ in whatever way it manifested itself previously was more a peace as a by-product of empire, possibly ‘achieved’ by accident or default, or imposed via hegemonic artifice by the empire du jour. In so many ways, in its more modern iteration, it’s not all that much different; as might be expected though, in the case of the US, there are some unique takes on the ‘pax’.

And given the character and personality of the tenant who's been occupying the Office the best part of the past two years or so, perhaps this reality has never more so obvious than in the here and now. 

To complete our short tour of the Narrative then, it is to the estimable Mark Twain we should look to for the last word. Methinks it will resonate loudly in the here and now (when most would argue it is most sorely needed) with the majority of those Americans HL Mencken referred to as "the plain folks of the land". 

‘Statesmen will invent cheap lies, putting blame upon the nation that is attacked, and every man will be glad of those conscience-soothing falsities, and will diligently study them, and refuse to examine any refutations of them; and thus he will by and by convince himself that the war is just, and will thank God for the better sleep he enjoys after this process of grotesque self-deception.’ *

(*From: Chronicles of Young Satan.) — GM

text:
Birthing of A Nation
Faith • Family • Freedom

DAILY SCRIPTURE
Saturday, November 14, 2026

THE HAND THAT LIFTS YOU

Psalm 34:18 (NLT)

“The LORD is close to the brokenhearted; he rescues those whose spirits are crushed.”

Have you ever reached a place in life where you felt you couldn’t take another step?

Maybe it was the loss of someone you loved, a marriage struggling to survive, financial burdens, betrayal, or simply carrying so much pain that nobody around you understood.

Sometimes the hardest battles are the ones nobody sees.

But today’s Scripture gives us a beautiful promise: God does not abandon the brokenhearted. He draws near to them.

Think about the woman who came to Jesus weeping, washing His feet with her tears. Others saw her past and judged her, but Jesus saw a heart reaching for mercy.

Where others saw a sinner, Jesus saw someone who needed forgiveness, restoration, and love.

He didn’t push her away. He welcomed her repentance and told her that her faith had saved her.

That’s the heart of Jesus Christ.

Perhaps you’ve been carrying something for years. You’ve learned how to smile in public while quietly falling apart behind closed doors.

You tell everyone you’re fine, but deep inside you’re exhausted.

Jesus sees beyond the smile. He sees the broken heart.

Imagine a father sitting alone in his truck after another difficult day. The bills are piling up, his family is struggling, and he doesn’t know what tomorrow will bring. Before walking into his house, he bows his head and whispers, “Lord, I can’t do this anymore. I need You.”

Nothing outside that truck may change immediately. The bills are still there. The problems haven’t disappeared.

But something changes when we surrender our burdens to Jesus. We discover we don’t have to carry them alone.

Jesus never promised a life without storms. But He promised His presence, and His grace is sufficient for us.

And sometimes God uses ordinary people to remind others that He hasn’t forgotten them.

A phone call. A visit. A helping hand. A prayer with someone who has lost hope.

You may be the encouragement someone has been praying for.

Don’t allow your own struggles to make you forget that Jesus is still near.

The same Saviour who went to the cross for our sins is able to restore our hearts, renew our strength, and lead us forward.

🎯 TODAY’S MISSION

Reach out to someone who may be struggling today. Don’t just ask how they’re doing—take time to listen. Offer encouragement, pray with them, or help carry a burden. And if you’re the one hurting, bring your heart honestly before Jesus.

🙏 PRAYER

Lord Jesus, thank You for being close to the brokenhearted. You know every silent tear and every burden we carry. Heal our hearts, renew our strength, and help us trust You even when we cannot see the way forward. Use us to bring Your compassion to someone today. In Jesus’ mighty name, Amen.

#DailyScripture #BirthingOfANation #FaithFamilyFreedom #JesusChrist #Psalm34 #HopeInJesus #Brokenhearted #GodIsNear #Healing #PowerOfPrayer #ChristianEncouragement #LoveOneAnother

text:
A Mother of 14 On How to Solve the Fertility Crisis
Last night, I had the pleasure of hearing tenured economics professor and mother of fourteen Catherine Pakaluk speak at the University of Virginia on "Faith, Fertility and the Future of Family."

I do my best to write about the causes and solutions to the birthrate crisis but ultimately, we need models of success. And there is no one better to help us understand high-functioning pronatalism - one that recognizes our values of education and success - than the Harvard-educated speaker and author Dr. Pakaluk.

Here are some highlights from her talk:

The Old World is Gone
There was a time when having children was the natural and largely inevitable result of coupling up. When men and women got romantically involved, one could expect at least a few children as a byproduct. Kids came and people had to figure things out.

The revolution has been gradual. There were rubber condoms in the 1800s, but they weren't very good. Latex condoms were invented in the 1920s and were much better. And on and on.

We've reached the point where children have to make their case and each child has to justify their own existence. And the math just isn't adding up.

So many costs
Pakaluk lists the huge costs of parenthood:
· Time
· Money
· Sleep
· Plans
· Status
· Accomplishments
· Freedom
· Hobbies
· Life
No wonder fertility is at all-time lows.

What can overcome all the costs?
Children need to offer a very high value proposition to meet all those costs.

This is why the religious are almost the only ones not experiencing a collapse in birthrates. They tend to have a worldview that values children profoundly.

Pakaluk, who interviewed successful mothers of many for her book Hannah's Children, uses quotes from those mothers to describe a particular outlook where children have extraordinary value, a value so high that all costs are overcome.
· “A child is the most worthwhile thing you can do”
· “Children are blessings from God”
· “Children are a unique gift, a light in the world”
· “Children are life’s greatest joy”
· “The salvation of the world is the birth of a child”

The Best Pronatal Policies?
Pakaluk is skeptical that common pronatal policies like cash incentives and tax relief will persuade people to have children. (Perhaps a bit too skeptical?)

What does she suggest? Religious liberty as family policy. School vouchers as a way to let people educate children according to their values. "Cultivate a world where Hannahs and their communities thrive." (Hannah = A reference to one of the bible's greatest stories.)

More pointers
· You can cultivate a desire for children. That is a value that can be taught and learned.
· Marriage should be a foundation, not a capstone.
· Plan your career around children, not children around your career.
· Pakaluk seems to have it all, but it didn't happen all at the same time. She began her tenure-track journey at 40, after many years of motherhood.

The greatest white pill
Demography can feel extraordinarily grim. Some of the greatest nations in the world are rapidly fading, and we confront the deep-down fear that civilization itself is dying.

But here is an antidote and it works completely.

Pakaluk is not only succeeding in this generation. Her children, highly educated and successful in the world, have given her around 35 grandchildren so far and there seem to be a whole lot more in the future. She's still so young!

The shift to the kinds of values embodied in those quotes is profound. But there are pockets of people who are making the shift, and it is really working! They will carry the world forward.

Amid our demographic winter, there are quiet flashes of spring, and the sight is incredible!

🚨 NVIDIA'S ₹47 LAKH CRORE AI LOAN MACHINE, EXPLAINED (1/3)

Everyone's yelling "AI bubble". Here's what's actually going on, with real numbers. Chai ready? ☕

🛺 THE RICKSHAW STORY
A rickshaw maker's customers have no cash. So he tells the bank: "Lend to my drivers. If one defaults, I'll cover part of your loss."

Bank lends → driver buys rickshaw → maker books a sale → driver repays from daily fares.

Works great… as long as fares keep coming.

Swap the names:
Rickshaw = AI chips (GPUs)
Maker = Nvidia
Drivers = AI firms like OpenAI
Bank = Wall Street
Fares = what people pay to use AI

🏭 WHY LOANS AT ALL?
AI runs in giant warehouses called data centres. One costs lakhs of crores. Big Tech alone is set to spend $730B+ this year, and even that isn't enough.

💰 THE $500B PLAN
Aug 2026: Nvidia signed MoUs with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR.

Aim: $500B (~₹47 lakh cr), mostly loans, with the chips as collateral. Nvidia offered to backstop up to 25% = up to $125B (~₹11.8 lakh cr).

⚠️ An MoU is a handshake, not money. 3 months later: zero deals closed.

🔥 THE OHIO BOMB
Separately, Nvidia promised to cover up to $105B (~₹9.9 lakh cr) on OpenAI's 20-year Ohio data-centre lease (built by SoftBank's SB Energy). If OpenAI stops paying, Nvidia pays the gap.

$105B ≈ ALL the cash Nvidia's business made in a full year ($102.7B in FY26).

text:
For two very important political reasons: The Atreides were granted a different type of fiefcompared to the Harkonnen, and House Atreides only had one ennobled Peer who could be granted fief.
To the first point, the Harkonnen were granted a demi-fief (a type of siridar-fief) over Arrakis, which gave them powers of stewardship as long as they kept the supply of Spice flowing to meet CHOAM demands, meaning that it was a limited and risky contract. One mistake, one lean year, and they would have been ousted to make room for another contender for the Mélange wealth. Which is partly why the Harkonnen stockpiled spice on Giedi Prime — a highly illegal action, but one that would have granted the Harkonnen greater political and economic stability, and power should production ever have fallen behind. The Atreides would not have to stoop so low — The Emperor granted them fief-complete — which essentially made Arrakis the sole property of House Atreides. It was a massive show of faith and support (ostensibly), because once accepted by House Atreides, it meant that even in times of low economic production, the Atreides would have the legal power to hold Arrakis as theirs (their home fief) regardless of the state of the economy of the Imperium. This plays in heavily to the political intrigue of the final chapters of the tale, which I will explain later.
To the second point I shall be brief: Duke Leto is, legally speaking, the only one of the Atreides House who holds Title. No-one, not even his son Paul, had been recognized as a Peer in Court, save for the hereditary classification of na-Duke (heir apparent to the Duchy), which is not sufficient to be entrusted with a fief. Since the Faufreluches of the Imperium is a feudal structure of government, only those with titles of nobility can oversee fiefdoms. The Baron could place his nephew Rabban as Regent-in-name of Arrakis because they were related by blood, and Rabban was a Count in his own right (of his father, Count of Lankiveil) — he had the legal power to oversee fief. This is because of the demi-fief that House Harkonnen was granted by the Emperor, and the special legal restrictions thereof, it was more beneficial and proper to install Rabban on Arrakis than the Baron himself. But Duke Leto had no such leeway — his fief-complete meant that he had to change the primary land fief of the entire House from Caladan to Arrakis, and being the only one able to take on the mantle, he was forced to move to Arrakis physically and make that the seat of his authority. Which is a deep bit of political intrigue, as not only is it an offer that he couldn't refuse, but it fundamentally uprooted a House from a territory that they knew and could defend well, to one that was hostile and unknown and under-developed in a military sense. It was literally asking a man to walk himself into an execution.
But Duke Leto did it anyways.
The deeper political intrigue was that the fief-complete was essentially a double-edged sword for the Emperor. Not only was he complicit in trying to remove a Great House from its legally-granted rightful seat by military force (which was a primal fear in the Imperium), but he also installed the Harkonnen onto this same legal fief in absentia, meaning that he declared emergency rights to keep spice production flowing on the caveat that the legal holder of the fief was not present or accounted for (his role in this fact was not made public) — essentially making the Emperor into a robber and an assassin. Thus when Paul re-emerged, he realized he was holding all the cards — not only would the Emperor be violently ousted from his throne by the Landsraad if there was ever proof of the Emperor's misdeeds, but that Paul Atreides was now the holder of enormous political and economic power as the sole owner of Arrakis. Which opened the door for an Atreides to ascend to the Lion Throne of the Imperium: The Padishah Emperor would be given an offer he couldn't refuse.

OUR ONEOK $OKE POST HAD THE NEW PIPELINE WRONG:

ONEOK (OKE) at $89.75, +$0.89 / +1.00% on Friday.

ONEOK is still on none of the Len5es we weigh, and we were factually incorrect about Blackcomb, the West Texas gas pipeline our post called still in testing. Blackcomb was already in service when we wrote. The futures market widened the discount on West Texas gas anyway, and it still prices that discount to grow through winter 2027-28. ONEOK then rose five sessions in a row with energy stocks while crude fell again, which our read on crude did not allow for. Its first 2027 forecast, due in February, is still the next date.

ONEOK is on none of the Momentum, Quality-Value, Deep-Value and Special-Situations, Hypergrowth or Income Len5es. Momentum wants a stock near its high with gains over one, three and six months; ONEOK now has one of the three:
- One month, from October 13: -3.9%.
- Three months, from August 13: -3.1%.
- Six months, from May 13: +1.1%.
- Against the September 8 closing high of $97.51: -8.0%.
What would put ONEOK on the Momentum Len5 is unchanged: a close above $97.51 with all three spans turned to gains. At about 15.6 times the 2026 profit ONEOK forecasts before a one-time tax benefit, it still offers the two value Len5es no discount. It has put out no new figures since our post, so what would put it on the Income Len5 and what keeps it off the Quality Len5 stand as we wrote them.

Blackcomb was already open when we wrote that it was still in testing. Enbridge (ENB) at $47.67, -$0.44 / -0.91% on Friday. Enbridge owns part of Blackcomb through a joint venture and said on its November 6 call, the day before our post, that the pipeline had entered service. Aegis Hedging, which advises gas producers on prices, says Blackcomb's flows build through 2027 to a full 2.5 billion cubic feet a day. Enbridge is on none of those five Len5es; Momentum wants a stock near its high, and Enbridge closed Friday 18% under its high of the past year.

The discount on West Texas gas grew with Blackcomb running. ONEOK's gas pipeline unit earns extra when gas at the Waha hub in West Texas sells far below the price near Houston, and the closest futures-market measure of that gap is Waha's discount to Henry Hub, the national benchmark. Prices on November 12, per Aegis:
- December delivery: $1.30 under Henry Hub, from about $1.22 in our post.
- Winter 2027-28: $2.14 under, from $2.08.
- Waha gas for immediate delivery: $1.865, from $1.39 on November 5.
Henry Hub gas for December delivery closed November 12 at $3.34, +$0.34 / +11.4% from November 6. Aegis said Waha's December price did not keep pace, so the discount widened even as West Texas gas got dearer. Aegis sees the greatest risk of full pipelines in early 2028, before the next new lines.

ONEOK won back part of its fall with energy stocks, not with crude.
- Since our post: +$4.56 / +5.4% from the $85.19 we quoted, five straight gains that won back 38% of the fall from October 30.
- Energy Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLE), a fund of large US energy companies, at $64.96, +$0.61 / +0.95% on Friday. October 30 to November 6: -12.0%; since: +5.4%.
- United States Oil Fund (USO), which tracks US crude, at $145.58, -$0.49 / -0.34% on Friday. October 30 to November 6: -12.1%; since: -1.9%.
Our premise was faulty: we read ONEOK's 12.2% fall as a trade on crude because the two fell together. Crude fell on three of ONEOK's five up days. ONEOK's path has matched the energy fund's both ways and crude's only on the way down.

Blackcomb is open, and West Texas gas is still priced at a bigger discount for winter 2027-28 than for this December. A discount that shrinks as Blackcomb fills would cut what ONEOK's gas pipeline unit earns on it in 2027. ONEOK has not dated the December-quarter report that carries its first 2027 forecast; last year's came February 23.
