Jensen Huang's resignation — what it means for NVDA and the AI industry
The resignation — verified:
Thursday, November 12, around 8:48 AM ET, Nvidia announced Jensen Huang resigned as President, CEO and board member, effective immediately, ending a 33-year tenure. He co-founded the company in 1993.
Interim CEO: CFO Colette Kress (EVP + CFO since September 2013, keeping the CFO role); the permanent search is internal and external. Harvey C. Jones was appointed the company's first-ever Chair of the Board.
The 8-K: the board accepted the resignation on November 11, effective immediately; the company gave no reason. "Firing" is Rep. Moolenaar's word, not the fact — his own statement's title says "Resignation."
Market reaction: Wednesday's close of $173.73 → pre-market $157.54 (-9.32%, about $400 billion of market value erased) → Thursday's close $165.77 → Friday $162.85 (-2.01%). NVDA fell 12.75% on the week.
Analysts: Ives $225 (without Huang) vs $300 (with him); Stifel $315 → $205; BofA $350 → $280; William Blair cut to Market Perform.
Rotation: AMD +18.93% on the week (Friday -8.75% to $534.06), AVGO up about 19% on the week (Friday $347.01, -4.76%). The NVDA–AMD spread is about -$371. Red pen: AMD trades at 38.44x forward earnings vs NVDA at 13.72x; the scale gap is about 11–13x (NVDA's data-center quarter is about $75 billion, AMD's $6.7 billion).
Three structural breaks for the AI industry:
The founder premium is gone: "Jensen is Nvidia" no longer holds, and the market has to re-price succession uncertainty.
A succession vacuum: Kress is an interim CEO from finance, with no product or visionary pull. In your framework: "NVDA doesn't need an operator, it needs a visionary."
The scrutiny continues: the Senate and House will investigate the Trump administration's approval of Nvidia chip exports to China; Huang has agreed to testify before Congress on the Alice Huang matter before Thanksgiving (no date set). The Warren + Coons preservation letter requires confirmation by November 17.
Rumors and investigations (reported, not established):
The NYT reported an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, his direct report; Reuters reported an intimate relationship with a second employee (two sources, unnamed). Both are allegations, not findings.
The Alice Huang spy case: CNN reported that intelligence to date "does not prove" she spied for Beijing (not an exoneration); the FBI probe is ongoing, with no official finding. CNBC reported she owned stakes in Chinese businesses that provided computing power to Huawei (source reporting, not a finding).
Your rule has fired: the November 11 rule — liquidate NVDA holdings once the CEO is replaced — has fired. The $200 calendar spread (long Jun 17, 2027 $200 calls / short Dec 24, 2026 $200 calls, $12.18 debit) is confirmed held, with a maximum loss of $1,218 per spread. The next test: NVDA earnings Tuesday after the close, Kress's first print facing analysts — watch data-center demand, H200 sales to China, and guidance.

Q3 (Nov 10, after the close): revenue $3.661 billion, +168% YoY, beating consensus of about $3.5 billion and the company's $3.4–$3.6 billion guide; GAAP EPS -$1.27, beating Zacks' -$1.45 (Finnhub shows -$0.95, a different basis); net loss $709 million.
Profits: adjusted operating income $379 million, beating the $200–$260 million guide; GAAP operating income $207 million. The Sankey: revenue $3.7B → gross profit $2.5B (68%) → operating profit $0.2B (6%) → interest $0.8B + tax and other $0.1B → net loss $0.7B.
Red pen: Q3 net interest expense of $846 million is more than 4x operating profit; Q4 interest is guided at $1.05–$1.15 billion; debt is $46.9 billion. R&D of $2.0 billion is 55% of revenue. 98% of revenue comes from committed contracts ($3.6B) — revenue quality is high; the problem is cost and leverage.
Guidance: backlog $132.5 billion (+138% YoY); FY26 revenue guided up to $13.0–$13.3 billion; capex $37–$39 billion; active power over 1.7 GW; operating cash flow $1.975 billion; cash $6.5 billion.
The stock: Nov 11 close $60.77 → Nov 12 $56.60 → Friday intraday $52.27 (-7.66%, low $49.24). A beat-and-raise sold off — that's the leverage story, not the revenue story.
The slide's numbers were checked against the official print; US $3.4B + rest of world $0.2B sums to $3.6B vs the $3.7B total — a $0.1B rounding difference.
Earnings breakdown: Nebius (NBIS) — a big beat, and the stock fell
Q3 (Nov 12, before the open): adjusted EPS $0.31, revenue $980.8 million; revenue +571% YoY (Q3 2025: $146.1 million) and +68% QoQ (Q2 2026: $582.3 million). Adjusted EBITDA $465.8 million.
Slide check: EPS consensus -$0.63 vs actual $0.31 (a 149% beat); revenue consensus $907.17 million vs actual $980.8 million (an 8% beat). The revenue consensus varies by vendor — the slide's $907.17 million matches MarketBeat, Finnhub's $925.68 million is the high outlier; the beat is large either way.
Red pen one: the slide's "EPS +178% YoY / +358% QoQ" uses the absolute-negative-base convention — the reality is a swing from loss to profit (YoY -$0.40 → +$0.31; QoQ -$0.12 → +$0.31). Don't say +178%.
Red pen two: FY26 revenue guidance was cut to the low end of the $3.0–$3.4 billion range (FactSet $3.35 billion); 2026 capex was raised to about $27 billion (from $20–$25 billion); 2027 capex is $40–$45 billion, far above the expected $28.77 billion; $7 billion-plus ARR was pushed from December to February; about $325 million of Q3 revenue was non-recurring.
Prepayments are the bright spot: Q3 new deals had prepayments covering over 100% of related capex (Q2: 50–60%); over 90% of Q3 contract value carries a prepayment (up about 20 points); deferred revenue on the balance sheet is $9.4 billion (from $1.6 billion at end-2025); payback on 1–3 year deals is 19 months (Q2: 22 months); 2027 prepayments are expected at $17–$20 billion (2026: $10 billion). Customers are paying to fund the build-out.
The stock: Nov 11 close $154.69 → Nov 12 $128.64 (-16.84%) → Friday intraday about $117 (-8.92%, low $109), about -24% in two days; one month -37.01%; 52-week high $299.86.
NBIS continued: 2027 revenue guidance is about 4x — but the market is pricing capex
Revenue trajectory: 2024 $92 million → 2025 $530 million → 2026 guide about $3.0 billion (low end of the range; analysts expect $3.37 billion) → 2027 guide $12–$13 billion, about 4x 2026 (analysts expect $11.98 billion). Q3 was $981 million, +571% YoY, beating the expected $908 million.
Quarterly outlook (VJN estimates): Q3 2026 about $0.9B, Q4 about $1.5B; 2027 Q1 about $2.2B, Q2 about $2.7B, Q3 about $3.2B, Q4 about $4.0B; 2028 Q1 about $4.6B, Q2 $5.2B. Everything after Q3 2026 is an estimate (e), not actuals.
Why a big beat still fell: revenue and EPS both beat big, but guidance was cut, capex jumped, ARR was delayed, and $325 million of revenue was non-recurring — the market is pricing the speed of the cash burn, not the speed of revenue. Prepayments covering 100%+ of capex are a guardrail, not a guarantee.
Against CRWV: both are "revenue exploding, interest and capex exploding faster" AI infrastructure stories; CRWV's interest is 4x its operating profit, and NBIS's capex guide is about 50% above expectations. This week the market chose to sell first and ask later.
Anthropic IPO — the price range is out; the seven giants are putting in $26 billion
Price range: $70–$78 (S-1/A No. 2, Nov 10); about 825 million shares offered, raising $57.75–$64.35 billion; on shares outstanding the valuation is about $916 billion–$1.02 trillion, midpoint about $968 billion — about equal to the May Series H mark of $965 billion.
Fully diluted: at $78, up to about $1.404 trillion (TechCrunch) — a different yardstick from the $1.02 trillion on shares outstanding; both numbers are real.
The $26B concurrent placement (Class N non-voting shares, at the IPO price): Alphabet $10 billion, NVIDIA $10 billion, AMD $2.5 billion, Broadcom $1 billion, Micron $1 billion, Microsoft $1 billion, TSMC $0.5 billion — exactly $26.0 billion in total. All seven buyers are also Anthropic's chip and cloud suppliers.
Timing: pricing reportedly Nov 18, first trade Nov 19 — unconfirmed; the filing carries no date. The founders keep 50.1% voting control through a single Class F share; the lock-up releases in stages (some non-founder insiders can sell 10% on day one).
Anthropic results: Q3 revenue $16.96 billion, compute ate 58%
Q3 2026: revenue $16.956 billion, +1,127% YoY, +47% QoQ (Q2 was +144% — growth is slowing); compute and infrastructure cost $9.863 billion, 58% of revenue; GAAP operating loss $567 million; adjusted operating income $2.463 billion, a 15% margin.
The Sankey: revenue $17.0B — consumption-based $13.2B (78%, API and app token usage), subscription $3.7B (22%, Claude fixed-fee plans); customers over $100K: 11,900+ (+1,153% YoY), net revenue retention 900%. Operating expenses $17.5B: compute $9.9B (58%), personnel $1.7B (10%), sales and marketing $2.4B (14%), other $3.6B (21%); operating loss $0.6B (-3% margin).
GAAP net loss of $23.29 billion is mostly a $21.9 billion non-cash note revaluation — not cash burned. Nine-month revenue is $33.24 billion, net loss $104.04 billion. Long-term commitments are about $900.9 billion (about $70.7 billion due within a year); the annualized run-rate at Oct 31 is about $81 billion; net proceeds are $84.6–$93.7 billion (including the placement).
Your position: you hold pre-IPO Anthropic shares (via Forge Global) and will not chase the IPO. On Nov 9, Claude Fable 5.2 + Mythos 5.2 launched ($8/$40 per million tokens, 20% cheaper than 5.1).
Against OpenAI: the same quarter, OpenAI had revenue of $10 billion and an adjusted operating loss of $10.9 billion (the loss exceeded revenue); Anthropic had revenue of $17 billion and an operating loss of $567 million. Both are burning money — Anthropic's unit economics are closer to breakeven.

text:
I LENT MY ROOMMATE $15,000 AND SHE VANISHED, THEN I SAW HER ON A HOME RENOVATION SHOW

My name is Kayla Brennan. I'm 33 and I live in Tucson, Arizona. I spent four years waiting for an apology from someone who never planned to give me one, and I found her again by accident on a Sunday night, with a bowl of popcorn in my lap.

Brooke and I roomed together our sophomore year of college and stayed close afterward. She was magnetic. She could walk into a room full of strangers and leave with three new friends and a free drink. I was the quiet one, so I was happy to stand next to her and take whatever light spilled over.

After graduation, she moved to Phoenix and I stayed in Tucson. We talked every week. When she called me one night in March, she sounded different, shaky and rushed. She told me she'd found a house she could flip, a real fixer-upper with great bones, and a contractor friend had offered to help. She just needed $15,000 to close before someone else grabbed it. She'd pay me back in six months, with interest.

That was almost every dollar I had. I'd been saving for years, partly for a down payment, partly because I'd grown up watching my parents panic over every unexpected bill. I told her I needed to think about it. She said, "Kayla, I wouldn't ask if I had anyone else." That was the sentence that did it.
I wired her the money the next day. She sent a string of heart emojis and a voice memo thanking me. I still have it.

For the first two months, she kept in touch. She sent photos of a gutted kitchen and told me about a leaky roof. Then the updates got shorter. Then she started answering my texts hours late, and eventually days late. When I asked about the repayment timeline, she said the project had hit "some delays" and she'd explain soon.

By month eight, she'd stopped replying altogether. I called, and it went to voicemail. I emailed, and nothing came back. I drove up to Phoenix and found the address she'd given me. A young couple with a stroller answered the door. They'd bought the house two years earlier and had never heard of her.
I sat in my car for twenty minutes. Then I called her mother, who said Brooke had "moved on to new things" and that she didn't think it was her place to interfere. Her tone made it clear I was the problem.
I stopped chasing. I told myself it was the price of learning something, and I started saving again from zero. My parents knew, and my mother said nothing, which was kinder than anything she could have said.
Four years passed.

Last month I was on my couch scrolling for something mindless, and I clicked on a home renovation show I'd never seen. Halfway through the episode, the host introduced the homeowners, a couple building a "dream farmhouse" outside Santa Fe. The wife turned to the camera and laughed. It was Brooke. Same laugh, same dimple, same way of tossing her hair. A caption at the bottom of the screen gave her name, and it wasn't the one I knew.

I paused the show and stared at it for a long time. Then I did something I'd never done before. I stopped letting it go.
I looked up the production company and found a listing for the property. I pulled old texts and the wire confirmation. I sent Brooke a message through a social account I managed to find under her new name. I wrote, calmly, that I knew who she was, that I had records of every transfer, and that I wanted my money back.

She called within an hour. Her voice shook. She said she'd been ashamed for years, that the house deal collapsed before she even closed, and that she'd used the money to cover debts she'd been hiding from everyone. She said she'd built a new life and was terrified of what would happen if people knew.
"I was going to pay you back," she said.
"When?" I asked.
She didn't answer.

text:
Our friend Cap-Hornier has put his finger on a very real problem: the rather peculiar British relationship with history, particularly naval history.

I have long been struck by the tendency of British historians to treat history almost as a national inheritance, something to be preserved, polished and occasionally rearranged for the greater glory of Britain. The Americans are much the same. Read a British account of the First World War and the French contribution is sometimes reduced to a supporting role. Read certain American accounts and one might imagine that the war was won almost single-handedly by the United States.

Neither interpretation does justice to history.

I remember, when I was working as a publisher, considering the acquisition of the French rights to a magnificent British illustrated history of naval warfare. I was astonished by its treatment of the Battle of Navarino in 1827. The author had devoted a splendid double-page spread to the battle, yet the French and Russian contributions had virtually disappeared.

Even the map was revealing: British warships were individually named, whilst the French and Russian vessels were reduced to anonymous black silhouettes! One might have thought that the Royal Navy had fought the entire battle single-handedly.

There is another example which has always fascinated me. The British never tire of celebrating the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588, a victory in which the weather played a considerable part.

Yet one of the greatest naval and amphibious disasters in British history, Admiral Vernon's catastrophic expedition against Cartagena de Indias in 1741, has virtually disappeared from British historical memory.

I have read the contemporary British accounts of that disaster, published in the 1740s. What astonishes me is not the scarcity but the absence of British books devoted specifically to this colossal defeat in the subsequent historical literature. To my knowledge, no British historian has published a dedicated monograph on the disaster since the mid-eighteenth century.

Richard Harding's Amphibious Warfare in the Eighteenth Century, published in 1991, certainly examines the expedition, but it is a specialised academic study of British amphibious operations in the West Indies, not a history devoted to the catastrophe of Cartagena itself.

The contrast is extraordinary. The Spanish Armada has inspired generations of British historians, countless books and endless patriotic celebrations. Cartagena, a disaster of enormous proportions, has been largely consigned to oblivion.

And Cartagena is hardly an isolated example.

The British invasions of the Río de la Plata in 1806 and 1807 offer another remarkable case. Two expeditions against Buenos Aires and Montevideo ended in British defeat, with consequences of considerable importance for the subsequent history of South America.

Yet those campaigns remained remarkably neglected in British popular historical literature for generations. It was not until 2013 that Ben Hughes published The British Invasion of the River Plate, 1806–1807, a modern narrative devoted to the subject.

Of course, every nation cultivates its victories and is rather less enthusiastic about commemorating its disasters. The French are hardly innocent of that temptation, and neither are the Spanish.

Still, there is something particularly entertaining about the British habit of transforming naval history into a magnificent procession of British victories, occasionally interrupted by unfortunate events which somehow never quite make it into the schoolbooks.

The Royal Navy has a glorious history. It is glorious enough without having to borrow everybody else's victories or mislay its own defeats.

The nationwide ground stop has been lifted ... but airline flight delays continue and it will take awhile to catch up. So what happened exactly? Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy speaking at the White House.: “3:36 p.m. we experienced instability for our radar and our communications in our centers and our trachons across the country. So if you don't know this, at airports we have towers, the next rung out is a trachon, after that we have en route centers. The trachons in the centers, we started to have inconsistency in the data from the radars and our communication with uh with airplanes. Blame an overloaded, outdated system. Flightaware says 7700 flights were cancelled after the FAA declared the nationwide ground stop. No indication of anything nefarious like a cyberattack. A software update, overwhelmed the nation's older air traffic control system. If you're flying in the next few days, make sure you check with your airline to make sure your flight is good to go.  Airlines don't have to give passengers any additional compensation....They do have to offer to rebook a flight or provide full refunds for people who decide to stay home.  NBA, NHL and College athletes scrambling to get to their destinations in time for games this weekend....some teams chartering busses....leagues bumping back start times.”

text:
Finally, all my interests have converged!

While I agree that this is being handled poorly by the SEC, it is largely out of the hands of Ole Miss. The Ole Miss charter situation is a bit different than that of most other programs.

Ole Miss charters via JetBlue operating out of Tupelo Regional Airport, an hour bus trip from Oxford. KTUP is a small airport with little scheduled commercial traffic, it is uncontrolled after 10pm, and is not a hub or base of operations for JetBlue.

Due to the nationwide ground stop, the JetBlue crew operating the Ole Miss charter certainly would have timed out their duty day before the aircraft could depart. 

Since it isn't a hub or base of operations, no relief crew would have been available to operate the charter tonight and no commercial flights departed from or arrived at KTUP after the ground stop was lifted so none could be flown in.

That means the earliest Ole Miss can depart would be when the rest period for the assigned crew is up, 10 hours, which only begins after the duty day ends. Depending on when that occurred, it is possible their next duty day couldn't even begin until after 8am. Add in an hour to bus/pre-flight, an hour to board, an hour and a half flight into Oklahoma City, an hour to load onto buses and half an hour to bus to Norman it would have been early afternoon before Ole Miss could get to OU.

Even if kick was delayed until evening, that would be pushing it in terms of player safety and it is also unclear if the SEC even offered a late Saturday kick time as an option.

Could an all-out last ditch effort made it work? Sure. But is an Ole Miss-Oklahoma game in mid-November worth making that all-out last ditch effort at the risk of player safety? I would personally say no. Unfortunately that means Oklahoma fans, through no fault of their own, get screwed. Knowing OU fans as I do, they'll find a way to make it hell on Ole Miss Sunday.

WHAT ARE THE REQUIREMENTS?

You must have successfully passed NCLEX-RN.
At least one year of recent nursing experience in a tertiary acute-care hospital with a minimum of 100 beds.
English-language competency examination.
Willingness to commit to a three-year employment contract.
You must satisfy the relevant licensing and immigration requirements.

STEP-BY-STEP APPLICATION PROCESS

Visit the official international recruitment portal:

Explore available Registered Nurse vacancies.
Select your preferred location. Opportunities are advertised across different US regions, including Florida and Colorado.
Read the job description carefully. Confirm the experience, NCLEX and English-language requirements.
Prepare your documents:

Updated nursing CV.
BNSc certificate.
Nursing registration and licence.
NCLEX-RN pass letter.
Evidence of employment and clinical experience.
English examination results.

Complete the online application and submit it through the official recruitment portal.
If shortlisted, proceed with the recruitment interview and subsequent employment screening.
If selected, you will receive an employment offer and guidance on the immigration and relocation process.

IMPORTANT INFORMATION

You do not have to be physically present in the United States to apply.

text:
NVIDIA $NVDA — JENSEN HUANG IS GONE. BUT IS NVIDIA'S LONG-TERM INVESTMENT THESIS BROKEN?
I've spent time reviewing the implications of Jensen Huang's departure from NVIDIA, including Tom Nash's bullish assessment and the latest developments surrounding US chip export restrictions.
I agree with much of the bullish argument. But there's one important distinction I don't think investors should overlook.
NVIDIA can remain the dominant AI infrastructure company without Jensen. That doesn't mean replacing him is a minor event.
I've been bullish on NVIDIA because of its technology, ecosystem, execution and ability to anticipate where computing is heading.
Jensen was central to building those advantages.
The question now isn't simply whether NVIDIA can continue selling GPUs. It's whether the company can sustain the strategic leadership, innovation and execution that made it so successful.
THE BULL CASE — WHY MY LONG-TERM CONVICTION REMAINS
🔹 1. AI DEMAND DOESN'T DISAPPEAR WITH JENSEN
Microsoft $MSFT, Amazon $AMZN, Alphabet $GOOGL and Meta $META continue investing heavily in AI infrastructure.
Their spending is driven by demand for training, inference, cloud services and enterprise AI applications.
Those requirements haven't disappeared because NVIDIA has changed leadership.
But hyperscaler capital expenditure isn't guaranteed future NVIDIA revenue. Customers can change suppliers, optimise infrastructure or moderate spending if returns disappoint.
🔹 2. CUDA REMAINS A FORMIDABLE COMPETITIVE ADVANTAGE
NVIDIA's moat extends well beyond GPUs.
CUDA, software libraries, networking, developer tools and integrated systems create an ecosystem that competitors cannot easily replicate.
Switching suppliers can require substantial changes to software, infrastructure and engineering workflows.
That competitive advantage remains intact today.
🔹 3. NVIDIA SELLS MORE THAN COMPUTE
NVIDIA has positioned itself across accelerated computing, networking, systems architecture and AI software.
Customers increasingly evaluate complete infrastructure economics rather than individual chip performance.
Performance per watt, networking efficiency, deployment speed and total cost of ownership all matter.
NVIDIA's integrated approach gives it an important competitive advantage.
🔹 4. INFERENCE COULD EXTEND THE GROWTH RUNWAY
I believe the expansion of AI inference could become another major source of computing demand.
As AI applications move into everyday business operations, the requirement for reliable, efficient computing infrastructure should increase.
But inference economics are different from training.
Customers will increasingly focus on cost per token, latency, energy efficiency and utilisation.
NVIDIA must continue proving its systems offer attractive economics as workloads evolve.
🔹 5. NVIDIA IS BIGGER THAN ONE PERSON
Jensen built an extraordinary organisation.
But NVIDIA also has thousands of engineers, established customer relationships, intellectual property and a substantial software ecosystem.
Its technology roadmap and existing products don't disappear with its founder.
That gives NVIDIA a strong foundation for its next chapter.
THE BEAR CASE — WHAT CONCERNS ME
🔹 1. JENSEN'S DEPARTURE IS A REAL STRATEGIC RISK
This is where I disagree most strongly with Tom Nash.
Jensen wasn't simply the public face of NVIDIA.
He helped shape its technological direction, organisational culture, customer relationships and willingness to invest years ahead of visible demand.
CUDA and NVIDIA's expansion into AI computing weren't accidental.
They reflected long-term strategic decisions made before the commercial opportunity became obvious.
Replacing that combination of technical understanding, commercial influence and strategic conviction will be difficult.
An excellent operator isn't necessarily an equally exceptional technology visionary.
And in an industry evolving as quickly as AI, that distinction matters.
🔹 2. COMPETITION IS ACCELERATING
AMD $AMD, Broadcom $AVGO and hyperscaler-designed accelerators are becoming increasingly important.
Google's TPUs and other custom silicon programmes demonstrate that major customers are willing to develop alternatives when the economics justify them.
NVIDIA could continue growing while gradually losing share in particular workloads.
That's why I'll be watching pricing power, gross margins and customer purchasing decisions, not just headline revenue growth.
🔹 3. THE AI CAPEX CYCLE MUST DELIVER RETURNS
Hyperscalers are committing enormous amounts of capital to AI infrastructure.
But spending cannot grow indefinitely without sufficient economic returns.
The investment chain matters:
Capital → Power → Data Centres → Compute → Utilisation → Revenue → Free Cash Flow → ROIC.
If utilisation disappoints, pricing weakens or returns fail to justify investment, customers may moderate spending or shift towards more economical alternatives.
That would affect NVIDIA's future growth trajectory.
🔹 4. EXPORT CONTROLS ARE BECOMING A BIGGER RISK
This is an area where the latest developments deserve particular attention.
Reuters reports that Jensen's departure has intensified scrutiny of Southeast Asia's role in providing access to advanced NVIDIA-powered computing.
US lawmakers are considering tighter restrictions on Chinese companies accessing AI computing through overseas data centres.
Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia could face additional licensing requirements and end-user verification.
Malaysia alone has approved approximately $94.7B in data centre-related investments since 2021.
That figure represents approved investment, not realised spending or NVIDIA revenue.
For me, the concern isn't simply whether demand for NVIDIA chips remains strong.
It's whether additional export restrictions, compliance requirements and shipment delays could affect how quickly that demand converts into revenue.
Tighter oversight could also favour operators with transparent customers and stronger compliance systems.
But proposed restrictions aren't the same as rules already implemented, and allegations involving particular companies shouldn't be treated as established wrongdoing.
AI demand can remain strong while regulatory barriers make that demand harder to monetise.
🔹 5. A LOWER SHARE PRICE DOESN'T AUTOMATICALLY MAKE NVIDIA CHEAP
Tom argues that NVIDIA's valuation has become exceptionally attractive.
I wouldn't reach that conclusion from a falling share price or a headline forward P/E alone.
The earnings assumptions matter.
If growth expectations fall, today's apparently attractive valuation may look very different.
I want to assess NVIDIA against sustainable earnings growth, gross margins, free cash flow and the risks surrounding its leadership transition.
WHAT'S CHANGING — THE POST-JENSEN NVIDIA
NVIDIA has appointed longtime CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO, while Harvey Jones becomes board chair.
The company expects operations, customer commitments and its product roadmap to continue without interruption.
That's encouraging.
But operational continuity isn't the same as long-term strategic leadership.
The next CEO must preserve NVIDIA's ability to execute today's roadmap while identifying the technologies that will define tomorrow's computing market.
There is also a capital allocation question.
NVIDIA's relationships with AI infrastructure providers, cloud companies and emerging AI businesses have become increasingly interconnected.
Under new leadership, investors will want to understand whether its investment and financing strategy changes.
That matters because supporting AI infrastructure demand through strategic investments is different from generating sustainable end-customer demand and attractive cash returns.
WHAT I'LL BE WATCHING NEXT
NVIDIA reports fiscal Q3 2027 earnings on November 17.
🔹 Revenue growth and forward guidance.
🔹 Gross margins and pricing power.
🔹 Hyperscaler demand and customer concentration.
🔹 Competition from custom AI accelerators.
🔹 Export restrictions and Southeast Asian deployment risks.
🔹 Strategic investments and customer financing exposure.
🔹 Senior engineering talent retention.
🔹 Permanent CEO selection and technological direction.
Most importantly, I want to see whether NVIDIA can continue translating its technology leadership into sustainable earnings and free cash flow.
MY TAKE — BULLISH, BUT NOT BLIND TO THE RISKS
I remain bullish on NVIDIA's long-term opportunity.
I agree with Tom Nash that demand for accelerated computing doesn't disappear because Jensen has left.
CUDA remains valuable. NVIDIA's engineering talent remains. Its ecosystem remains.
But I disagree with treating Jensen's departure as merely temporary noise.
Jensen didn't just manage NVIDIA's success. He helped create the technological direction that made its success possible.
That contribution cannot be replaced overnight.
Equally, I don't believe everything NVIDIA achieved should be attributed to one individual.
The organisation he built has substantial competitive advantages and the potential to continue growing.
My conviction in the AI infrastructure buildout remains strong.
My conviction in NVIDIA's existing competitive advantages remains strong.
But my assessment of its future leadership and execution risk has changed.
That's why I wouldn't automatically sell because Jensen has departed, nor would I automatically buy simply because the share price has fallen.
I want evidence that the next leadership team can maintain NVIDIA's technological lead, protect margins, execute its roadmap and deliver attractive returns on capital.
THE BIGGER QUESTION
Can NVIDIA preserve Jensen Huang's technological vision while building a leadership structure capable of delivering the next decade of innovation?
Because the greatest risk isn't necessarily losing today's GPU customers.
It's losing the ability to anticipate the next major computing transition before competitors do.
NVIDIA's past success was built on seeing the future early.
Its next chapter will be judged by whether it can continue doing so.
I remain bullish on $NVDA. But Jensen's departure has made the leadership question impossible to ignore.

text:
Flights across America brought to a standstill—all by one line of code throwing an error...

So even the superpower has come to this: the eve of the Roman Empire’s collapse. Planes across the United States, grounded just like that.

A ground stop, put simply, means not a single plane is allowed to take off. Passengers stranded at airports, flights canceled, tens of millions of people’s travel plans ruined. The U.S. homeland security secretary came out to respond, but offered no real explanation.

This all looks awfully familiar. In August 2003, a massive blackout hit the northeastern United States and Canada, leaving 50 million people in the dark and bringing several states’ economies to a halt for two days. The Financial Times dissected it at length back then: years of underinvestment in the power system, one failure triggering a chain reaction, and finally the whole grid going down. The U.S. energy secretary at the time said something blunt but true—the cost of fixing the system would ultimately land on every customer’s bill.

Twenty years later, swap electricity for aviation. Americans themselves know better than anyone how badly their infrastructure has deteriorated. The American Society of Civil Engineers grades the country’s infrastructure every four years. Since 1998, it has never earned a passing grade, languishing around a D for years—bridges operating beyond their intended lifespan, pothole-riddled roads, aging power grids, outdated airport facilities. Out comes the report, and every year brings calls for investment, arguments in Congress, and ultimately nothing.

America’s infrastructure is the world’s most luxurious used car.

It looks impressive on the outside: airports everywhere, airlines filling the skies. But underneath, the aging systems, code, and equipment have long been patches piled on patches. Things that should have been upgraded ten or twenty years ago keep going unreplaced, because replacement costs money, spending needs congressional approval, and congressional approval depends on election-year politics. So nobody wants to be the one who spends the money—until one day a line of code throws an error and America’s entire aviation network stalls.

One day of grounded flights means direct losses ranging from hundreds of millions to billions of dollars, before even counting disrupted freight, stranded passengers, and cascading delays. Yet a complete overhaul of that old system would actually cost about as much as a single grounding. The problem is that fixing it means paying now for benefits that won’t show up until much later; leaving it alone means the risks won’t blow up until much later either. Politicians always choose the latter, because by the time disaster hits, they’ll be long out of office.

Now compare that with China. Over the past twenty years, China has built more than 40,000 kilometers of high-speed rail, expanded its airports again and again, and developed the world’s most reliable power grid. Some people are always calling China’s infrastructure spending a waste. Today’s U.S. flight shutdown shows you that money went exactly where it was needed. Infrastructure doesn’t lie: neglect it for years, and one day it will collect everything you owe, with interest.

Where has America’s money gone? Annual military spending of $800–900 billion, more than the next several countries combined—yet decades of tinkering still haven’t fixed the aging systems at its own airports. This is the classic American disease: it would rather pour money into wars overseas than build roads, bridges, and airports for its own people. Arms-industry lobbying and the interests of the military-industrial complex steer the budget toward the war machine year after year, while infrastructure serving people at home gets pushed aside. In the end, aircraft carriers swagger across the seas while airports sit paralyzed on the ground.

America talks every day about containing China, cutting off its access to critical technologies, and leading the world in high tech, yet it can’t even get its own air traffic control system into shape. How can a country that can’t even get its flights off the ground talk about leading the world?

This won’t be a one-off performance. Next time it could be the power grid, the railways, or the drinking water supply. The day it finally exhausts what previous generations built will be the final reckoning for the “New Rome”...

(Reference: Financial Times, FT Lessons, coverage of the 2003 U.S.–Canada blackout)

▫️FY27 revenue target of ~₹48 Cr reiterated (FY26: ₹30.65 Cr)
💠H1 achieved ₹21.17 Cr, 44% of target; H2 requires ~₹26.8 Cr (56%)

💠H2 is the stronger half; demand is higher in H2

▫️Margin outlook: EBITDA margin of at least 35% for the next two years

💠Rising Unit II utilisation through H2 FY27 to support margins
💠Vertical integration plans over the next two years not expected to change margins

▫️Raw material cost pass-through: hard to pass on mid-project, as OEM customers do not revise prices within an approved budget
💠Revised prices are taken up at next order finalisation or repeat order
💠Significant impacts are taken back to the customer

▫️Growth roadmap: FY28 plan ~₹80 Cr with Unit I and II at full capacity
💠FY32 aspiration ~₹300 Cr, supported by Unit III, assemblies and new plants
💠Targeted growth of 50–55% annually
💠Aspiration of ₹500 Cr retained; ₹300 Cr by FY32 is the committed plan, the larger figure depends on a prospective project at a very initial stage

▫️Revenue mix: defence ₹12.86 Cr (60.7%, +56.2% YoY), aerospace ₹5.79 Cr (27.3%, +26.5%), healthcare ₹2.24 Cr (10.6%, vs ₹0.75 Cr), others 1.4%

👉Order book / projects and pipeline:
▫️Order book: ₹31.8 Cr as on 30 Sep 2026, 1.5x H1 revenue
💠Defence ₹16.83 Cr (53%), aerospace ₹9.94 Cr (31%), healthcare ₹4.36 Cr (14%), others ₹0.66 Cr (2%)
💠Bid pipeline: minimum ₹100 Cr maintained, with conversion of ~30–35%

▫️Unit II (Hi-Tech Aerospace & Defence Park, Bengaluru):
💠Inaugurated 14 Aug 2026; 20,000 sq ft; 15 machines and 45+ employees as on 30 Sep
💠Utilisation ~30–35% in September and October, as installation and commissioning continue; total of 30 machines planned
💠Expected to contribute ~₹15 Cr in H2 FY27
💠Revenue potential at 100% utilisation in FY29: ₹50–60 Cr, with a further ₹5–6 Cr on a stretch towards more complex parts
💠Unit II plans support 50–55% annual growth till FY29

▫️Unit I (Peenya):
💠8,500 sq ft; 18 machines and 80 employees
💠100% utilised

▫️Combined capacity:
💠Unit I and II can deliver up to ₹80 Cr from machining business
💠Vertical integration can stretch this to ₹90–95 Cr
💠Assemblies and other services can add at least 10–15% revenue from Unit II itself

▫️Unit III:
💠40,000 sq ft greenfield near Aerospace Park; construction planned from FY29
💠Focus on complex machined components, ~80% of business vs ~60% in Units I and II, with maximum automation
💠Business plan under preparation; capex and funding to be communicated later
💠Additional land of ~40,000 sq ft near Aerospace Park is available; decision on Unit III or expansion within existing facilities expected around the beginning of next financial year
💠Land use being considered for vertical integration, mainly mechanical assemblies and medium-critical components

▫️Capex and IPO proceeds:
💠₹23.33 Cr invested in H1 including capital advances, in advanced CNC machines and inspection equipment for Unit II

▫️New opportunities:

💠Design and testing at sub-module level under consideration

text:
Folks that populate the weapons world tend to have one eye on the future while assuming that the past shall always find a way to enter our lives. The humble shotgun, often laughed at by many forces, found its way back into the battlefield & what an entry that was. The CUAS battle will never be able to give up on “hard kill”. There is a detection & localization conundrum that’s been keeping us at @sssdefence very busy.  Here we are pushing the boundaries of tech. At the other end, we saw the beauty of the shotgun far ahead of time & built the T12. The T12 is the only indigenously designed & manufactured CUAS semi-auto shotgun to be inducted into the Indian Army in good numbers. We are not very far from the Italians & Americans in this area & clearly far ahead of the 🇹🇷 (just cheap crap) & 🇷🇺 (unwieldy & lacking in ergonomics). The ammunition too had to be worked on & what an internal collab this turned out to be. 
We were late to many parties for weapons because we decided to do things on our own. Everybody including the govt licensed their tech but we bucked the trend. But when the user called and none but us could offer a solution, all of that effort paid off.  Weapons like the T12 & its ammunition suite are step children of the weapon’s world. But we love them because they signify that that battlefield survival tech evolution is not always linear forward. They can also run into the past.
Every foreign expo brings us face to face with OEM’s that have sold to India. A few days back came face to face with somebody who wanted to push their CUAS hard kill weapons into India. This time, I did fire away “how exciting. Call me when you’re around. We’ll be the ones already serving the market”

text:
SA TECH NEWS: THE WEEK THAT WAS 
(09–13 November)

A week in which South Africa’s digital rails moved faster than the rules that govern them. Three signals for founders, investors and policymakers:

/ Identity is moving onto private rails. Home Affairs now offers Smart ID replacements at 753 bank branches, four months ahead of target, taking its footprint to 967 service points. When national biometric identity runs through commercial #bank systems, *who audits* those operators matters as much as who builds the enabling digital rails.

/ Connectivity is waiting on a #courtroom. Sakeliga's challenge to ICASA’s 30% ownership rule is before the Pretoria High Court, and Telkom has asked ICASA to allow alternatives for all licensees, not just newcomers like Starlink. ICASA says change needs Parliament. Until the court, the regulator, or Parliament moves, satellite capital waits.

/ Capital is getting selective. @Yoco_ZA secured a $100m private credit facility for SME lending, while @EnzaCapital reached a $21m first close for African AI, where the median round is just $1.9m. Credit seems to flow to proven rails, but AI #founders still raise seed-sized cheques, though.

BREAKING (13 Nov): Minister @DrBladeNzimande joins the Silicon Valley delegation, with #cybersecurity now explicitly on the agenda. This is interesting. I wonder why you left me out @SpokespersonRSA 🤔. Ask any AI chatbot who the top "AI in Cybersecurity" scholars in South Africa are, and my name will be in the top two.

Anyway, South Africa is building digital infrastructure faster than we can govern it, and that gap is where both the *risk* and the OPPORTUNITY lie.

I think the most important dimension here is the assumption that economic pressure can indefinitely substitute for a political settlement. A blockade is not really a neutral status quo, it is an active instrument of coercion and one that inevitably creates its own escalation dynamics. 
The underlying miscalculation may be treating Iran's willingness to absorb economic costs as evidence that it will eventually abandon its strategic position. Economic pressure can constrain a state, but it does not automatically translate into political capitulation. In fact, when diplomacy offers no meaningful concessions and military action remains on the table, the space for miscalculation becomes considerably wider.
A blockade may postpone the decision to go to war, but it cannot resolve the political conditions that keep bringing war back onto the table.

text:
Operation Paperclip (formally evolving from the shorter Operation Overcast) was a classified US program, roughly 1945–1959, that brought more than 1,500–1,600 German and Austrian scientists, engineers, and technicians (plus families) to the United States for government employment.
Core Purpose and Mechanics
The explicit goal was dual: accelerate US capabilities in rocketry, aeronautics, chemical weapons, and related fields while denying the same expertise to the Soviet Union. The Joint Intelligence Objectives Agency (JIOA) managed it. Scientists were identified from lists (including one compiled by German engineer Werner Osenberg), offered contracts, and moved under military control. An initial rocket group of about 125, led by Wernher von Braun, arrived at Fort Bliss, Texas, in 1945–46; the team later relocated to Redstone Arsenal in Huntsville, Alabama. Most participants eventually became US citizens.
President Truman’s directive required that recruits not have been ardent Nazis or involved in war crimes. In practice, the JIOA frequently sanitized files—minimizing or omitting Nazi Party membership, SS ranks, and links to forced labor—so that valuable specialists would clear immigration and security review. The “paperclip” name referred to the marker placed on cleaned dossiers.
Wernher von Braun and the V-2 Program
Von Braun was the most consequential recruit. He joined the Nazi Party in 1937 and the SS in 1940, rising to Sturmbannführer (major equivalent). He directed technical development of the V-2 (A-4) ballistic missile at Peenemünde and later at the underground Mittelwerk factory near Nordhausen. Production at Mittelwerk relied on slave labor from the Mittelbau-Dora concentration camp complex. Historians estimate more than 20,000 prisoners died there from starvation, disease, executions, and death marches—more than the number of people killed by V-2 strikes on Allied cities.
Von Braun visited the facility multiple times, was aware of the conditions, and was involved in decisions about the use of forced labor. He and key colleagues surrendered to US forces in 1945, bringing technical documents and hardware. In the US he led development of the Redstone and Jupiter missiles and, after transfer to NASA, the Saturn V that launched Apollo to the Moon. NASA’s own materials now acknowledge his SS membership and awareness of slave-labor conditions.
Outcomes and Ethical Record
Technically, the program delivered results. Paperclip personnel accelerated US ballistic-missile work and contributed to Explorer 1 and the Apollo program. Parallel Soviet efforts (including Operation Osoaviakhim) sought the same talent, so the competitive logic was clear. Ethically, the program involved deliberate concealment of war-crimes connections. Contemporary critics included Albert Einstein and Eleanor Roosevelt. Later investigations (1970s–80s) led to the Justice Department’s Office of Special Investigations; Arthur Rudolph, a key V-2 production manager who later worked on Saturn V, left the US in 1984 and renounced citizenship rather than face proceedings. Most Paperclip recruits faced no such accountability.
Relation to the Current Analogy
Paperclip was a state-directed, supervised absorption of former enemy specialists under military and later civilian-agency control. Records were altered specifically to enable entry and employment. The “forgiveness” was operational and incomplete: talent was retained under oversight, not restored to unrestricted private power or given a clean public slate. Later scrutiny of figures such as Rudolph shows the ethical compromise was never fully settled. The historical episode is therefore a case study in prioritizing capability over full accountability during a great-power contest, not a model of unrestricted absolution.

text:
The Tree of Life

God did not keep Adam and Eve from the Tree of Life because the tree was evil. He kept them from it because of the condition they were now in.

Look  at Genesis 3:22:

“Behold, the man is become as one of us, to know good and evil: and now, lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever…”

Notice what the God says: “lest he… eat, and live for ever.”

The concern is not simply that Adam might eat fruit. It is that he might obtain everlasting life while remaining in his fallen condition.

1. The problem was not life. It was the condition in which humanity would live forever.

Before the fall, humanity had access to God's creation without shame, fear, alienation, or death.

After eating from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil, the story changes:

They become aware of their nakedness and feel shame.
They hide from God.
They become afraid.
Their relationship with one another is damaged.
They are expelled from the garden.
Death enters the human story.

Now imagine that humanity could eat from the Tree of Life and continue forever in that condition.

The consequences of the fall would become permanent. Humanity would have endless existence, but not the restored life it originally had.

That is one way to understand God's action: He prevents fallen humanity from making its broken condition everlasting.

2. Being denied the tree may actually be an act of mercy

This is an important distinction.

God does not destroy the Tree of Life. He places cherubim and a flaming sword to guard the way to it (Genesis 3:24).

The way is closed, but the tree remains.

That leaves an interesting possibility within the biblical narrative: humanity is not necessarily being denied life forever. Humanity is being denied access to everlasting life in its present condition.

The separation creates a period of waiting for restoration.

3. This makes Jesus' promise in Revelation especially interesting

Remember what Jesus says:

Revelation 2:7

“To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the midst of the paradise of God.”

Now compare the sequence:
Genesis
Revelation
Humanity loses access to the Tree of Life.
The faithful are promised access to it.
Humanity is expelled from paradise.
Paradise is restored.
Death becomes part of human existence.
The tree is associated with life and healing.
The way to the tree is guarded.
The tree is accessible to the redeemed.
And Revelation 22:3 adds something crucial: the curse is no more, and the throne of God and the Lamb is in the restored creation.
The condition has changed.

4. 
In John 11:25, Jesus says:

“I am the resurrection, and the life.”

He does not say, "I know where the Tree of Life is." He identifies himself as the source of resurrection and life.

In John 6:51, he says:

“I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever.”

There is a striking parallel:

In Genesis, eating from the Tree of Life would allow humanity to live forever.

In John, Jesus offers everlasting life through eating the living bread.

In Revelation, the Tree of Life is available again to those who overcome.

This raises a profound theological possibility: Jesus is not necessarily rejecting the Tree of Life. He is showing that everlasting life cannot be separated from restoration to God.

The tree was never the ultimate answer to humanity's broken condition. Living forever while separated from God would not solve the problem.

Jesus offers something different: not merely an endless existence, but resurrection and reconciliation.

What if the central issue in Genesis was never simply that humanity gained knowledge?

What if the deeper issue was that humanity acquired knowledge of good and evil while losing its proper relationship with the source of life?

That would explain why the story ends not with humanity discovering another way to live forever, but with humanity needing to be restored before access to the Tree of Life is given again.

And notice: in Revelation, the tree returns only after the curse is removed.

The sequence matters: restoration first, access to everlasting life afterward.

text:
THE KNOWLEDGE THAT REPLACED US
A Lesson from the Book of Enoch, Penemue, and the Age of Artificial Intelligence

Central teaching: When humanity transfers its natural abilities to external tools, it risks losing the ability to exercise those faculties within itself.

1. The Original Human Faculties

Imagine a humanity that did not need to write everything down, calculate every answer, or rely on external systems to navigate the world.

Human beings learned through observation, memory, experience, and direct understanding.

Their knowledge lived within them.

We cannot establish from the Book of Enoch that the first humans possessed perfect memory or abilities beyond those we have today. But the ancient text does raise a question about the relationship between humanity, knowledge, and the consequences of acquiring it.

2. Penemue: The Angel Who Taught Writing

In 1 Enoch 69:8–11, Penemue is identified among the Watchers who taught humanity.

His teachings included:

The distinction between bitter and sweet.
The secrets of wisdom.
Writing with ink and paper.

The passage connects this knowledge with humanity's corruption and destruction.

Notice what makes this interesting: the text does not simply describe weapons or violence. It also identifies wisdom and writing.

Why?

Perhaps the danger was not knowledge itself, but what happens when knowledge becomes separated from wisdom, righteousness, and responsibility.

3. When Knowledge Leaves the Human Mind

Consider what happens when a human faculty is transferred into a tool.

Memory becomes writing.

Mental calculation becomes a calculator.

Navigation becomes GPS.

Research becomes search engines.

Expression becomes automated writing.

Each tool offers convenience. Each can also reduce the amount of practice we give the original ability.

There is an important distinction between preserving a capability and exercising it.

A person can possess thousands of books without possessing the wisdom contained in them.

A person can access unlimited information without knowing how to distinguish truth from falsehood.

4. The Second Danger: Knowledge Can Be Forged

Once knowledge is stored externally, it can be manipulated.

Written records can contain lies.

Historical accounts can be altered.

Evidence can be fabricated.

Information can be removed, rewritten, or presented out of context.

5. Artificial Intelligence: The Modern Penemue Question

We are now entering another stage of this process.

Artificial intelligence can:

Remember information for us.
Write for us.
Calculate for us.
Create images for us.
Analyze information for us.
Make recommendations for us.
Produce answers that we may accept without examining.
Remove history.

AI can be an extraordinary instrument of learning.

But it can also become a substitute for learning.

Writing preserves truth, but it can also preserve falsehood. Whoever controls records can influence what future generations believe.

The very system created to preserve knowledge can become a system for controlling knowledge.

This is one of the most important lessons we can draw from the story of Penemue.

The ability to preserve information does not guarantee that the information is true.

If we stop questioning, reasoning, remembering, creating, and investigating because a machine can do these things for us, we risk weakening the very faculties that make us human.

The greatest danger is not that AI becomes intelligent.

It is that humans become unwilling to exercise their own intelligence.

6. Information Is Not Wisdom

There are three different things:

Information: Knowing what something says.

Knowledge: Understanding what the information means.

Wisdom: Knowing how to judge, apply, and question what you understand.

AI can provide information and assist with knowledge.

But human beings must retain responsibility for judgment, discernment, and moral choices.

We should never confuse an answer with understanding.

7. The Lesson

Perhaps the most important question is not what technology can do for humanity.

It is what humanity stops doing for itself when technology takes over.

Every generation receives new tools. Every generation must decide whether those tools will serve human development or replace it.

We should use writing without abandoning memory.

We should use calculators without abandoning mathematics.

We should use AI without abandoning independent thought.

We should preserve knowledge without surrendering our ability to recognize truth.

The lesson is not to reject knowledge or technology.

It is to remain capable of thinking, remembering, questioning, and discerning without them.

FINAL REFLECTION

If you allow a machine to remember for you, what happens to your memory?

If you allow a machine to think for you, what happens to your reasoning?

If you allow a machine to tell you what is true, what happens to your discernment?

And if you eventually cannot distinguish what you know from what a machine has told you, who is directing your understanding?

The greatest loss may not be the knowledge we forget. It may be the human faculties we stop exercising.

Use the tools. Preserve the faculties. Never surrender your judgment.

🚨 SKYROOT AEROSPACE IS TAKING INDIA'S PRIVATE SPACE INDUSTRY GLOBAL. @SkyrootA 

THIS COMPANY REMINDS ME OF $RKLB'S EARLY DAYS.

I was so happy to see $RKLB successfully complete Electron's 100th launch today that I thought I'd share another company I'm excited about.

I've been closely keeping my tab on this company for a few months now. 

Skyroot Aerospace is making some serious moves in India's growing private space industry and I think it's a company worth keeping an eye on.

And full credit goes to @PawanKChandana, Co-Founder and CEO and Naga Bharath Daka, Co-Founder and COO, for what they're building at Skyroot Aerospace.

THEIR LATEST BRAZIL PARTNERSHIP IS ANOTHER BIG STEP.

I'm surprised how quickly Skyroot is moving from proving its rocket technology to securing international customers and expanding its launch ambitions.

SKYROOT AND BRAZIL'S CONCERT TECHNOLOGIES ARE WORKING ON A NEW SATELLITE LAUNCH VEHICLE.

Under a two-year MoU signed in October, the companies will explore jointly developing a launcher capable of carrying at least 100 kg into low Earth orbit.

The opportunity goes beyond the rocket itself.

Brazil's Alcântara launch location, close to the equator, could offer launch-efficiency advantages and another geographical option for satellite customers.

It's still an early-stage agreement but I like that Skyroot is already thinking beyond India's domestic launch market.

1. NOVEMBER 2022: VIKRAM-S MADE HISTORY.

Skyroot became India's first private company to launch a rocket into space.

It was a suborbital mission, but an important validation of its propulsion, avionics and launch operations.

2. JULY 18, 2026: VIKRAM-1 REACHED ORBIT ON ITS FIRST ATTEMPT.

This was the real breakthrough.

Skyroot became the first Indian private company to successfully launch an orbital rocket from Indian soil, deploying payloads into approximately 450 km low Earth orbit.

Vikram-1 is designed to carry around 350 kg to LEO.

What interests me here is the engineering. Vikram-1 combines carbon-composite structures, solid propulsion stages and a 3D-printed liquid engine.

For a company founded in 2018, reaching orbit in eight years is impressive.

3. OCTOBER 14: SKYROOT SECURED TWO DEDICATED LAUNCHES FOR REFLECT ORBITAL.

One mission will use Vikram-1 and the other its upgraded Vikram-1U, designed for approximately 550 kg to LEO.

This is what I like. Skyroot is attracting international customers who need dedicated launch capacity rather than depending entirely on rideshare schedules.

4. NOVEMBER 2026: SKYROOT IS PREPARING ITS SECOND ORBITAL FLIGHT.

The company has completed its Raman-1 thruster test campaign and is preparing another Vikram-1 mission for December 2026 or early January 2027.

I'm watching the final vehicle integration, hardware readiness and launch preparations.

The first successful flight proved the technology. The next few flights need to prove Skyroot can deliver consistently.

5. Q1 2027: VIKRAM-1U COULD BE THE NEXT IMPORTANT UPGRADE.

Skyroot is targeting the first flight of Vikram-1U, designed to carry approximately 550 kg to LEO.

That's roughly 57% more payload capacity than Vikram-1.

It could open up a broader range of satellite missions without requiring customers to move to much larger launch vehicles.

6. LATE 2027: VIKRAM-2 IS THE BIGGER OPPORTUNITY.

Skyroot is targeting Vikram-2 with payload capability of up to 900 kg and cryogenic propulsion.

The company also wants to reach one launch per month by the end of 2027.

Those are ambitious targets and I want to see how quickly its manufacturing and launch operations can scale.

7. YOU KNOW WHO SKYROOT REMINDS ME OF? ROCKET LAB IN ITS EARLY DAYS.

I keep thinking about Peter Beck and how he built Rocket Lab. $RKLB

He started with Electron, gradually established launch reliability and then expanded into spacecraft manufacturing, components and a much larger space business.

Skyroot seems to be following a similar approach with its Vikram rocket family.

Both companies started with smaller rockets, focused on dedicated satellite launches and looked beyond their home markets for customers.

Of course, Rocket Lab is years ahead. Electron has approached its 100th launch and Rocket Lab has already built a substantial Space Systems business.

Skyroot hasn't proved that level of repeatability yet but that's precisely why I'm excited in watching its next few missions.

GUYS, JUST SEE THE PROGRESSION.

In 2022, Skyroot was proving it could reach space.

In July 2026, it proved it could reach orbit.

Now it's securing international launch customers, preparing follow-on missions, developing larger rockets and exploring overseas partnerships.

The next six months will be important. I want to see the second orbital mission completed, the transition toward fully commercial launches and meaningful progress on Vikram-1U.

One successful orbital launch doesn't make a mature launch business. Skyroot still has to prove reliability, competitive economics and its ability to manufacture rockets at a higher rate.

But I genuinely think India could have its own Rocket Lab story developing here.

And if Skyroot can execute on these plans, the opportunity could extend far beyond India's satellite launch market.

🚨From the Radical Left to Fringe Isolationists:
How Anti-American Extremes Meet at the Bottom of the Horseshoe

For years, mainstream media pundits have tried to paint the MAGA movement as a radical fringe. Yet a closer look at today’s political landscape reveals a very different reality: while America First conservatives are focused on commonsense border security, economic nationalism, and peace through strength, the true extremes on both ends of the political spectrum have curved around the "political horseshoe" to meet in the middle—united by a shared hostility toward American leadership, constitutional order, and traditional allies.

THE UNHOLY ALLIANCE OF DSA & WOKE REICH
At first glance, the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the paleolibertarian Ron Paul Institute, and online New Christian Right podcasters appear to come from completely different worlds. One preaches Marxist wealth redistribution; the others claim to speak for constitutional liberty or religious tradition.

Yet when it comes to practical policy, they repeatedly land in the exact same place:

⚠️Undermining American Strength Abroad:
The DSA platform explicitly demands defunding the Pentagon, closing overseas U.S. military bases, and cutting off all support to democratic allies like Israel. At the exact same time, the Ron Paul Institute and New Christian Right influencers push the very same isolationist agenda—calling for the dismantling of the U.S. defense apparatus and abandoning key allies abroad.

⚠️Weakening Our Borders:
While MAGA fights to secure the southern border, finish the wall, and enforce the rule of law, the DSA calls for abolishing ICE and granting mass amnesty—a position mirrored by the Ron Paul Institute’s push for open borders and ending border enforcement.

⚠️Attacking the Constitutional Republic:
Both the socialist left and hardline fringe groups seek to tear down the American system from within. The DSA wants to abolish the Electoral College and the U.S. Senate to cement permanent one-party rule, while self-described "post-Trump" Christian nationalists openly reject the American founding and call for scrapping secular constitutional protections altogether.

WHY MAGA STANDS APART AS THE COMMON SENSE MAJORITY 🇺🇸
Unlike fringe internet subcultures and socialist radicals, the MAGA agenda is rooted in practical results for working-class families and the preservation of our Constitutional Republic:

▶️Peace Through Strength, Not Retreat:
MAGA opposes endless, wasteful foreign wars, yet recognizes that a weak America invites global chaos. Rather than gutting the military or abandoning allies like Israel, America First policies rebuild our defense industrial base, modernize the armed forces, and deter adversaries through strength.

▶️Protecting American Workers:
Where socialist radicals want government takeovers of industry and libertarians want unrestricted globalist free trade, MAGA uses strategic tariffs, deregulation, and domestic energy dominance to bring manufacturing jobs back to the U.S. heartland.

▶️Law, Order, and Sovereignty:
A nation without borders isn't a nation at all. MAGA champions legal immigration, secure borders, support for law enforcement, and constitutional judges who defend the rights of everyday citizens.

DEFENDING THE MOVEMENT AGAINST RADICAL DISTRACTIONS
As conservative voters look toward the future, fringe commentators and self-proclaimed purists continue trying to divide the Republican coalition from the outside. Whether they are attacking mainstream leaders, flirting with antisemitic tropes, or echoing far-left talking points against American allies, these factions share one thing in common: they offer zero electoral path to victory and zero solutions for working families.

In the end, the political horseshoe makes one thing clear. While extremists on the far left and far right echo each other from the sidelines, the MAGA movement remains the true mainstream voice of American strength, sovereignty, and common sense.

NEHRU AND THAROOR: THE ENDURING IDEA OF INDIA
TWO GENERATIONS, ONE SHARED CONVICTION: INDIA'S UNITY MUST REST UPON PLURALITY, ITS NATIONALISM UPON INCLUSION, AND ITS FUTURE UPON EQUAL BELONGING.
Mr. Jawaharlal Nehru and Dr. Shashi Tharoor belong to different historical moments, yet their intellectual engagement converges on one fundamental question: What holds together a nation as extraordinarily diverse as India?
In his essay Democracy at 55 (18 August 2002), Dr. Tharoor offered a particularly evocative interpretation of Nehru's vision:
“Jawaharlal Nehru articulated it as pluralism vindicated by history, seeing the country as an ‘ancient palimpsest’ on which successive rulers and subjects had inscribed their visions without erasing what had been asserted previously.” https://t.co/dfrA4VwjJU
For Mr. Nehru, the challenge was to translate the aspirations of the freedom movement into the foundations of a modern republic. His vision rested upon secularism, scientific temper, economic modernisation, institutional development and a national identity transcending religious and linguistic divisions.
Dr. Tharoor does more than carry this vision forward. Drawing upon his diplomatic experience, historical scholarship and literary understanding, he brings his own intellectual perspective to India's civilisational pluralism, constitutional morality, individual liberty and religious tolerance.
Their approaches are not identical, but their philosophical common ground is unmistakable. Both reject the reduction of Indian identity to a single religious, linguistic or cultural narrative. Both recognise that India's diversity is integral to its national character, not an obstacle to national unity.
Where Mr. Nehru helped give institutional and political expression to an inclusive national vision, Dr. Tharoor brings renewed intellectual engagement to its interpretation, defence and contemporary relevance.
Ultimately, the idea of India belongs neither to one generation nor to one political personality. It is a continuing national conversation in which every Indian must have an equal stake.
INDIA DOES NOT NEED TO CHOOSE BETWEEN UNITY AND DIVERSITY. ITS ENDURING GREATNESS LIES IN THE ABILITY TO EMBRACE BOTH.
