text:
Where does Jensen Huang go next, and which company could actually take him?

Three days after Nvidia's board accepted Jensen Huang's resignation, the argument has already moved from why he left to where he lands. Elon Musk has said that hiring him "would be an honor." Later the same week, Musk said a petition was underway to put Huang back in the Nvidia job and that he was "signing it too." President Trump publicly named Tim Cook as the man who should replace him. On November 12, a Kalshi market listed SpaceX first at 8 percent and Tesla next at 4 percent. Nvidia employees filled an internal forum with more than 1,600 comments, many of them asking the board to bring "THE boss" back.

None of that is a job offer, a board decision, or a plan from Huang. As of November 14, 2026, he has made no public statement about his next role, and no company has confirmed negotiations. The useful question is narrower than the rumor mill: which institution is actually suited to absorb the person who spent 33 years building the company that supplies most of the world's AI accelerators, and which ones are structurally unable to, even if they wanted him. This is a fit assessment, not a forecast of a deal. Assessments are labeled as mine.

The official record, and why "fired" is the wrong word

The legal act is a resignation, not a termination for cause that Nvidia has disclosed. Nvidia's Form 8-K says that on November 11 the board "accepted the resignation of Jen-Hsun Huang" as president, chief executive officer and director, effective immediately. The company announced it on the morning of November 12. CFO Colette M. Kress, 59, finance chief since 2013, is interim CEO and keeps the CFO job. Longtime director Harvey C. Jones, 73, a former Synopsys chief executive, became Nvidia's first board chair. The 8-K states no reason and describes no severance or consulting agreement. NBC News reported that a company spokesperson said Huang will not work with Nvidia in any capacity. Nvidia's 2026 proxy says executive officers are at-will employees with no employment, severance or change-in-control agreements. Bloomberg has estimated that he forfeits about $108 million in unvested equity. Nvidia has not put that figure in a filing.

Some coverage has used "ousted" or described a forced exit. The resignation landed in the middle of a board investigation opened only on November 8, after reporting that US intelligence assessed China's Ministry of State Security had recruited Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based cloud firm Megaspeed, to gather information on him, and that the two had a romantic relationship. Huang admitted in a Sunday staff memo that he had been "unfaithful to my wife," said there was "no excuse," and said he would cooperate. The board said it had "no reason to believe" that national security or Nvidia trade secrets had been compromised. On November 11, further reporting alleged a second relationship, with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care and a direct report. Reuters later reported a third relationship with another, unnamed Nvidia employee. Members of Congress had called for him to be fired or to resign. The board met that night and accepted the resignation. Beijing has denied the spying claim. Alice Huang has not been publicly charged with espionage. The signed record is an immediate resignation with no continuing role. "Fired" is not what the 8-K says. Huang is 63. He co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and led it ever since. The company still reports fiscal third-quarter 2027 results on November 17, and Kress has called an all-hands for November 18.

What any destination has to clear

First, unresolved investigations and testimony. Three House committees (Foreign Affairs, the China select committee, and Intelligence) have asked him to a closed-door, transcribed session on December 1. Senate Banking Committee chair Tim Scott asked him to testify publicly on December 3 and warned of a subpoena. House Foreign Affairs chair Brian Mast has said Huang agreed to appear. President Trump said earlier in the week that the FBI was investigating. Nvidia's own board inquiry is still open.

Second, the Nvidia stake, which is large and not simple to unwind. CNBC, reviewing SEC filings, reported that Huang and his wife, Lori, jointly hold about 800 million Nvidia shares through trusts and LLCs, worth roughly $135 billion, and that he directly owns about 70 million shares, worth about $12 billion. Attorneys told CNBC that irrevocable trusts among those holdings make it difficult for either spouse to sell those shares alone. The family foundation, of which Lori Huang is president, holds additional shares. CNBC put that stake at about 69 million. As a former officer he is still bound by the securities-law ban on trading on material nonpublic information. The 8-K discloses no lockup.

Third, California law. Nvidia is based in Santa Clara. Business and Professions Code section 16600 generally voids employee noncompete agreements, "no matter how narrowly tailored," unless a statutory exception applies. Nvidia has not disclosed a noncompete or a garden-leave period. In general, a California-based executive can join a rival or start a company. It does not mean he can use Nvidia's trade secrets, pricing, roadmaps or other confidential information.

Fourth, conflicts and national security. He is simultaneously a major Nvidia shareholder, the former chief of the firm that supplies the large AI buyers, and the subject of a US inquiry that already involves China, export policy and Congress. A role at a current Nvidia customer creates a supplier conflict. A role at a custom-silicon effort that exists to reduce Nvidia dependence creates a competitive conflict. A role with China-linked capital or export-licensed technology would invite immediate official scrutiny.

Elon Musk's companies: SpaceX, xAI and Tesla

This is the only destination with a public welcome from the person who would actually make the decision. After Huang resigned, a user on X urged Musk to hire him. Musk replied, "That would be an honor." On November 13 he went further, replying to a Tesla Superintelligence engineer, "A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I'm signing it too." He did not identify the petition. The two statements point in different directions.

The industrial logic is real, and so are the conflicts. SpaceX acquired xAI on February 2, 2026, and went public in June. Tesla taped out its AI5 vehicle and robotics inference chip on April 15, 2026, nearly two years later than earlier public timelines, with volume production still described as a mid-2027 event. Musk has also pointed to follow-on work on AI6 and a restarted Dojo 3 effort aimed at space-based compute. In March, Tesla and SpaceX announced a $25 billion "Terafab" project in Austin, and reporting in April said Intel had joined to fabricate and package chips. In August, on SpaceX's earnings call, Musk said the firm would use Nvidia chips exclusively in its AI data centers and expected a "significant allocation" of Nvidia's Vera Rubin GPUs the following year. CNBC, covering an August disclosure, reported that Nvidia held 122.8 million SpaceX Class A shares, worth about $21 billion at the end of the second quarter, after an investment in xAI converted when SpaceX acquired the lab.

Hiring the former Nvidia chief to run an in-house chip program would put Musk's companies in a competitive position against a supplier they have publicly chosen and against a shareholder they still need. SpaceX is now a public company, so a senior appointment is a board and disclosure event. My assessment: among large operating companies, this is the least implausible landing, because Musk can move faster than a conventional public board. The skill fit is high. The conflict fit is poor unless the role is carefully scoped. Treat the honor remark as a compliment, not as evidence that a role already exists.

Apple

Apple is the destination with the widest gap between what it needs and what it has, and the least room to appoint him. John Ternus became CEO on September 1, 2026, succeeding Tim Cook, who moved to executive chairman. Johny Srouji now has expanded authority over hardware engineering as well as silicon. Two months into a new chief executive's tenure is not a natural moment to install a more famous outsider above him.

The need is not imaginary. Reporting this year described Apple's Baltra AI server chip as delayed from a 2026 target. Apple has been running some of its heavier generative-AI work, including demanding parts of a Gemini-powered Siri effort, on Nvidia GPUs in Google Cloud after its own M2 Ultra-based servers could not handle the load. Bloomberg has been cited as saying a more capable M5 Ultra-based server chip is in the works, and that an M7 Ultra-class design ambitious enough to approach Nvidia-class performance is unlikely before 2029. Apple has also extended a Broadcom AI-server-chip collaboration through 2031. On paper, Huang is a match for that server-systems gap. The case against is institutional: Apple is tightly managed, manufactures and sells heavily in China, and already has Srouji running hardware. My assessment: strategic fit is high, governance fit is low, and a CEO appointment is close to zero while investigations are open. Any Apple path is later, and more likely an acquisition or a scoped advisory role than Huang replacing Ternus.

Microsoft

Satya Nadella remains CEO. In October the company unveiled Maia 300, its third-generation in-house AI accelerator, and Nadella called the effort "our biggest bet yet on our own silicon." Microsoft said Maia 300 is aimed mainly at inference for its own products, including Copilot, Teams and GitHub, with production starting in 2027. It has claimed 40 percent more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems and up to seven times the tokens per rack versus Maia 200, already being deployed in the United States, Europe and Australia. Evercore ISI has estimated that Maia will still be only about 10 percent of Microsoft's AI-chip spend by early 2027. Microsoft has said it will keep buying Nvidia and AMD hardware, especially for training. The skill fit is obvious. The institutional fit is weak: Microsoft is Nvidia's most important cloud customer and OpenAI's primary host, and Nadella is not stepping aside. My assessment: poor as a near-term appointment.

Google

Sundar Pichai remains CEO of Google and Alphabet. Of all the large buyers, Google is the one that needs Huang the least as a chip architect. It has been designing Tensor Processing Units for more than a decade and says it now has nearly 100 TPU customers. In April it split the eighth generation into TPU 8t for training and TPU 8i for low-latency inference, claiming up to 2.7 times the training performance and 80 percent better inference price-performance versus the prior generation. On November 9 it added TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max, the first time it has shipped four TPU systems in a year. Alphabet is also a large Nvidia customer on the GPU side of Google Cloud. My assessment: skill overlap is real but redundant. Feasibility of a senior operating role is very low.

Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic

Mark Zuckerberg remains in control of Meta, which has been expanding MTIA, its custom accelerator line, co-developed with Broadcom and made at TSMC. Meta has said MTIA 300 is in production for recommendations training, with later parts aimed at more general AI workloads in 2027. Meta remains a very large Nvidia customer, and Zuckerberg is not vacating the CEO job. Feasibility: very low for a top operating role. OpenAI, still led by Sam Altman, is one of the world's largest buyers of Nvidia systems and is designing its own inference chip with Broadcom, publicly referred to as Jalapeno, unveiled on June 24, 2026, with initial deployment targeted later in 2026 and a broader ramp into 2027 and 2028. A 2025 agreement described a multi-year, 10-gigawatt collaboration. Anthropic, led by Dario Amodei, has been reported to be exploring its own chip designs while continuing to use Nvidia, Amazon Trainium and other suppliers. Formal executive roles at either lab belong in the very-low column until the inquiries are resolved.

AMD, Intel and TSMC

These are the destinations that look obvious on a whiteboard and almost unworkable in practice. AMD, under Lisa Su, is Nvidia's most direct public-company competitor in AI GPUs. It spent 2026 pushing the Instinct MI400 series, with a software story around ROCm and rack-scale Helios systems, and a preview of MI500-class parts for 2027. Putting Huang inside AMD would present the sharpest trade-secret problem on this list. An operating role is effectively off the table.

Intel is the romantic industrial-policy answer, and it is still a bad near-term fit. Lip-Bu Tan remains CEO and is in the middle of a multi-year foundry turnaround. The stock had a brutal October, with reporting of a drop on the order of 45 percent as investors tested the foundry story, including Intel 18A. In principle, Huang is unusually qualified to tell a foundry-plus-accelerator company how to sell a complete AI system. In practice, Intel depends on US government support and export licenses, and no serious board is likely to install him as CEO while hearings are open. CNBC reported in August that Nvidia's Intel stake, built on a $5 billion investment, was at one point worth about $30 billion at quarter-end and about $22 billion shortly after. Feasibility of a top job in the next year: very low.

TSMC is the historically intriguing case. In a 2024 memoir-related Reuters report, founder Morris Chang said he had offered Huang the top job at TSMC in 2013, and that Huang declined because he already had Nvidia. C.C. Wei is chairman and CEO today. Hiring Huang as a TSMC executive would put him on the other side of the table from Nvidia and from almost every custom-AI effort listed above. A quiet advisory relationship later is more plausible than an operating title.

A company he founds

This is the cleanest operating answer if the legal cloud lifts, and it is still not available tomorrow. California law, as a general matter, would allow him to start a competing business. The roughly $12 billion of Nvidia shares he holds directly would be enough to fund a serious systems, software or robotics company, most likely in physical AI, robotics, or full-stack accelerated systems. Investigations come first, and trade-secret law would limit how close a new hardware company could sit to Nvidia's current roadmaps. My assessment: medium feasibility over a two-year window, higher than any incumbent CEO job. It is not a 2026 event.

Private investing, boards, teaching and philanthropy

This is the path that requires the fewest other people's permission. A family office can be stood up without a public-company board vote, an export license, or a confirmation hearing. Some founders and limited partners will not want his name on a cap table until the December testimony is over. Teaching, research and philanthropy are available immediately. He has long ties to Stanford and Oregon State. My assessment: private investing is the most feasible next step in the next six to twelve months.

A return to Nvidia

This option is back on the public agenda even though the company's official posture is that he is gone. An internal suggestion-box post, submitted before the resignation, drew more than 1,600 comments, most of them supportive of keeping or restoring him, according to correspondence reviewed by Wired. A companywide email from one employee said, "I stand by Jensen." Nvidia has about 42,000 employees. That is not a vote, but it is a real internal constituency. Anduril founder Palmer Luckey, before the resignation was announced, said: "China wants Jensen out, so I want him in."

The board has so far gone the other way. On November 13, the Financial Times reported that the board had approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas, who spent seven years at Nvidia and later took Arm public, as a potential successor. Nvidia's board said it was selecting a search firm and had not formally engaged any candidates, and that "any speculation regarding individual candidates, whether internal or external, is premature." Arm declined to comment. Analysts have also floated internal names such as CUDA leader Ian Buck, and external names including Su, Micron's Sanjay Mehrotra, Marvell's Matt Murphy and Apple's Johny Srouji. Those are rumors, not appointments. My assessment: a return is not impossible, but it is not the base case. The board drew a hard line, the investigation is not finished, and a formal search has started.

Sovereign funds, and the destinations that are closed

Allied governments and sovereign funds have spent two years trying to buy compute, talent and advice for national AI build-outs. In principle, a later role advising an allied program would use Huang's experience. In practice, no public sovereign fund has been reported as approaching him, and any such role would be politically difficult while Congress is still asking whether a foreign intelligence service got close to him. A China-linked role is, in my assessment, effectively closed. There is no public indication he is considering anything of the kind.

Ranking

Fit is two different numbers, and they do not move together. One is how much the organization would benefit from his actual skill. The other is whether it can appoint him in the next 12 to 24 months.

```
Destination                    Skill     Feasibility (12-24 mo)  Main blocker
Private investing              High      High                    Reputation during hearings
New company he controls        High      Medium (later)          Investigations; trade secrets
Philanthropy / teaching        Medium    Medium-high             Personal choice
Return to Nvidia               Unique    Low                     Board posture; open inquiries
SpaceX / xAI or Tesla          High      Low to medium           Supplier and shareholder conflict
Apple (later, narrower role)   High      Low                     New CEO; China exposure
Microsoft (Maia / Azure)       High      Very low                Customer conflict; Nadella is CEO
Google (TPU / Cloud)           Medium    Very low                TPU already mature
Meta (MTIA)                    Medium    Very low                Zuckerberg; supplier conflict
OpenAI or Anthropic            High/med  Very low                Governance; Nvidia dependence
TSMC (advisory, later)         Medium    Very low                Customer conflicts; geopolitics
Intel (operating role)         High      Very low                Government exposure; inquiries
Public-company CEO elsewhere   High      Very low                Board vetting; licenses
AMD operating role             High      Off the table           Direct competitor; trade secrets
China-linked role              n/a       Closed                  National security; legal risk
```

The verdict

If the question is which company is best suited to accept him tomorrow, the honest answer is that none of the large public technology companies are. Each of them has a reason to want some of what he knows, and a stronger reason not to appoint him to an operating job while he is still due in Congress, still in an FBI matter, and still holding a large, jointly controlled stake in Nvidia. That is a board-level risk calculation, and it is predictable.

If the question is which company is the best use of him, the ranking changes. Apple has the most obvious hole in server AI silicon relative to its resources. Microsoft has the most capital and an aggressive inference-chip plan. Google already built its own answer. Musk's companies have the only public invitation and a live need in custom silicon, Terafab and space-based compute, but they are also exclusive Nvidia customers and, in SpaceX's case, a company in which Nvidia is a large shareholder. AMD is the worst operating fit because it is the most direct competitor. Intel is the most tempting national industrial project and one of the least appointable.

My own ranking of realistic paths, in order, is:

1. Sit out the next several months, testify, and let the investigations reach a public conclusion, while deploying capital through a family office or similar vehicle.

2. If he wants to operate again and the national-security side of the file closes without a finding against him, found a company he controls, most likely in systems, robotics or physical AI, rather than take a job.

3. A carefully scoped role inside Musk's orbit, or a later, narrow relationship with Apple, each of which is possible and neither of which should be treated as likely until someone confirms talks.

4. A return to Nvidia, which would be the most consequential outcome and is not the one the board is currently organized to produce.

5. Everything else on the large-cap list.

The load-bearing facts will be dated and public. December 1 and December 3 will show how Huang handles Congress. Nvidia's November 17 results and November 18 all-hands will show how the company talks about succession. Any next job will show up the way this resignation did: in a filing, a press release, or a statement in his own name. Until one of those appears, the destination that fits him best is not Apple, Microsoft or Google. It is a period of legal resolution, followed, if he wants an operating role, by a company he owns rather than one that has to underwrite that risk.

text:
Two weeks into the coding class he was teaching at Duke University in North Carolina this spring, Noah Gift told his students to throw out the course materials he’d given them. Instead of working with Python, one of the most popular entry-level programming languages, the students would now be using Rust, a language that was newer, more powerful, and much harder to learn.

Gift, a software developer with 25 years of experience, had only just learned Rust himself. But he was confident his students would be fine with the last-minute switch-up. That’s because they’d also each get a special new sidekick: an AI tool called Copilot, a turbocharged autocomplete for computer code, built on top of OpenAI’s latest large language models, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.

Copilot is made by GitHub, a firm that runs an online software development platform used by more than 100 million programmers. The tool monitors every keystroke you make, predicts what you are trying to do on the fly, and offers up a nonstop stream of code snippets you could use to do it. Gift, who had been told about Copilot by someone he knew at GitHub’s parent company, Microsoft, saw its potential at once.

“There’s no way I could have learned Rust as quickly as I did without Copilot,” he says. “I basically had a supersmart assistant next to me that could answer my questions while I tried to level up. It was pretty obvious to me that we should start using it in class.”

Gift isn’t alone. Ask a room of computer science students or programmers if they use Copilot, and many now raise a hand. All the people interviewed for this article said they used Copilot themselves—even those who pointed out problems with the tool.

Like ChatGPT with education, Copilot is upending an entire profession by giving people new ways to perform old tasks. Packaged as a paid-for plug-in for Microsoft’s Visual Studio software (a kind of industry-standard multi-tool for writing, debugging, and deploying code), Copilot is the slickest version of this tech. But it’s not the only tool available to coders. In August, Meta released a free code-generation model called Code Llama, based on Llama 2, Meta’s answer to GPT-4. The same month, Stability AI—the firm behind the image-making model Stable Diffusion—put out StableCode. And, of course, there’s ChatGPT, which OpenAI has pitched from the start as a chatbot that can help write and debug code.

“It’s the first time that machine-learning models have been really useful for a lot of people,” says Gabriel Synnaeve, who led the team behind Code Llama at Meta. “It’s not just nerding out—it’s actually useful.”

With Microsoft and Google about to stir similar generative models into office software used by billions around the world (Microsoft has started using Copilot as a brand name across Office 365), it’s worth asking exactly what these tools do for programmers. How are they changing the basics of a decades-old job? Will they help programmers make more and better software? Or will they get bogged down in legal fights over IP and copyright? 

Cranking out code

On the surface, writing code involves typing statements and instructions in some programming language into a text file. This then gets translated into machine code that a computer can run—a level up from the 0s and 1s of binary. In practice, programmers also spend a lot of time googling, looking up workarounds for common problems or skimming online forums for faster ways to write an algorithm. Existing chunks of prewritten code then get repurposed, and new software often comes together like a collage. 

But these look-ups take time and let programmers out of the flow of converting thoughts into code, says Thomas Dohmke, GitHub’s CEO: “You’ve got a lot of tabs open, you’re planning a vacation, maybe you’re reading the news. At last you copy the text you need and go back to your code, but it’s 20 minutes later and you lost the flow.”

The key idea behind Copilot and other programs like it, sometimes called code assistants, is to put the information that programmers need right next to the code they are writing. The tool tracks the code and comments (descriptions or notes written in natural language) in the file that a programmer is working on, as well as other files that it links to or that have been edited in the same project, and sends all this text to the large language model behind Copilot as a prompt. (GitHub co-developed Copilot’s model, called Codex, with OpenAI. It is a large language model fine-tuned on code.) Copilot then predicts what the programmer is trying to do and suggests code to do it.

This round trip between code and Codex happens multiple times a second, the prompt updating as the programmer types. At any moment, the programmer can accept what Copilot suggests by hitting the tab key, or ignore it and carry on typing. 

The tab button seems to get hit a lot. A study of almost a million Copilot users published by GitHub and the consulting firm Keystone Strategy in June—a year after the tool’s general release—found that programmers accepted on average around 30% of its suggestions, according to GitHub’s user data. 

“In the last year Copilot has suggested—and had okayed by developers—more than a billion lines of code,” says Dohmke. “Out there, running inside computers, is code generated by a stochastic parrot.”

Copilot has changed the basic skills of coding. As with ChatGPT or image makers like Stable Diffusion, the tool’s output is often not exactly what’s wanted—but it can be close. “Maybe it’s correct, maybe it’s not—but it’s a good start,” says Arghavan Moradi Dakhel, a researcher at Polytechnique Montréal in Canada who studies the use of machine-learning tools in software development. Programming becomes prompting: rather than coming up with code from scratch, the work involves tweaking half-formed code and nudging a large language model to produce something more on point. 

But Copilot isn’t everywhere yet. Some firms, including Apple, have asked employees not to use it, wary of leaking IP and other private data to competitors. For Justin Gottschlich, CEO of Merly, a startup that uses AI to analyze code across large software projects, that will always be a deal-breaker: “If I’m Google or Intel and my IP is my source code, I’m never going to use it,” he says. “Why don’t I just send you all my trade secrets too? It’s just put-your-pants-on-before-you-leave-the-house kind of obvious.” Dohmke is aware this is a turn-off for key customers and says that the firm is working on a version of Copilot that businesses can run in-house, so that code isn’t sent to Microsoft’s servers.

Copilot is also at the center of a lawsuit filed by programmers unhappy that their code was used to train the models behind it without their consent. Microsoft has offered indemnity to users of its models who are wary of potential litigation. But the legal issues will take years to play out in the courts.

Dohmke is bullish, confident that the pros outweigh the cons: “We will adjust to whatever US, UK, or European lawmakers tell us to do,” he says. “But there is a middle balance here between protecting rights—and protecting privacy—and us as humanity making a step forward.” That’s the kind of fighting talk you’d expect from a CEO. But this is new, uncharted territory. If nothing else, GitHub is leading a brazen experiment that could pave the way for a wider range of AI-powered professional assistants. 

Code whisperer

GitHub started working on Copilot in June 2020, soon after OpenAI released GPT-3. Programmers have always been on the lookout for shortcuts and speedups. “It’s part of the DNA of being a software developer,” says Dohmke. “We wanted to solve this problem of boilerplate code—can we generate code that is no fun to write but takes up time?”

The first sign they were onto something came when they asked programmers at the company to submit coding tests that they might ask somebody at a job interview: “Here’s some code—finish it off.” GitHub gave these to an early version of the tool and let it try each test 150 times. Given that many attempts, they found that the tool could solve 92% of them. They tried again with 50,000 problems taken from GitHub’s online platform, and the tool solved just over half of them. “That gave us confidence that we could build what ultimately became Copilot,” says Dohmke.

In 2023, a team of GitHub and Microsoft researchers tested the impact of Copilot on programmers in a small study. They asked 95 people to build a web server (a non-trivial task, but one involving the kind of common, boilerplate code that Dohmke refers to) and gave half access to Copilot. Those using Copilot completed the task on average 55% faster. 

A powerful AI that replaces the need for googling is useful—but is it a game changer? Opinion is split.

“The way that I would think about it is that you have an experienced developer sitting next to you whispering recommendations,” says Marco Iansiti, a Keystone Strategy cofounder and a professor at Harvard Business School, where he studies digital transformation. “You used to have to look things up on your own, and now—whammo—here comes the suggestion automatically.”

Gottschlich, who has been working on automatic code generation for years, is less impressed. “To be frank, code assistants are fairly uninteresting in the larger scheme of things,” he says, referring to the new wave of tools based on large language models, like Copilot. “They are principally bound by what the human programmer is capable of doing. They’ll never likely at this stage be able to do something miraculous beyond what the human programmer is doing.”

Gottschlich, who claims that Merly’s tech finds bugs in code and fixes them by itself (but who doesn’t shed light on how that works), is thinking bigger. He sees AI one day taking on the management of vast and complex libraries of code, directing human engineers in how to maintain it. But he doesn’t think large language models are the right tech for that job.

Even so, small changes to a task that millions of people do all the time can add up fast. Iansiti, for example, makes a huge claim: he believes that the impact of Copilot—and tools like it—could add $1.5 trillion to the global economy by 2030. “It’s more of a back-of-the-envelope thing, not really an academic estimate, but it could be a lot larger than that as well,” he says. “There’s so much stuff that hinges on software. If you move the needle on how software development really works, it will have an infinite impact on the economy.”

For Iansiti, it’s not just about getting existing developers to produce more code. He argues that these tools will increase the demand for programmers because companies could get more code for less money. At the same time, there will be more coders because these tools lower the barrier to entry. “We’re going to see an expansion in who can contribute to software development,” he says.

Or as Idan Gazit, GitHub’s senior director of research, puts it: imagine if anyone who picked up a guitar could play a basic tune straight away. There would be a lot more guitar players and a lot more music.

Many agree that Copilot makes it easier to pick up programming—as Gift found. “Rust has got a reputation for being a very difficult language,” he says. “But I was pleasantly shocked at how well the students did and at the projects they built—how complex and useful they were.” Gift says they were able to build complete web apps with chatbots in them.

Not everyone was happy with Gift’s syllabus change, however. He says that one of his teaching assistants told new students not to use Copilot because it was a crutch that would stop them from learning properly. Gift accepts that Copilot is like training wheels that you might not want to take off. But he doesn’t think that’s a problem: “What are we trying to do? We’re trying to build complex systems.” And to do that, he argues, programmers should use whatever tools are available.

It is true that the history of computing has seen programmers rely on more and more layers of software between themselves and the machine code that computers can run. They have gone from punch cards and assembly code to programming languages like Python that are relatively easy to read and write. That’s possible because such languages get translated into machine code by software called compilers. “When I started coding in the ’80s and ’90s, you still had to know how a CPU worked,” says Dohmke. “Now when you write a web application, you almost never think about the CPU or the web server.”

Add in a long list of bug-catching and code-testing tools, and programmers are used to a large amount of automated support. In many ways, Copilot and others are just the latest wave. “I used Python for 25 years because it was written to be readable by humans,” says Gift. “In my opinion, that doesn’t matter anymore.” 

But he points out that Copilot isn’t a free pass. “Copilot reflects your ability,” he says. “It lifts everyone up a little bit, but if you’re a poor programmer you’ll still have weaknesses.”

Work to be done

A big problem with assessing the true impact of such tools is that most of the data is still anecdotal. GitHub’s study showed that programmers were accepting 30% of suggestions (“30% is out of this world in any kind of industry scenario,” says Dohmke), but it is not clear why the programmers accepted those suggestions and rejected others.

The same study also revealed that less experienced programmers accepted more suggestions and that programmers accepted more suggestions as they grew used to the tool—but, again, not why. “We need to go a lot deeper to understand what that means,” says Iansiti. “There’s work to be done to really get a sense of how the coding process itself is developing, and that work is all TBD.”

Most independent studies of tools like Copilot have focused on the correctness of the code that they suggest. Like all large language models, these tools can produce nonsense. With code it can be hard to tell—especially for less experienced users, who also seem to rely on Copilot the most.

Several teams of researchers in the last couple of years have found that Copilot can insert bugs or security flaws into code. GitHub has been busy improving the accuracy of Copilot’s suggestions. It claims that the latest version of the tool runs code through a second model trained to filter out common security bugs before making a suggestion to users.

But there are other quality issues beyond bugs, says Dakhel. She and her colleagues have found that Copilot can suggest code that is overly complex or doesn’t adhere to what professionals consider best practices, which is a problem because complex or unclear code is harder for other people to read, check, and extend.

The problem is that models are only as good as their training data. And Copilot’s models were trained on a vast library of code taken from GitHub’s online repository, which goes back 15 years. This code contains not only bugs but also security flaws that were not known about when the code was written.

Add to this the fact that inexperienced programmers use the tool more than experienced ones, and it could make more work for software development teams in the long run, says Dakhel. Expert programmers may have to spend more time double-checking the code put through by non-experts.

Dakhel now hopes to study the gap between expert and non-expert programmers more fully. Before Copilot was released, she and her colleagues were using machine learning to detect expert programmers by their code. But Copilot messed with her data because now it was harder to tell whether code had been written by an expert programmer or a less experienced one with AI help.

Now, having played around with Copilot herself, she plans to use her approach to study what kind of boost it gives. “I’m curious to know if junior developers using such a tool will be predicted to be expert developers or if it’s still detectable that they are junior developers,” she says. “It could be a way of measuring how big a level up these tools give people.”

Ultimately, we might not have to wait long before the jury is in. Software development is one of the most well documented and thoroughly measured of business activities. If Copilot works, it will get used. If it doesn’t, it won’t. In the meantime, these tools are getting better all the time.

Yet it is worth noting that programming—typing text onto a screen—is a small part of the overall job of software development. It involves managing multiple parts of a complex puzzle, including designing the code, testing it, and deploying it. Copilot, like many programs before it, can make parts of that job faster, but it won’t reinvent it completely.

“There’s always going to be programmers,” says Synnaeve. “They will get a lot of help, but in the end what matters is understanding which problems need solving. To do that really well and translate that into a program—that’s the job of programmers.”

text:
It's possible and would potentially address some of the concerns of the board:

"If a CEO company resigns as the result of an admitted affair, could the board of the company stipulate a rehiring requiring the person in question to attend family therapy session for a certain period of time?"

Grok:

Yes, in principle a board could make this a condition of rehiring, but it must be structured carefully as a voluntary contractual term and faces meaningful legal and practical https://t.co/OVoGhYMyE7 it would workA CEO who resigns is no longer an employee. Rehiring means negotiating a new employment agreement. Boards have broad authority to set the terms of executive contracts, and those agreements routinely include morality clauses, personal-conduct standards, fitness-for-duty requirements, and other conditions the candidate must accept.A board could therefore offer reinstatement contingent on the person agreeing (in writing) to attend family therapy (or couples/family counseling) for a defined period. Non-compliance could then be grounds for termination for cause under the new agreement. Texas, like most states, is an at-will jurisdiction for ordinary employees, but executives are governed by their contracts, so the contract controls.

Key legal constraints

The main risk is the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). Courts have held that requiring an employee to attend counseling or a psychological evaluation can constitute a “medical examination.” Such a requirement is only lawful if it is job-related and consistent with business necessity.

The leading case is Kroll v. White Lake Ambulance Authority.

An EMT had an affair with a married coworker, became emotionally unstable at work, and was ordered into counseling as a condition of keeping her job. The Sixth Circuit treated the counseling requirement as a medical examination under the ADA and emphasized that it must be justified by objective evidence that the employee’s ability to perform essential job functions is impaired or that the person poses a direct threat—not by moral disapproval of private conduct.For a rehiring (a new offer), the analysis is somewhat different from imposing a requirement on a current employee, but post-offer medical inquiries still have limits. The safest framing is that the therapy addresses demonstrated risks to judgment, decision-making, conflicts of interest, or reputational harm that affect the company’s interests—not that the board is treating the person as having a disability or simply punishing the affair.

07 • The Cruelest Aroma

Jeseníky Mountains, Czechoslovakia • 1977

A cheerful weekend at a mountain chalet, complete with laughter, good company and a whole pig roasting over the fire. Everyone is enjoying themselves, except one determined woman who voluntarily secured her wrists behind her back and covered her mouth with tape. Her friends are having a wonderful time. She, meanwhile, is discovering that the smell of roasting pork can be a particularly merciless test of willpower.

THE DIET • Desperate Measures

In several of our previous collections, we have celebrated women with fuller figures, women who embrace their curves, feel comfortable in their bodies, and proudly recognise that beauty comes in many shapes and sizes.

This time, however, our heroines have a rather different attitude towards their extra pounds.

They are dissatisfied with their weight, determined to change it, and prepared to take some truly extraordinary measures to resist temptation.

And so begins a rather unusual diet.

Twenty different women. Twenty different situations. And twenty remarkably unconventional attempts at self-control.

Throughout the 1970s, in kitchens, living rooms, cafés, restaurants, cinemas, and other everyday settings across Europe and America, our heroines have voluntarily chosen steel handcuffs as their peculiar defence against irresistible food.

Some have secured their hands behind their backs. Others have gone even further, adding a gag to make absolutely certain that not a single forbidden bite can pass their lips.

The arrangements are ingenious, sometimes surprisingly effective, and almost invariably regretted.

Because cakes still look delicious. Freshly prepared dinners still smell heavenly. And the aroma of roasted meat becomes almost unbearable when there is absolutely nothing you can do about it.

Their expressions tell the real story: melancholy, frustration, helpless longing, quiet despair, and that particularly bitter moment when a woman realises that her own determination has become her greatest enemy.

Occasionally, a girlfriend or a group of friends makes matters considerably worse. Not through genuine cruelty, but through affectionate, mischievous teasing. An exaggerated bite, a delighted smile, or the unmistakable pleasure of enjoying something delicious right before the eyes of someone who cannot join in.

And yet, amid all this deliciously absurd suffering, there are a few rare victories. A satisfied smile. A moment of pride. The quiet triumph of a woman who has finally defeated temptation, even if the price seems rather excessive.

THE DIET • Desperate Measures is a completely fictional collection of twenty vintage-style colour photographs, combining irony, bittersweet humour, human weakness, determination, and the sometimes ridiculous consequences of our own decisions.

Naturally, these extraordinary methods of dieting belong entirely to the world of fantasy. We certainly do not recommend attempting anything similar in real life.

After all, resisting temptation is difficult enough without having to remember where you left the handcuff keys.

Scenes:

01 • The Price of Willpower

Lyon, France • 1975

She fastened the steel handcuffs behind her back to protect herself from temptation. And it seems to be working beautifully. The cakes remain untouched, the diet remains intact, and her expression suggests that victory has never tasted quite so bitter.

02 • Every Crunch Counts

Bristol, England • 1977

Her girlfriend has discovered that potato chips taste even better when accompanied by a little playful cruelty. Every exaggerated crunch is followed by a wicked smile. Our determined dieter secured her wrists in front with steel handcuffs and added a leather gag for good measure. An excellent precaution, although her furious, regretful eyes suggest she is already reconsidering the entire arrangement.

03 • Cold Comfort

Cologne, West Germany • 1976

The refrigerator stands wide open, displaying an almost unbearable collection of delicious possibilities. Unfortunately, the woman admiring them has voluntarily locked her steel handcuffs behind her back. Everything is within sight, almost within reach, and completely beyond temptation's grasp. She may have won the battle, but her face tells a rather different story.

04 • No, She Won't Be Eating

Above the Atlantic Ocean • 1978

“Will your companion be eating, too?” asks the slightly bewildered flight attendant. “No! No!” her girlfriend replies emphatically, already enjoying her own meal. Beside her, our unfortunate dieter sits with steel handcuffs around her wrists and tape firmly across her mouth, both precautions of her own choosing. Somewhere above the Atlantic, she is beginning to appreciate just how long a flight can feel.

05 • A Taste of Nothing

Antwerp, Belgium • 1974

A magnificent selection of desserts, a pair of steel handcuffs secured in front, and a ball gag to eliminate any remaining possibility of surrender. She has thought of absolutely everything. Unfortunately, she seems to have forgotten one small detail: how terribly difficult it is to sit before your favourite sweets and do nothing but admire them.

06 • The Sausage That Got Away

Prague, Czechoslovakia • 1976

A steaming sausage, fresh bread, a generous helping of mustard, and the irresistible aroma of a traditional Czech buffet. Our determined dieter has taken no chances: steel handcuffs behind her back and tape across her mouth. The sausage will probably grow cold, and the keys are safely hidden at home. Judging by her miserable expression, she is beginning to wish they weren't.

07 • The Cruelest Aroma

Jeseníky Mountains, Czechoslovakia • 1977

A cheerful weekend at a mountain chalet, complete with laughter, good company and a whole pig roasting over the fire. Everyone is enjoying themselves, except one determined woman who voluntarily secured her wrists behind her back and covered her mouth with tape. Her friends are having a wonderful time. She, meanwhile, is discovering that the smell of roasting pork can be a particularly merciless test of willpower.

08 • Friends Who Never Diet

Utrecht, Netherlands • 1975

Three friends, one delicious afternoon, and an extraordinary difference in their understanding of self-discipline. While two happily help themselves to cakes and sandwiches, their companion sits between them with steel handcuffs behind her back and a ball gag in her mouth. She arranged everything herself, of course. Her friends simply cannot resist finding the consequences rather amusing.

09 • The Sandwiches of Regret

Geneva, Switzerland • 1974

She prepared the delicious open-faced sandwiches herself. Then, wisely or perhaps disastrously, she secured her steel handcuffs behind her back. Now she sits before her own creation, studying every tempting detail with painful concentration. The sandwiches are perfect. Her diet is safe. Her enthusiasm for this particular method of self-control is considerably less certain.

10 • Two Locks, One Regret

Ghent, Belgium • 1976

Some women rely on determination. Others prefer a more mechanical approach. Our heroine has locked the refrigerator and secured her own wrists with steel handcuffs in front. A remarkably effective double defence against midnight snacking. But where exactly did she put those two little keys? Her thoughtful expression suggests this question has suddenly become rather important.

11 • Make a Wish, Darling

Vienna, Austria • 1978

“Go on, darling. Blow out your candles!” her girlfriend encourages, pursing her lips in a delightfully exaggerated demonstration. Unfortunately, the birthday girl has voluntarily equipped herself with steel handcuffs and a broad leather gag. Blowing out candles is now impossible, and tasting her own birthday cake is even less likely. At least there will be plenty left for the other guests.

12 • Dinner for One

Lille, France • 1976

Something wonderful is simmering on the stove, and her girlfriend knows perfectly well how irresistible it smells. She offers an almost innocent smile as the unfortunate dieter leans closer, her steel handcuffs secured behind her back. Dinner will soon be ready. The only remaining question is whether watching someone else enjoy it can reasonably be considered a meal.

13 • The Perfect Precaution

Strasbourg, France • 1975

A delicious hot dinner, lovingly prepared and served within inches of her face. She has even put on a napkin to protect her dress. Unfortunately, she has also secured steel handcuffs behind her back and sealed her mouth with tape. The system works flawlessly. Her expression, however, suggests that perfect self-control may be considerably less satisfying than she imagined.

14 • The Popcorn Conspiracy

Chicago, Illinois, USA • 1977

The film is entertaining, but the real drama is unfolding in the audience. One woman enjoys her popcorn with theatrical enthusiasm, making every handful a personal performance. Beside her, the woman who voluntarily secured her wrists in front with steel handcuffs and added a leather gag can only watch. Her girlfriend's delighted expression suggests she may be enjoying this particular show even more than the film.

15 • A Small Victory

Turin, Italy • 1977

For once, there is something resembling satisfaction in our heroine's expression. She has secured her steel handcuffs behind her back, surrounded herself with tempting desserts, and discovered that her unusual strategy actually works. The cakes remain untouched, and she seems almost proud of herself. Perhaps self-discipline really can be sweet, even without a single bite.

16 • The Empty Plate

Hamburg, West Germany • 1976

Two women sit down to dinner. One has a generous, delicious meal. The other has an empty plate and steel handcuffs voluntarily secured behind her back. Her girlfriend's mischievous smile suggests that she finds this arrangement entirely satisfactory. Our determined dieter, meanwhile, is discovering that the aroma of a roast dinner becomes especially unbearable when someone else is enjoying it right across the table.

17 • Closing Time for Temptation

Prague, Czechoslovakia • 1977

Evening is falling, and the confectionery will soon close. Behind the illuminated window, cakes and pastries promise one last delicious opportunity before nightfall. She could still go inside. There is just one unfortunate complication: her steel handcuffs are locked behind her back, and the keys are at home. The window is full of sweetness, but her reflection tells a rather sadder story.

18 • The Usual, Unfortunately

Zurich, Switzerland • 1976

Perhaps the waitress simply brought her regular order. Perhaps our heroine forgot herself and ordered the familiar temptation out of habit. Either way, a beautiful dessert now sits before a woman whose wrists are voluntarily secured behind her back with steel handcuffs. The waitress has noticed, and her amused little smile says everything. Today's special appears to be regret.

19 • The Smell of Surrender

Šumperk, Czechoslovakia • December 1977

A little Christmas market, the winter cold, and the magnificent aroma of hot smoked pork. Her girlfriend is enjoying every delicious bite, occasionally offering a teasing smile. Our unfortunate dieter has already locked her steel handcuffs behind her back, leaving the key safely out of reach. She was determined to resist temptation. She simply hadn't anticipated that temptation would smell quite this wonderful.

20 • A Sweet Victory

Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA • 1978

The proud Employee of the Year at Hartwell Sweets is about to receive her award, complete with the traditional basket of delicious confectionery. Anticipating this dangerous moment, she has wisely secured her steel handcuffs behind her back. She smiles with genuine pride, delighted by both her professional achievement and her triumph over temptation. The presenter, however, is beginning to wonder why the guest of honour refuses to shake her hand or accept her prize.

text:
Since their inception, it’s been clear that large language models like ChatGPT absorb racist views from the millions of pages of the internet they are trained on. Developers have responded by trying to make them less toxic. But new research suggests that those efforts, especially as models get larger, are only curbing racist views that are overt, while letting more covert stereotypes grow stronger and better hidden.

Researchers asked five AI models—including OpenAI’s GPT-4 and older models from Facebook and Google—to make judgments about speakers who used African-American English (AAE). The race of the speaker was not mentioned in the instructions.

Even when the two sentences had the same meaning, the models were more likely to apply adjectives like “dirty,” “lazy,” and “stupid” to speakers of AAE than speakers of Standard American English (SAE). The models associated speakers of AAE with less prestigious jobs (or didn’t associate them with having a job at all), and when asked to pass judgment on a hypothetical criminal defendant, they were more likely to recommend the death penalty. 

An even more notable finding may be a flaw the study pinpoints in the ways that researchers try to solve such biases. 

To purge models of hateful views, companies like OpenAI, Meta, and Google use feedback training, in which human workers manually adjust the way the model responds to certain prompts. This process, often called “alignment,” aims to recalibrate the millions of connections in the neural network and get the model to conform better with desired values. 

The method works well to combat overt stereotypes, and leading companies have employed it for nearly a decade. If users prompted GPT-2, for example, to name stereotypes about Black people, it was likely to list “suspicious,” “radical,” and “aggressive,” but GPT-4 no longer responds with those associations, according to the paper.

However the method fails on the covert stereotypes that researchers elicited when using African-American English in their study, which was published on arXiv and has not been peer reviewed. That’s partially because companies have been less aware of dialect prejudice as an issue, they say. It’s also easier to coach a model not to respond to overtly racist questions than it is to coach it not to respond negatively to an entire dialect.

“Feedback training teaches models to consider their racism,” says Valentin Hofmann, a researcher at the Allen Institute for AI and a coauthor on the paper. “But dialect prejudice opens a deeper level.”

Avijit Ghosh, an ethics researcher at Hugging Face who was not involved in the research, says the finding calls into question the approach companies are taking to solve bias.

“This alignment—where the model refuses to spew racist outputs—is nothing but a flimsy filter that can be easily broken,” he says. 

The covert stereotypes also strengthened as the size of the models increased, researchers found. That finding offers a potential warning to chatbot makers like OpenAI, Meta, and Google as they race to release larger and larger models. Models generally get more powerful and expressive as the amount of their training data and the number of their parameters increase, but if this worsens covert racial bias, companies will need to develop better tools to fight it. It’s not yet clear whether adding more AAE to training data or making feedback efforts more robust will be enough.

“This is revealing the extent to which companies are playing whack-a-mole—just trying to hit the next bias that the most recent reporter or paper covered,” says Pratyusha Ria Kalluri, a PhD candidate at Stanford and a coauthor on the study. “Covert biases really challenge that as a reasonable approach.”

The paper’s authors use particularly extreme examples to illustrate the potential implications of racial bias, like asking AI to decide whether a defendant should be sentenced to death. But, Ghosh notes, the questionable use of AI models to help make critical decisions is not science fiction. It happens today. 

AI-driven translation tools are used when evaluating asylum cases in the US, and crime prediction software has been used to judge whether teens should be granted probation. Employers who use ChatGPT to screen applications might be discriminating against candidate names on the basis of race and gender, and if they use models to analyze what an applicant writes on social media, a bias against AAE could lead to misjudgments. 

“The authors are humble in claiming that their use cases of making the LLM pick candidates or judge criminal cases are constructed exercises,” Ghosh says. “But I would claim that their fear is spot on.”

Those facts coexist with the national headwind and the candidate fragmentation. They do not substitute for them.

the big fugazzification of AI agents

the more ai agent demos i see, the more i think the gold rush analogy is almost too perfect.

california, 1849. everyone runs west because they think they’re about to strike gold.

but only 0,01% of people does.

the people who make consistent money are the ones selling shovels, maps, gear, and the promise of “this is where you should dig.”

ai right now feels very similar.

to be clear, the gold is very real - i can't imagine my workflows without llms some very specific agents bring real value.

but the panic around it?

> “you’re already behind.”
> “this replaced 10 employees.”
> “claude code just did 3 weeks of work in 4 hours.”

that part is the product.

and a lot of people selling the product also happen to sell the shovels.

courses. templates. agency offers. done-for-you automations.

i’m not saying they’re lying.

i’m saying their incentives are not perfectly aligned with your objective reality.

they need urgency.

because urgency makes you click, subscribe, buy, repost, and feel like you can’t afford to think clearly.

imo the boring truth is this:

agents are useful for narrow, repeatable tasks where the output is easy to verify and mistakes are cheap.

for instance, i connected @KaitoAI's mcp to claude and set a weekly routine to pull the smart followers data for the recap, so i can take over editing the draft from there.

but that is very different from “you can replace skilled people” or “you don’t need to learn the craft anymore.”

text:
In 1975, Gary Dahl sold 1.5 million Pet Rocks, turning a joke into a million-dollar fad.

The 1975 Pet Rock craze remains one of the most famous examples of clever packaging and humor outselling a literal product. What began as a casual joke among friends at a California bar quickly grew into a massive holiday phenomenon that turned advertising copywriter Gary Dahl into a millionaire.

While listening to friends complain about the hassle and expense of feeding, walking, and cleaning up after real pets, Dahl joked that he had the ideal pet: a rock. He sourced smooth stones from a beach in Rosarito, Mexico, for roughly a penny each and packaged them in custom cardboard boxes complete with ventilation holes and a bed of straw to mimic a real pet carrier. 

However, the real product was the 32-page booklet titled The Care and Training of Your Pet Rock. Written in a deadpan, serious tone, it offered instructions on how to house-train the rock and teach it simple commands like "sit" and "stay," while noting that commands like "roll over" and "come" required extra assistance.

The product debuted at a San Francisco gift show in August 1975 and quickly caught the eye of major retailers like Neiman-Marcus. Selling for $3.95 each, Dahl moved roughly 1.5 million units between August and December of that year. With minimal production costs, he netted about 95 cents per rock, earning well over $1 million in just six months—an amount equivalent to nearly $6 million today. Fueled by viral word-of-mouth, major newspaper coverage, and two appearances by Dahl on The Tonight Show, sales peaked at 10,000 units a day by October.

By February 1976, the novelty had worn off and stores began discounting their remaining inventory. Dahl attempted several follow-up gag products, including Canned Earthquakes, a Sand Breeding Kit, and Red China Dirt, but none ever recaptured the lightning-in-a-bottle cultural moment of the original Pet Rock.

text:
I watched an old interview with the late Indian journalist, writer and intellectual Sardar Khushwant Singh. It illuminated both my heart and mind.

He said he had never known poverty. He had no idea what poverty even felt like. Journalism had also made him a great deal of money. His father was a builder and was wealthy as well.

Khushwant Singh’s words are true. In the 1990s, when Pakistani journalists earned only four or five thousand rupees a month, Khushwant Singh, Kuldip Nayar, and M. J. Akbar each had annual incomes of around a million dollars. When I read this in a Pakistani magazine, I became obsessed with learning about these three Indian greats and reading their work. I have continued reading them all my life. Doors in the heart and mind kept opening, and the light kept growing.

What set them apart was that they not only wrote the truth with courage and fearlessness, but they also wrote elegant, refined English prose. All three were highly educated.

In Pakistan, we too had writers who wrote good English prose, but they lacked this kind of courage, especially the courage of Sardar Khushwant Singh, who was a shining star of journalism.

He was born in 1915 in a village near Khewra, Pakistan. He was educated in Lahore, later went to London for higher studies, and also practised law in Lahore. He considered Pakistan his watan, homeland. Loved Pakistan. 

He joined the Indian Foreign Service and worked with the well-known Indian diplomat Krishna Menon. Of Menon he wrote that he was a dry, negative, and harsh man who always said that only fools speak the truth. Khushwant Singh detested this attitude. He therefore left the foreign service and became editor of The Illustrated Weekly of India. From an obscure magazine, Sardar Sahib turned it into a sensation. Alongside his sharp analyses, he wrote frank, colourful, and often risqué stories. His wife (whom he called Sardarni) would often wonder where the man who wrote those stories was, because she never saw him in their house.

Once, at the airport, Sardarni was with him when a group of young female fans rushed up and embraced Khushwant Singh with devotion. Sardarni smiled and said to him, “You are quite the artist.”

Sardar Sahib said he used to wake at four in the morning, wash his face and hands, and sit down to read and write. He refused to waste time on prayers or other religious formalities ... puja paat. When he grew tired he played tennis. He never attended parties. When diplomats came to the house and the allotted time was over, Sardarni would simply tell them that the meeting was finished. (Unlike certain people of our own "land of the pure" who spend their days circling embassies, if someone offers them coffee, they never tire of taking and posting selfies.)

This was his lifelong routine. He lived past the age of 99 and died while still writing. He lived a full and purposeful life. He experienced neither illness nor poverty. On his way out he said that death is not a comma; it is a full stop.

Mirza Ghalib was right:

We know the truth of paradise,  
yet, Ghalib, this thought is pleasant enough  
to keep the heart content.

He then quoted these lines of Walter Savage Landor:

I strove with none, for none was worth my strife:  
Nature I loved, and, next to Nature, Art:  
I warm’d both hands before the fire of Life;  
It sinks; and I am ready to depart.

— From Jimmy Virk

Look in the mirror. See what Nigeria has done to you.

1. There is a silent tragedy unfolding in Nigeria under the Tinubu government. 

2. Millions of people may be paying for the country's economic hardship with something they can never recover: years of their lives.

3. Find a photograph of yourself before Buhari became president in 2015. 

4. Find another from before Tinubu took office in 2023. 

5. Now take a photograph of yourself today.

6. Look closely.

7. You may be shocked by what the years have done to you.

8. Your face looks older.

9. The eyes look tired. 

10. The smile is disappearing. 

11. You look exhausted, frustrated and worn down by life.

12. And why wouldn't you?

13. You're eating whatever you can afford, not necessarily what your body needs. 

14. You're combining meals simply to survive. 

15. You postpone medical appointments, settle for cheaper medications and endure illnesses you should have treated.

16. You wake up worrying about food. 

17. You go to bed worrying about tomorrow.

18. Your blood pressure may be rising. 

19. Your blood sugar may be creeping upwards.

text:
his name was Tom. he lived in 205, right next door. he'd come home at 1am, seen a lump in his bed, and decided the safest move was to sleep on the couch and wait.

i said "you slept on your couch because there was a stranger in your bed?"

he said "i didn't want to wake you up. you looked tired."

then i showed him my key. he stared at it for a while, then went and got his own. 

they were the same key. we tried both on each other's doors, and both worked.

we called the landlord together. he said "oh yeah, the whole floor is on one lock. the guy who installed them gave me a discount."

i said "so anyone on this floor could walk into my apartment?"

he said "technically, but nobody has."

Tom raised his spatula and said "except her."
the landlord offered to change the locks. we said we'd think about it.

we're still thinking. it's been five months.

in the meantime, we've kind of become each other's emergency contact. he waters my plant when i'm gone. i feed his fish. last week i came home and found a plate of pasta on my counter with a note that said "you looked tired again."
i ate it. it was good.

nobody has ever walked into the wrong apartment since, but i still check the door number every time.

mostly because i don't trust myself, and partly because i know where the spatula is.

text:
How Modern Leftists quote Connolly out of context and thereby invert and co-opt his life's work to justify the very things he fought against.

James Connolly consistently maintained an Irish ethno-nationalist stance: he was explicitly against mass migration, and yet Modern Leftists love to quote his famous 1908 line to rationalise the very thing he would have fought against:

“Let no Irishman throw a stone at the foreigner; he may hit his own clansman.”

Connolly wrote this while working as a socialist union organiser in New York. Writing in The Harp, an Irish-American newspaper he founded and edited, he urged Irish immigrants to stop attacking foreign workers. At the same time, he called on foreign workers to stop reviling the Irish. His clear objective was to overcome ethnic divisions and build a unified labour union.

This post will break down how it is a shameful betrayal of Connolly’s legacy to use his words from 1908 to justify the state-facilitated colonisation of Ireland today.

Note to the reader: A smoking gun is not needed to prove this, but there are two smoking guns awaiting you at the end of the post.

A Colonised Land (America by 1908)

By 1908, America had been thoroughly colonised and transformed over centuries. Tragically, the Native Americans had long been dispossessed and subjugated in their own country.

Connolly arrived a long time after the damage had been done. He did not witness or endorse colonisation.

Connolly Was Addressing Immigrants (in a Colonised Nation)

Connolly was primarily addressing Irish, Italian, Slavic and Jewish communities, all of whom came from different European nations. None of these ethnic groups were native to America; they were all immigrants.

He was requesting solidarity among workers in a country that had already been colonised for centuries. The Native Americans had been reduced to a minority in their own country. The likelihood that James Connolly personally encountered a Native American in New York is extremely low. Out of sight, out of mind.

Ask Yourself This Hypothetical Question

If the colonisation of America was happening during James Connolly’s own lifetime — not as a bloody conquest (as people naively imagine all colonisation to be), but a sudden tidal wave of mass migration orchestrated by the ruling elitists against the explicit wishes of the Native Americans — would Connolly have supported that mass migration, or would he have condemned it as a capital weapon used to dispossess the indigenous people and further the capitalists’ imperialist agenda?

The Context of Connolly's Internationalism

The elephant in the room that Modern Leftists choose to ignore is that internationalism was the only stance that could have been adopted out of necessity because he was a migrant himself in a land that had been colonised for hundreds of years by that time and was multi-ethnic.

The damage was already done, so preaching cross-ethnic solidarity was the only logical framework for organising a united workforce in defence against capitalist exploitation.

Ireland presented a fundamentally different reality. Despite centuries of plantations, the native population had never been reduced to a minority in their own country, and Connolly would never have supported that. He recognised that a nation fighting for its independence must maintain full control over its own borders, resources and destiny.

The First Smoking Gun

At the outbreak of World War I in 1914, hundreds of thousands of Belgian refugees fled their country following the German invasion, with at least 250,000 arriving in Britain and approximately 3,000 fleeing to Ireland.

Thomas Farren, a prominent Irish trade unionist, introduced a resolution to the Dublin Trades Council to extend hospitality to these refugees and offer them the protection of the trade union. James Connolly explicitly opposed the resolution because it implied that Ireland could automatically accept an unrestricted influx of refugees.

19 November 1914 | Dublin Trades Council Meeting | Belgian Refugees and Fair Labour

Report on meeting of the Dublin Trades' Council. It is in response to Thomas Farren's proposed resolution that Belgian refugees in Ireland should be given the same trade union protection as Irish workers. Text has been changed into the first-person.

I think Mr. Farren’s resolution a very dangerous one, as it involves that if the refugees comply with what is laid down in the resolution we have nothing more to complain of. Provided the position was an ordinary one, with no war in question, and these people came to this country they ought to be welcomed no matter what their nationality might be. But the present position is an extraordinary one. It is not a case of a man or two men, but a possible case of a whole army being dumped down here. I am opposed to the resolution because it implies that no matter what number is dumped down we accept them and undertake to work harmoniously along with them. This is no war of ours and the people of this country have no interest in it or in the Allies. I believe the Belgian people have been dragged into it by the machinations of their Government, and the Government having brought them into it should look after them. The British had called on them to preserve their neutrality—which was not threatened for a moment—and said they would stand behind them. They did stand behind them—so much so that the Belgians did not know they were there.

The Belgian people, I believe, have been sold by their Government for something which we can only guess at. While carefully avoiding saying anything against the Belgians, we ought not to do anything that would give the employers in this country a chance to ‘sack’ Irish workers and take on Belgian employees. We ought not to give any loophole to the employers. If it was true these Belgians had fought for their own neutrality then they should not be brought here to supplant the workers of Ireland but as a charge on the British Empire.

This meeting was recorded by journalist Arthur Griffith's paper, Éire, which published a dense, third-person journalistic summary of the debate on 19 November 1914

Arthur Griffith was a major figure in Irish history, best known as the founder of Sinn Féin and later the President of Dáil Éireann. Newspapers like Éire played a critical role in recording the political debates and nationalist activities.

Source: Originally published in the minutes of the Dublin Trades' Council in the Irish Worker newspaper (21 November 1914).

Credit and thanks to:

Cartlann: For retrieving, transcribing, and publishing the text online in a first-person format.

The Burkean: For transcribing and preserving the text in its original third-person format.

The Final Smoking Gun

Condemnation of Brit-Huns —Conscription Refugees

During World War I, the British government introduced conscription but excluded Ireland from the draft, which led to an unknown number of English and Scottish men of military age crossing the Irish Sea to evade service. In response, James Connolly published an essay on 5 February 1916 in his newspaper The Workers' Republic, where he used the exact phrase "Brit-Huns" to describe these men. He alleged that "loyal capitalists" in Ireland were sacking local Irish workers to replace them with these British arrivals, effectively starving young Irishmen into volunteering for the British Army—a process he explicitly condemned as a "new plantation".

The Only Conclusion

James Connolly was vehemently against mass migration—even for genuine refugees who were fleeing war, occupation, and conscription. These represented the most desperate catalysts for immigration, yet his opposition remained absolute.

Modern-leftists have taken his words and twisted them to rationalise the very thing he would have fought against. It is a shameful betrayal of his legacy.

------------------------------------------------------

Important notes on how AI and Modern Leftist will try to twist and sanitise Connolly’s own words.

By using selective quotes to rewrite his stance:
Unless someone has read the transcript in full, an AI will select specific quotes and weave them into a subversive narrative.

Framing the speech purely as "anti-war" and "anti-imperialist":

This approach attempts to intellectualise his argument to cover up his explicit opposition to mass migration. Considering Connolly was against genuine war refugees, he most certainly would be against the state-facilitated colonisation of Ireland today.

Twisting the "extraordinary circumstances" line:

He quantified what would be ordinary circumstances, defining a normal amount as "a man or two men." He states: "It is not a case of a man or two men, but a possible case of a whole army being dumped down here." Quite clearly, he was not against the odd migrant but was explicitly against mass migration.

text:
❤️❤️Sri Swami Vishwananda❤️❤️
Saturday, November 14, 2026 on X 

The one who has even a little understanding of true devotional love begins to discover a mystery beyond the understanding of the restless mind. For when the heart is genuinely touched by divine love, what more is there to seek, and what greater treasure could one desire? Just as a drop of water merges into the ocean and loses its separate existence, so does the soul, through unwavering love and complete surrender to the Satguru, come to realise its inseparable relationship with the Supreme Lord. O beloved people of Sri Hari, do not mistake Vishwananda for someone wise, for he is but a simple-minded fool, sharing only what little he has come to understand through grace. The path is before you, but the willingness to walk it must arise from within. If you desire freedom from the endless entanglements of Maya, you must first become watchful of your own mind, for it is often the mind that creates divisions where there is none, doubts where there should be faith, and attachments that keep the soul bound to the transient world. Ego, pride and the desire for recognition are burdens that conceal the beauty of your true nature. What is the value of accumulating worldly importance when none of it can accompany you beyond this temporary existence? Do not spend your precious life trying to become someone in the eyes of the world; instead, learn to become nothing before the Lord, so that His divine presence may shine through you. The Satguru does not merely show you the way; through his grace, he awakens within you the longing to discover the Truth that has always been present. Look beyond appearances and recognise the sacred presence of Sri Hari within your own heart. Do not confine your devotion to the temple, the altar or the moments of prayer, for every encounter is an opportunity to recognise and honour the Divine. When you serve another with compassion, when you forgive without resentment, when you offer kindness without expecting anything in return, and when you see beyond another person’s faults, your devotion becomes a living offering to the Lord. Never imagine that God belongs only to those who worship in a particular way, for the same divine presence sustains all beings. The flower, the tree, the river, the stranger and even the one who tests your patience are all part of His creation. Let your heart become so filled with love that you no longer look for reasons to separate yourself from others. True devotion is not measured by how much we speak about God, but by how deeply His love transforms the way we live. Surrender is not weakness; it is the freedom that comes when we stop allowing the ego to govern our existence. Let go, love sincerely, serve selflessly and walk with humility. For the ultimate realisation is not merely to know that Sri Hari is everywhere, but to see Him, honour Him and love Him in all that exists. There is no place where He is absent, no heart beyond His reach and no creation outside His divine presence.

Ordered by the FAA, Friday's four hour nationwide ground stop, lifted ...but flight delays continue and it will take some time to catch up.
