text:
I initially understood the British Army’s agreement with Tariq Halal Meats to be a contract for supplying meat. Having examined the reporting, I accept that it concerns the Armed Forces Covenant. Accuracy matters, and that distinction must be acknowledged.

However, correcting that misunderstanding does not remove my objection.

A public signing involving a senior Army officer gives the company prestige and legitimacy. Whatever the formal disclaimers, the public message can reasonably be understood as endorsement by association.

As a Christian priest, my objection is theological: Christians must abstain from food offered to idols. The apostolic instruction in Acts 15:29 is explicit, and Paul’s teaching must be read alongside that instruction and his prohibition against participation in idolatrous worship. His permission to eat marketplace meat without investigating its origins (1 Cor 8) does not amount to unrestricted permission knowingly to consume food identified as religiously dedicated. The invocation over halal-slaughtered meat is bringing it within that prohibition. On that understanding, abstention is a matter of obedience to Scripture, not merely personal preference.

My concern is the growing institutional adoption of halal meat without clear disclosure or meaningful choice. Accommodating Muslim dietary convictions should never mean disregarding the convictions of Christians or others who object. People deserve to know what they are eating and to have an appropriate alternative.

Supporting veterans, reservists and military families is commendable. But that worthy purpose does not put the Army’s choice of commercial association beyond scrutiny. In my view, this association lends institutional approval to practices that remain seriously contested.

Respect for Muslim fellow citizens does not require approval of halal practices. Our national institutions should respect freedom of conscience consistently, including the conscience of those who oppose them.

text:
The age of 7 is not arbitrary. It comes directly from Catholic canon law, and this is the part nobody teaches.

Canon law since Gratian (1140) and the Decretals of Gregory IX (1234) fixed the "age of reason" (aetas discretionis) at 7. Thomist doctrine, at 7, a child can distinguish good from evil, can sin, can receive first communion, and therefore can legally consent to sponsalia de futuro, binding engagements. The age of marriage consummation was 12 for girls, 14 for boys.

When Henry VIII broke with Rome in 1534, he did not abolish canon law. He nationalized it. English ecclesiastical courts kept applying the same categories. Blackstone codified them in his Commentaries (1765-1769). The 13 American colonies inherited the whole architecture at independence. Delaware at 7 in 1890 was not a local aberration. It was the direct application of Thomist doctrine, transmitted through English canon law, to American civil code.

Every argument the 1895 legislators used against reform was canonical in origin.

"Girls matured early enough to consent" is the secular version of attigit aetatem nubilem.
"Southern chivalry offered sufficient protection" is the medieval doctrine that female protection belonged to masculine charity (patria potestas, chivalry, paternalism), not to positive civil law.
"Working girls might blackmail employers" is the canonical presumption of crimen falsae accusationis, which required heavy proof for any sexual accusation by a woman.

And the proposal to deny protection to assaulted girls unless they could prove prior virginity comes directly from the canonical doctrine of bona fama. A girl who had already lost her virginity was no longer protected because she was already dishonored in canonical terms.
Why did Rome fix the age so low in the first place? 2 reasons.
First, demographic strategy. Early marriages meant more baptisms, more sacramental revenue, more ecclesiastical jurisdiction over families. Lowering the nubile age served the institution.
And also, patriarchal continuity. Fixing the age at 7 for engagement and 12 for marriage ensured girls passed from paternal to marital control with no window of juridical autonomy between them. No moment where a woman existed as adult outside male tutelage.

Helen Hamilton Gardener and the 1000s of women who raised the age of consent between 1885 and 1920 did something the history books underplay. They legally pulled millions of little girls out of canon law transmitted through common law. It is one of the most important fights in feminist history, and it is one of the least taught, precisely because recognizing it would mean recognizing the canonical source of the problem, and therefore the underground jurisdiction of Rome in modern civil law.

The witches burned at the stake and the little girls legally available at 7 are 2 faces of the same architecture. The visible face and the invisible face of the same extraction of the female body by the same institution.

All roads lead to Rome. Including the ones that run under the civil code.

A pre-loved barong Tagalog gets a second life as a tote bag, a skirt, or Christmas décor. Traditional Pampanga parols bring generations of lantern-making craftsmanship into homes. And every purchase offers a way to support the Filipino makers behind these creations.

These are among the stories at this year's PRESENTE by ArteFino, which is expanding to two locations for the holidays following its 10th anniversary celebrations in August.

The first fair runs from Nov. 26 to 29 at The Fifth at Rockwell, followed by a second edition at Alabang Town Center from Dec. 10 to 13. Together, the fairs will feature 135 Filipino artisanal brands, including 17 exclusive to the Alabang leg.
But beyond the shopping, several projects put the spotlight on local craftsmanship, livelihood, and community.

One of the fair's featured projects is Barong Yugto, Barong Buhay, an initiative led by designer and ArteFino Maker’s Lab mentor Zarah Juan.

The project transforms pre-loved barong Tagalogs into bags, clothing, and holiday décor, with the pieces handcrafted by persons deprived of liberty in Quezon City.

Launched through ArteFino's 2025 Maker's Lab #TotallyUpCycledChallenge, the initiative brings together SparkPH, the Quezon City local government, and design students from SOFA Design Institute. Old barongs are collected and reworked into new designs, which the PDLs then cut, sew, and assemble by hand.

The name draws from the Filipino phrase "bagong yugto, bagong buhay." The project gives discarded garments another purpose while offering their makers an opportunity for a fresh start.

The collection will be available at the HeArteFino booths at both fairs.

PAROL TRADITION

PRESENTE will also showcase Christmas lanterns made by master artisans from Pampanga, the country's Christmas Capital.

Developed with the Makati City Office of Cultural Affairs, the special collection will be available at The Fifth at Rockwell. The same artisans have also been sharing their lantern-making skills with communities in Makati.

At Alabang Town Center, visitors can find more handcrafted parols through the Tukod Foundation, founded in 2020 by the late National Artist for Architecture Francisco “Bobby” Mañosa. The organization champions Filipino design and craftsmanship, cultural heritage, and sustainable community development.

The Alabang fair will also feature a performance by the children's choir of the Tuloy Foundation on Dec. 13.

HANDOG NG PASKO

ArteFino's community work extends beyond the fair itself. On Nov. 12, it held Handog ng Pasko with Saints Peter and Paul Parish in Makati, bringing together brand partners, media friends, and collaborators to share Noche Buena packs and activities with 100 families from barangays Poblacion, Olympia, and Valenzuela.

The fairs will also feature new HeArteFino collaborations, including fresh colorways from IslaTek, a farm-to-fabric initiative exploring the possibilities of Filipino tropical textiles.

Proceeds from HeArteFino product sales and ticket sales from ArteFino fairs support the program's grantees and their projects.

Shoppers can browse clothing, accessories, home goods, fragrances, and handcrafted keepsakes from established and emerging Filipino brands at either venue. The fair also offers a chance to discover the people and processes behind the products—making each find more than just another Christmas present.

(✍️: radar Lifestyle)

Last week’s local government elections delivered a clear verdict - South Africans are finished with incompetence and corruption.

They have also signalled that diversity of parties and approaches must form part of the solution if we are to pull our metros and municipalities out of the hole. 

The biggest gains went to ActionSA, the Democratic Alliance, the MKP and the SACP. The SACP’s low single digit result is humbling after years of alliance politics, yet it shows the party can sustain a modest independent presence.

One reading of the shifts is that voters, outside Cape Town, eThekwini and Buffalo City, have bought into the service delivery visions offered by ActionSA and the DA. In eThekwini the pattern points toward an MKP led arrangement. In Buffalo City voters appear willing to see the ANC continue in some form of co-governance. This is not pure arithmetic; it is an interpretation of where support moved and what voters seem to be asking for.

A second, purely numerical reading allows coalitions that seize power. That route leans heavily on arithmetic. It is the easy way out. It spares parties the deeper introspection their records require, keeps them temporarily in the power equation, and softens the pain of rejection by constituents who have become more colour blind in their pursuit of basic services. The easy way, as the saying goes, often leads straight back in.

Tshwane illustrates one outcome of this path: ActionSA gained from the collective work of a coalition ably led by Dr Nasiphi Moya. 

Cape Town shows the longer term version of the same dynamic. In 2006 the DA, as the largest party, formed a multi-party coalition under Helen Zille. The next local government elections in 2011 delivered an outright DA majority, which the party has held and, for a period, expanded ever since. 

Consistent leadership and delivery can convert coalition support into durable majorities. 

Johannesburg shows the other side: service delivery failures have rightly landed on the door of the mayor, Dada Morero, damaging the ANC. In all these cases the party that leads the coalition receives the credit for progress or carries the blame for failure.

This is the strategic trap. Parties that aspire to lead metros and municipalities in the longer term must ask themselves a hard question: if they will not lead the coalition, is propping up a competitor the best use of their seats? 

The quick route to irrelevance is to lend weight to a government run by the party they ultimately hope to displace. The harder, and right, choice is to sit on the opposition benches. Sitting in opposition also helps citizens: it creates real accountability, keeps pressure on those in power to deliver, and gives voters a credible alternative when the next election arrives. It allows parties to build the credibility and record that future majorities require.

The hard thing to do and the right thing to do are usually the same thing. Voters have shown they will reward delivery and punish its absence. 

Parties that treat this election as an invitation to short term arithmetic rather than long term accountability risk missing the deeper message. #ProudlySA

As airlines work this morning to untangle thousands of residual delays and cancellations following yesterday’s four-hour nationwide ground stop, the lessons from Friday’s telecommunication outage offer a stark case study in modern systems engineering. Officials confirmed that yesterday’s shutdown—only the third nationwide halt in United States aviation history—was not a cyberattack, but rather an internal legacy network failure in which newer equipment and data streams overloaded older switches and routers across Air Route Traffic Control Centers.

That modernization challenge was already documented before yesterday's breakdown. In September, the Government Accountability Office reported that the FAA’s Brand New Air Traffic Control System initiative lacked an integrated master schedule for its first phase. Instead, the agency was managing 11,389 individual project schedules that were not integrated, creating potential conflicts among installations at the same sites and avoidable disruption to controller operations. While those are construction and deployment schedules rather than the operational data moving through the network, both require disciplined management of dependencies. When massive public infrastructure falters in this manner, it happens because agencies try to bolt high-frequency modern capabilities onto fragile, tightly coupled legacy pipes without a canonical state layer sitting in between.

My perspective comes from developing JATS™, where the core architectural question is how to turn continuously changing observations into a verified state that downstream systems can evaluate and act upon consistently. The principle I would carry into the infrastructure discussion is straightforward: receiving new data and authorizing a change in operational state should be separate steps.

Of course, the analogy has clear limits. A market framework evaluating one- and five-minute observations against a fifteen-minute cadence cannot supply the real-time timing requirements for aviation. Air traffic systems must meet their own rigorous safety requirements, millisecond response deadlines, and certification standards. What transfers across domains is the fundamental design question: which observations are sufficiently current, coherent, and trustworthy to justify the next action?

Applying that architectural discipline to critical government systems provides three structural guarantees that legacy networks currently lack. First, it establishes noise and patch isolation at the edge; rather than allowing erratic sensor feeds or aggressive network updates to cascade directly into core national operations, an intermediate state-evaluation engine absorbs the turbulence, requiring every state change to pass deterministic cycle gates and cryptographic hash verification against its prior state before any downstream consumer acts on it.

Second, this model replaces fragmented legacy tools with a single canonical state bus. Instead of forcing uncoordinated subsystems or dozens of regional air traffic control centers to communicate through brittle point-to-point connections, every component publishes standardized, self-contained state snapshots onto one immutable bus. If a single regional node lags, degrades, or goes stale, explicit age tracking and degradation notices isolate that partition mathematically, allowing the rest of the national grid to remain safely operational rather than forcing a blunt nationwide shutdown.

Third, a deterministic snapshot architecture provides auditable, replayable governance. In large-scale public infrastructure failures, root-cause investigations routinely drag on for months because diagnostic logs are scattered across disparate contractors and aging mainframes. Self-contained state snapshots with built-in lineage and content hashing give regulators and engineers an exact, bit-for-bit replay of what the network knew, the precise timestamp it knew it, and the exact rule that triggered every state transition.

Modernization requires explicit rules for validating information, containing failures, and reconstructing decisions. By treating critical national infrastructure as a deterministic state machine rather than a reactive web of wires, federal agencies could safely upgrade individual components at speed while containing and isolating disruption whenever it occurs.

text:
LETTERS FROM STOCKHOLM
Nigeria Has the Talent. Why Do We Keep Recycling Failure?
By Kio Amachree

Nigeria is approaching a quarter of a billion people, yet we are continually asked to believe that our future depends on the same small circle of political veterans, power brokers and professional survivors. UNFPA put our population at 237.5 million in 2025. Among so many Nigerians, are we seriously expected to believe that this is the best leadership we can produce?
I refuse to believe it.

I know Nigerian men and women whose education, sophistication, experience and judgement would put much of our political establishment to shame. Friends and members of my own family have managed complex institutions, built businesses and earned international respect. Nigeria invested heavily in developing generations of capable people. Too many now serve the rest of the world while their own country remains trapped in the politics of patronage.

Nobody can repair Nigeria with a wave of the hand. But there are Nigerians who understand what competent government requires—and who would approach the responsibility with considerably more seriousness than the familiar faces demanding another opportunity.

My objection to the present assortment of presidential hopefuls is straightforward: too many offer the same old song and dance. New campaign colours, new alliances, new slogans—and the same exhausted political habits.

I have lived long enough, and known enough Nigerian leaders personally, to recognise the difference between public responsibility and naked ambition.

I grew up around members of the old northern establishment. General Hassan Usman Katsina taught me polo in 1968. Later, when I was at Eton, he visited to see how I was progressing with my studies.

He had more important official responsibilities than checking on a Nigerian schoolboy. Yet he understood that my education carried an obligation beyond personal advancement. In his eyes, a young Nigerian entering an institution associated with the British governing establishment was also representing his country.

Eton was founded in 1440 and has educated twenty British prime ministers. During my years there, its history already stretched back more than five centuries. For a newly independent African country, having its children enter such institutions carried considerable symbolic weight.

As I remember it, General Gowon and General Hassan Katsina wanted to ensure that the Amachree boy did not let Nigeria down.

I also remember the uproar when another Nigerian pupil left the school unexpectedly. General Hassan’s reaction, in my recollection, was fierce. He regarded the matter as an embarrassment to the country and summoned the boy’s father for a dressing-down at the Lagos Polo Club.

The message was unmistakable: opportunity came with responsibility.

I was also close to Umaru Shinkafi and knew other prominent northerners. These relationships gave me a view of an establishment that understood authority, preparation and the weight of national office.

That generation had its failures. Military government deserves scrutiny, and personal affection cannot erase history. But I remember individuals who believed that Nigeria’s reputation mattered and that those entrusted with opportunity had a duty to justify it.

Today, I too often see political survival presented as statesmanship.

Where is the presidential quality? Where is the seriousness? Where is the willingness to tell powerful friends that the public purse belongs to the public?

Ali Modu Sheriff’s place in Tinubu’s political operation illustrates my frustration with the endless recycling. Sheriff, a former governor of Borno, has been reported campaigning for Tinubu’s re-election. Nigerians are entitled to ask what this familiar alliance offers beyond the preservation of established political networks.

A photograph beside a president is no substitute for an account of a politician’s record.

Then there is the tribal poison.

As a man with a Yoruba mother and an Ijaw father, I find the ethnic policing of political opinion particularly absurd. Criticise Tinubu and some supporters immediately decide that you must be Igbo—as though an Igbo identity were an accusation and a Yoruba identity required obedience.

I have received vile insults directed at my late parents. I have received threats from people presenting themselves as Yoruba defenders of Tinubu. Some messages are so repulsive that I will not reproduce them.

Those responsible must answer for their conduct. They cannot claim to speak for an entire people, and I will not surrender my mother’s heritage to political bullies.

But I will say this plainly: leaders who benefit from ethnic intimidation have a responsibility to confront it unequivocally.

The intimidation of Igbo and other non-Yoruba voters in Lagos is documented. The United States’ human-rights reporting on the 2023 elections described threats against ethnic Igbo voters and the obstruction of non-Yoruba voters at polling stations. Human Rights Watch likewise recorded election violence and failures by security personnel to protect voters.

This is a national disgrace.

No Nigerian should have to establish an ancestral claim to a city before exercising a constitutional right there. No political party owns Lagos. No ethnic group owns the presidency. Citizenship must mean something wherever a Nigerian chooses to live.

My standards also apply to the opposition.

I have been abused by supporters of Peter Obi because I question what I regard as his excessively cautious approach to entrenched power. Supporting an opposition candidate does not require surrendering one’s judgement.

Obi must explain how he intends to confront the machinery of corruption. Nigerians need more than a reassuring personality. We need an operational plan: independent investigations, transparent procurement, protected witnesses, credible prosecutions and consequences that reach powerful people.

The reported attack surrounding the ADC gathering in Benin City in February 2026 underlines the danger of political intimidation. Police confirmed an attack on the party secretariat and reported damage at John Odigie-Oyegun’s residence; Obi’s representatives described gunmen following the politicians. Responsibility must be established through investigation, but the need for protection and accountability is already clear.

A reforming president must be relentless within the law. Courage must translate into institutions strong enough to confront people accustomed to escaping consequences.

Consider Gilbert Chagoury.

His business interests and proximity to successive Nigerian governments deserve sustained scrutiny. Bloomberg reported that the Lagos–Calabar coastal highway, then estimated at $13 billion, was awarded to Hitech, a company owned by Chagoury, a longstanding Tinubu ally.

Then came the GCON, Nigeria’s second-highest national honour, reported in January 2026. Premium Times also recounted Chagoury’s 2000 Swiss conviction for money laundering and aiding a criminal organisation.

What message does this send about the standards Nigeria rewards?

The relevant questions concern access, competition, public value and accountability. Publish the contracts. Explain the procurement decisions. Disclose relevant ownership interests. Demonstrate that the public received value for money.

I want to hear that demand clearly from anyone asking to become president, including Peter Obi.

And to those who behave as though office guarantees lifelong immunity, I suggest studying what has happened elsewhere.

Isabel dos Santos once appeared almost inseparable from Angola’s ruling establishment. A British court nevertheless imposed a worldwide freezing order covering up to £580 million of her assets, and her appeal was dismissed in September 2024. Britain subsequently imposed an asset freeze and travel ban under its anti-corruption sanctions regime. She disputes allegations of wrongdoing.

A freezing order is distinct from confiscation or a criminal conviction. But its practical lesson is clear: political influence at home does not guarantee unrestricted access to wealth abroad.

Charles Taylor offers a different example involving international crimes. The former Liberian president was convicted by the Special Court for Sierra Leone and sentenced to fifty years’ imprisonment. His former office did not prevent his trial.

These cases involve different laws and circumstances. Neither makes the arrest of any Nigerian politician inevitable. They do demonstrate why powerful people should be cautious about assuming that accountability can always be postponed until it disappears.

To Tinubu, Wike, David Umahi, the Senate leadership and every other holder of public authority, my message is simple: exercise power as though your decisions may one day be examined independently.

Contracts leave records. Financial transfers leave records. Public statements survive their speakers’ convenience.

I will continue watching the Washington litigation concerning records associated with the investigation in which Tinubu was named. Judge Beryl Howell’s October 30, 2026 opinion concerns access to FBI and DEA investigative material under freedom-of-information law. It is a disclosure case, rather than a criminal conviction, and its significance should be assessed through the actual court record. Nigerians deserve access to whatever the law requires to be disclosed.

We do not need invented intelligence dossiers to demand accountability. The documented questions are serious enough.

And we certainly do not lack examples of Nigerian ability.

My cousin Adebayo Ogunlesi helped build Global Infrastructure Partners into a business acquired by BlackRock in a transaction announced at approximately $12.5 billion and completed in October 2024. He subsequently joined BlackRock’s board and was appointed to OpenAI’s board in January 2025.

Here is a Nigerian whose judgement has been entrusted with major international responsibilities.

Business success alone does not establish fitness for the presidency. But Ogunlesi’s career exposes the absurdity of pretending that Nigeria lacks people capable of operating at the highest level.

We produce them. We educate them. We export them.

Then our political system too often rewards the people most skilled at controlling delegates, assembling patronage networks and financing the next campaign.

Why should Nigerians accept this?

I will support a candidate who makes clear commitments to the Nigerian people: open public contracting, independent law enforcement, credible elections, protection against political violence, and appointments based on competence.

That candidate must also explain how those commitments will survive pressure from financiers, party elders and personal friends.

I want to know what happens when the investigation reaches your ally. What happens when the contract belongs to your sponsor? What happens when the thug threatening voters wears your party’s colours?

Your answer to those questions tells me more than a hundred campaign speeches.

I have defended Nigerian unity because I believe our diversity can be a source of strength. But unity requires a functioning bargain between citizens and the state.

People cannot be asked indefinitely to endure insecurity, humiliation and deprivation while being lectured about the sanctity of a national arrangement that fails to protect them.

Another decade of this behaviour would deepen the damage to the Nigerian idea itself.

Those of us who believe in the country should be the most demanding of its leaders. Our commitment deserves a government that makes belonging worthwhile.

Nigeria has the people. Nigeria has the ability. Nigeria has citizens who understand service and responsibility.

The political establishment must stop treating those citizens as spectators while the same exhausted actors divide the stage.

I am tired of being offered another version of failure and told to call it hope.

Kio Amachree

text:
Moscow 1980 — The Olympics the World Boycotted, but Who Could Forget Misha?

A Letter from Olympic History

There are moments in history when politics casts such a long shadow over the affairs of ordinary people that even the Olympic Games, supposedly the greatest celebration of international friendship, cannot escape its reach.

And so, it was in #Moscow in the summer of 1980.

The Soviet Union had invaded #Afghanistan the previous December, and President Jimmy Carter, determined that the #Kremlin should not be rewarded with the prestige of hosting the world's greatest sporting spectacle, led an international boycott.

Some 65 nations stayed away, making the Moscow Games one of the most extensively boycotted #Olympics in modern history. Only 80 countries sent athletes to compete. ¹

The Cold War had arrived at the Olympic stadium.

Yet, amid the political arguments, the absent athletes and the unmistakable atmosphere of international confrontation, there appeared a rather extraordinary little character who seemed blissfully unaware of the quarrels between Washington and Moscow.

His name was Misha.

Or Mishka, as he was affectionately known in Russian — Мишка — the Olympic bear whose cheerful expression and disarming innocence made him one of the most memorable mascots in sporting history.

He was the creation of Viktor Chizhikov, a talented Soviet children's book illustrator who had somehow managed to give a simple brown bear a personality that no committee of politicians could ever have manufactured. 

His design was selected from some 60 artistic proposals following a public campaign that attracted approximately 45,000 letters from across the Soviet Union. ²

Misha wore a colorful belt bearing the five Olympic rings. He had large, kindly eyes, a mischievous smile and the unmistakable appearance of a creature who would much rather offer you a warm embrace than engage in an ideological argument.

And perhaps that was precisely his charm.

For while the world's governments debated #communism, #capitalism, #Afghanistan and the balance of global power, this little bear seemed to be offering a far simpler message: that friendship between ordinary people need not depend upon agreement between their governments.

Then came the closing ceremony on 3 August 1980.

In Moscow's great Lenin Stadium, now known as Luzhniki, thousands of spectators watched as an enormous image of Misha appeared in the stands.

And suddenly, rather wonderfully, a tear rolled down the bear's face.

It was a carefully choreographed moment, of course, but no less moving for that.

Then an enormous inflatable Misha, lifted by colorful balloons, rose slowly above the stadium and drifted into the evening sky, waving farewell to Moscow and to the world. ³

It remains one of the most touching farewells in Olympic history.

And there is something rather revealing about the fact that, more than four decades later, many people who have forgotten the medal tables, the political speeches and even the names of the winning athletes can still remember that smiling bear disappearing into the Moscow sky.

Four years later, the #SovietUnion and most of its Eastern Bloc allies would boycott the Los Angeles Olympics, proving once again that political leaders could find reasons to quarrel even when the world's athletes simply wished to compete. ⁴

But Misha had already achieved something that neither Washington nor Moscow could accomplish through diplomacy.

He had made people smile across the Iron Curtain.

And perhaps that is the enduring little lesson of Moscow 1980.

Governments may boycott the Olympic Games. Politicians may turn sporting occasions into instruments of foreign policy. Empires may rise and fall, and ideological divisions may disappear into the history books.

But sometimes, the thing people remember most is not the politics, the flags or the speeches.

It is a little Russian bear named Misha, with a tear in his eye, waving goodbye to a world that could never quite agree with itself.

Historical Sources and References

1. United States Department of State — The Olympic Boycott, 1980

Official United States government historical account of President Jimmy Carter's decision to lead the boycott following the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan. Confirms that 65 countries did not participate and 80 countries sent athletes to Moscow.
https://t.co/5xDJDFXB7s

2. International Olympic Committee — Olympic Summer Games Mascots: Moscow 1980
Official Olympic historical publication documenting the creation of Misha by Viktor Chizhikov, the public consultation that attracted approximately 45,000 letters, and the selection of the bear from 60 artistic designs.
https://t.co/QZezzUIBOF

3. Foundation of the Hellenic World — Moscow 1980: Misha's Tear
Historical account of Misha's appearance at the Moscow Olympic Games, including the emotional closing ceremony and the celebrated image of the bear shedding a tear.
https://t.co/iuAfMfxLH6

4. International Olympic Committee — The Olympic Movement, the IOC and the Olympic Games
Official Olympic historical overview confirming the Moscow Games' participation figures and the subsequent Soviet-led boycott of the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics.

The midterms complicate Trump's search for an Iran deal

https://t.co/FfGGIfCTPx

♦️ Democrats' sweeping victory in the November 2026 US midterm elections has changed the political landscape for President Donald Trump, giving them control of both chambers of Congress from January and greater power to scrutinise his war with Iran, its military objectives and its growing economic costs.

♦️ Despite the election setback, Trump retains considerable authority over military operations and may see foreign policy as an opportunity to secure a major achievement before leaving office. A deal that reopens the Strait of Hormuz, restricts Iran's nuclear programme and lowers energy prices could help him claim that military pressure delivered results.

♦️ However, reaching such an agreement would require significant economic concessions to Tehran, including sanctions relief, the release of frozen Iranian assets and an end to the US blockade. Democratic control of Congress could make these commitments harder to guarantee, particularly where sanctions imposed by legislation are concerned.

♦️ Iran is also under mounting economic pressure, with the US blockade severely restricting its oil exports and the rial falling to around 2.7 million to the dollar in early October. Tehran is demanding economic relief before making further nuclear and maritime concessions, while insisting that any agreement must offer lasting access to international markets.

♦️ Negotiations remain complicated by disagreements over the sequence of concessions. Iran wants Washington to lift the blockade and ease restrictions before reopening the Strait of Hormuz, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has rejected elements of Tehran's demands. The collapse of the June memorandum of understanding exposed how difficult it is for both sides to agree on who should move first.

♦️ Three possible outcomes could emerge: a comprehensive agreement involving nuclear restrictions and substantial sanctions relief; a limited ceasefire restoring maritime traffic while postponing difficult questions; or prolonged escalation that keeps energy markets unstable and increases economic pressure on both sides.

♦️ Gulf countries have a major stake in the outcome, as disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz threaten oil and gas exports, shipping and regional investment. Ultimately, Trump's biggest challenge is not simply negotiating a deal with Tehran, but securing concessions that Washington can legally deliver and politically sustain beyond his presidency.

text:
Film Noir: After the War — The Uncertain Return

The Blue Dahlia (1946) George Marshall
Somewhere in the Night (1946) Joseph L. Mankiewicz
Cornered (1945) Edward Dmytryk

The end of World War II created a powerful expectation of renewal. Victory promised the restoration of ordinary life, the recovery of familiar identities, and a future freed from the violence of the past. Yet postwar film noir questions the assumption that history can be divided so neatly into before and after. Its returning veterans confront a society eager to resume normality, while their experiences have unsettled the very meanings of home, belonging, and moral certainty. The contradiction is not simply that war has damaged these men, but that peace demands a continuity their lives can no longer sustain.

In The Blue Dahlia, Johnny Morrison (Alan Ladd) discovers that the bonds of loyalty forged during military service have no secure equivalent in civilian life. His disillusionment exposes a fracture within the ideal of homecoming itself. The domestic world, traditionally imagined as the reward for sacrifice, offers neither emotional stability nor moral reassurance. What survives the war is not necessarily the life that preceded it, but the solidarity of men who have shared experiences that separate them from the society to which they return. The film suggests that belonging is no longer guaranteed by marriage, home, or familiar social roles. It must be sought among those who understand a past that civilian life cannot easily accommodate.

In Somewhere in the Night, George Taylor’s (John Hodiak) amnesia gives this rupture a more radical form. His lost memory is not merely a mystery to be solved but a challenge to the assumption that identity possesses an essential continuity. The investigation into his former life raises an unsettling possibility: recovering the past may not mean recovering an authentic self. The person George once was exists largely through the testimony, interests, and judgments of others, making identity something reconstructed rather than simply remembered. Mankiewicz turns the returning veteran into a figure of postwar uncertainty, caught between the desire to know his origins and the fear that knowledge may undermine the person he is becoming. His predicament suggests that beginning again may require something other than the restoration of what has been lost.

In Cornered, Laurence Gerard (Dick Powell) confronts the moral inadequacy of victory itself. The defeat of fascism has not extinguished its surviving networks, nor has it resolved the personal suffering inflicted by the war. Gerard’s pursuit of his wife’s murderer exposes the distance between historical justice and individual retribution. His determination appears morally justified, yet the violence of his obsession threatens to reproduce the destructive logic he seeks to confront. Dmytryk presents a world in which political evil survives through concealment and adaptation, while the individual who attempts to oppose it risks becoming imprisoned by the need for revenge. Peace, in this vision, is a political condition rather than a guarantee of moral resolution.

These three films approach the aftermath of war through different crises: the loss of belonging, the instability of identity, and the impossibility of complete moral closure. Their protagonists are not simply men struggling to adjust to civilian life. They reveal the inadequacy of a society’s expectation that military victory should restore personal order.

What postwar noir ultimately questions is the reassuring idea that the end of a historical catastrophe marks the beginning of a new and unburdened existence. The past survives in relationships, identities, and moral obligations that cannot be dissolved by the declaration of peace. The war ends collectively, but its consequences must be lived individually.

#SciFeature 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗣𝗛𝗜𝗟𝗜𝗣𝗣𝗜𝗡𝗘𝗦 𝗔𝗧 𝗡𝗜𝗚𝗛𝗧 🌃

Ever wondered what the Philippines looks like from space after dark? From the bright sprawl of Metro Manila to the flickering dots of far-flung islands, each cluster of light tells a story of life and activity. Can you spot your community in the glow?

This map was created using nighttime light data from NASA's Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS), which captures the brightness of artificial lights from space. With a resolution of 15 arc seconds, equivalent to about 500 meters at the equator, VIIRS data allows us to visualize the distribution of human activity across the country.

The intensity and spread of these lights closely align with populated areas, especially urban centers. Aside from Metro Manila, some of the brightest regions include Baguio City, Iloilo City, Cebu City, and Davao City. In many areas, the illuminated patterns resemble networks of nerves, tracing major roads, highways, and coastal outlines, which are particularly evident in northern Luzon and across various islands.

Remote sensing of nighttime lights offers a valuable tool for understanding human presence and development. It can reveal differences in access to electricity, track changes in economic activity, and support decision-making where ground-level data is limited. It also helps assess light pollution, which can affect ecosystems and stargazing in darker regions. #LightPollution #Nighttime

text:
Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, @ReichlinMelnick.

The studies say something narrower than your claim that "study after study" has "proven empirically" that sanctuary policies have no effect on crime or reduce it.

A result that is "not statistically distinguishable from zero" is not a result of zero. Hausman (2020) found no significant effect across 224 large counties, but its confidence bounds still allow increases of about 5% for violent crime and 6% for property crime relative to the median. https://t.co/d8M22WUYm0

Otsu (2020) found no significant increase, yet one specification shows robbery up 3.6%, and the 95% upper bound for rape is +9%. https://t.co/jH8MInippH

A follow-up on New York City by Otsu (2024), covering 75 precincts, found recorded rape 34.7% higher in the highest-immigrant-share precincts. The paper attributes this to reporting, but its own tests do not establish that. https://t.co/m8UKpZOPUT

The data are also old and thin. Otsu's city data end in 2010. Martínez-Schuldt and Martínez cover 1990 to 2010 (https://t.co/zTTvwowYK5). Manning and Burkhardt (2022) stop in 2016 (https://t.co/ZJYGOULNzg).

The California study by Kubrin and Bartos (2020) has a single post-policy year (https://t.co/pdFXyIkSEf).
A study of victim reporting by Martínez-Schuldt and Martínez (2021) uses survey data that end in 2004 (https://t.co/BeSzym59TM).

Several findings are fragile. Otsu's property-crime decline disappears in some specifications, and Manning and Burkhardt's significant effects are concentrated in violent crime, aggravated assault, and robbery.

Explanations offered by authors are often untested. Ascherio (2022) writes, "I do not have the data to test the specific mechanism" (https://t.co/KQVIwNpVb2). Manning and Burkhardt say they "cannot disentangle the mechanisms." And no study I reviewed tests whether police in sanctuary places record crime differently. Eleven of the 16 sources I reviewed rely on police-recorded crime, so that question stays open in both directions.

Definitions also vary. Some studies define "sanctuary" by detainer refusal, and others by city ordinance. Wong (2017) is a cross-sectional analysis (rather than a "before-and-after" study), and the author explicitly frames his methodology as a way to establish causal effects (https://t.co/uux3TQuuNf).

text:
MY HUSBAND QUIT HIS JOB WITHOUT TELLING ME, AND FOR FOUR MONTHS HE KEPT LEAVING THE HOUSE EVERY MORNING

My name is Allison Reyes. I'm 38 and I live in Sacramento, California. My husband, Mark, and I have been married twelve years, and we have a daughter, Chloe, who's ten. 

I found out he'd lost his job by accident, and what hurt most wasn't the job.
Mark was a sales manager at a medical supply company. He'd been there fourteen years. Every morning he put on a collared shirt, kissed Chloe on the head, grabbed his travel mug, and left at 7:40. Every evening he came home around six, tired, and told us about his day in vague terms. I never questioned it. Why would I?
In June, 

I had a dentist appointment near his office, so I texted him to ask if he wanted to grab lunch. He took a long time to answer. Finally he wrote, "Can't today, slammed." I decided to stop by his building anyway and bring him a sandwich as a surprise.

The receptionist at the front desk was someone I'd met at the holiday party. She smiled at me, then went pale. I asked for Mark, and she said, very carefully, "Mrs. Reyes, Mark doesn't work here anymore."
I laughed, because I thought she'd mixed him up with someone else. She said he'd been let go in February. They'd restructured the sales division. He'd gotten a severance package and cleaned out his desk in an afternoon.
February. It was June.

I sat in my car for a long time. Then I did the math, and I couldn't stop doing it. Four months of mornings. Four months of travel mugs and collared shirts and dinner-table stories about clients I now realized he'd made up.

I didn't call him. I drove home and waited. At 5:50 he walked through the door like always, set down his bag, and asked what was for dinner.
"How was work?" I said.
"Fine. Busy."
"Mark, I went to your office today."
He stood very still. He didn't try to deny it. He just sat down at the kitchen table and put his face in his hands, and I realized he'd been waiting for this conversation for months, dreading it and hoping for it at the same time.

He told me everything. They'd laid off a third of the division, and he'd been one of them. He'd gone home that night intending to tell me, and I'd been in the middle of planning Chloe's tenth birthday party. I'd mentioned how excited I was and how I'd put a deposit on the venue. He decided it could wait a week. 

Then a week became a month, and every day he didn't say it, saying it got harder.
"So where did you go?" I asked. "Every morning?"
He said he drove to a public library about twenty minutes away. He sat in the same corner and applied for jobs. Some days he walked around a park because he couldn't stand to look at a screen. He ate lunch in his car. He said he'd gotten two interviews and no offers, and he'd been quietly spending down our savings to cover the gap, so nothing would look different at home.

That was the part that undid me. Not the lie itself, though it was a big one. It was that he'd carried the whole thing alone while I slept next to him every night, and I'd had no idea.

I was furious. I told him he'd made me a stranger in my own marriage, that I'd have understood a layoff, and that what I couldn't understand was why he didn't trust me with it. He said he was ashamed. He said he'd always been the one who held it together, and he didn't know who he was without the title.

We argued until midnight. Somewhere around eleven, I stopped being angry and started being scared, because I realized how close we'd come to real trouble. We had about three months of savings left. He'd have kept going until it ran out.

The next morning I made a spreadsheet. I'm not proud of how cold I was, but it helped. We cut expenses, and I picked up extra shifts at the clinic where I work as an office manager. Mark looked into contract work in his field and landed a three-month gig in August. It paid less, but it was something.

"Give us wealth, and the home shall exist. But that is a very imperfect and inglorious solution of the problem, and therefore no solution. “Give us wealth.” You ask too much. Few have wealth, but all must have a home. Men are not born rich; and in getting wealth the man is generally sacrificed, and often is sacrificed without acquiring wealth at last. Besides, that cannot be the right answer;—there are objections to wealth. Wealth is a shift. The wise man angles with himself only, and with no meaner bait. Our whole use of wealth needs revision and reform. Generosity does not consist in giving money or money’s worth. These so-called goods are only the shadow of good. To give money to a sufferer is only a come-off. It is only a postponement of the real payment, a bribe paid for silence, a credit system in which a paper promise to pay answers for the time instead of liquidation. We owe to man higher succors than food and fire. We owe to man man. If he is sick, is unable, is mean-spirited and odious, it is because there is so much of his nature which is unlawfully withholden from him. He should be visited in this his prison with rebuke to the evil demons, with manly encouragement, with no mean-spirited offer of condolence because you have not money, or mean offer of money as the utmost benefit, but by your heroism, your purity and your faith. You are to bring with you that spirit which is understanding, health and self-help. To offer him money in lieu of these is to do him the same wrong as when the bridegroom offers his betrothed virgin a sum of money to release him from his engagements. The great depend on their heart, not on their purse. Genius and virtue, like diamonds, are best plain-set,—set in lead, set in poverty."

— Ralph Waldo Emerson, feat.

text:
Our lives among the tents… an endless ache, a suffering that begins anew with every sunrise. 💔

This is what our daily lives in Gaza have become: a reality beyond words, a reality in which we have been stripped of even the most basic necessities of a dignified life. Tents that offer no protection from the summer heat or the winter cold, days weighed down by fear and anxiety, and endless nights in which we no longer know what it feels like to rest or feel safe.

Every day, we wake up to the same suffering, struggling to find something to satisfy our hunger, a place to shelter us, and even a little of the peace of mind we have lost amid all this pain.

We are exhausted by a life that no longer feels like living, and by waiting for each new day to be a little less cruel than the one before. We are not asking for luxury or grand dreams. All we want is a roof over our heads, a meal to ease our hunger, warmth to protect us, and our most basic right to live with dignity and safety.

How much longer must we endure this suffering? How much longer will our most basic human rights remain distant dreams?

Gaza needs more than words of sympathy. It needs people who feel the pain of its people, who see their suffering, and who help them reclaim their right to live. 💔

The Reality

After a week of euphoria where the world witnessed Americans begin to reclaim their power against the corrupt Trump regime, reality is slowly creeping back in.

As I told an audience gathered in London at a post-midterm elections Byline Times event at The Cockpit theatre in Marylebone: “I have always said, ‘Diversity is America’s superpower’, and if it took high gas prices to get there, so be it.”

I was referring to the historic flipping of deeply red states – the poetic justice of Scott Colom’s win in Mississippi, making him the state’s first Black Senator in 140 years. I also shared with the audience that Kiesha Lance Bottoms, who was elected to Georgia and is the first Black female governor in US history, is the daughter of blues musician Major Lance, who was hugely influential to the Beatles. 

These are dramatic days, as Democrats take both houses of Congress in January. Their new majorities give them full investigatory powers – the ability to subpoena records and force people to testify before lawmakers. 2027 offers endless opportunities to further shame Trump in the court of public opinion, compelling people to testify about his endless shady ties and Russian dealings.

As political philosopher Dr Michael MacKay told the Byline Times: “The midterms euphoria is starting to be tempered by recognition of the way things are. 
 For example, that a new government doesn't actually take power for almost two months. And that's the result of the US's odd 18th century Constitution. And then there's also the realization that foreign policy remains in the hands of Trump, and that there still is the imperial presidency.” 
MacKay said that people are “looking for a seriousness in Democrats in  Congress to tackle corruption and treason.”

“We have this horrible window where we're starting to see some of the worst excesses,” he said, noting that this week, the Trump regime again throttled the Elon Musk-owned Starshield satellite system in Ukraine. 

“This means, Ukrainians no longer have early warning of ballistic missile attacks,” he said. “Zelensky said Wednesday that all of the patriot missile batteries are empty. Trump has withheld all of the Interceptors that Europe and Canada already bought and paid for. Thursday, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were in Moscow, trying to cook up a corrupt deal… Now they're shopping this Russian imperialist talk about a new European security arrangement, which is just a repackaging of Russian imperialism.”

text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

Many people in AI will be familiar with the story of the Mechanical Turk. It was a chess-playing machine built in 1770, and it was so good its opponents were tricked into believing it was supernaturally powerful. In reality, the machine had space for a human to hide in it and control it. The hoax went on for 84 years. That’s three generations! 

History is rich with examples of people trying to breathe life into inanimate objects, and of people selling hacks and tricks as “magic.” But this very human desire to believe in consciousness in machines has never matched up with reality. 

Creating consciousness in artificial intelligence systems is the dream of many technologists. Large language models are the latest example of our quest for clever machines, and some people (contentiously) claim to have seen glimmers of consciousness in conversations with them. The point is: machine consciousness is a hotly debated topic. Plenty of experts say it is doomed to remain science fiction forever, but others argue it’s right around the corner.

For the latest edition of MIT Technology Review, neuroscientist Grace Huckins explores what consciousness research in humans can teach us about AI, and the moral problems that AI consciousness would raise. Read more here.

We don’t fully understand human consciousness, but neuroscientists do have some clues about how it’s manifested in the brain, Grace writes. To state the obvious, AI systems don’t have brains, so it’s impossible to use traditional methods of measuring brain activity for signs of life. But neuroscientists have various different theories about what consciousness in AI systems might look like. Some treat it as a feature of the brain’s “software,” while others tie it more squarely to physical hardware.

There have even been attempts to create tests for AI consciousness. Susan Schneider, director of the Center for the Future Mind at Florida Atlantic University, and Princeton physicist Edwin Turner have developed one, which requires an AI agent to be isolated from any information about consciousness it could’ve picked up during its training before it’s tested. This step is important so that it can’t just parrot human statements it’s picked up about consciousness during training, as a large language model would.  

The tester then asks the AI questions it should only be able to answer if it is itself conscious. Can it understand the plot of the movie Freaky Friday, where a mother and daughter switch bodies, their consciousnesses dissociated from their physical selves? Can it grasp the concept of dreaming—or even report dreaming itself? Can it conceive of reincarnation or an afterlife?

Of course, this test is not foolproof. It requires its subject to be able to use language, so babies and animals—manifestly conscious beings—would not pass the test. And language-based AI models will have been exposed to the concept of consciousness in the vast amount of internet data they have been trained on. 

So how will we really know if an AI system is conscious? A group of neuroscientists, philosophers, and AI researchers, including Turing Prize winner Yoshua Bengio, have put out a white paper that proposes practical ways to detect AI consciousness based on a variety of theories from different fields. They propose a sort of report card for different markers, such as flexibly pursuing goals and interacting with an external environment, that would indicate AI consciousness—if the theories hold true. None of today’s systems tick any boxes, and it’s unclear if they ever will. 

Here is what we do know. Large language models are extremely good at predicting what the next word in a sentence should be. They are also very good at making connections between things—sometimes in ways that surprise us and make it easy to believe in the illusion that these computer programs might have sparks of something else. But we know remarkably little about AI language models’ inner workings. Until we know more about exactly how and why these systems come to the conclusions they do, it’s hard to say that the models’ outcomes are not just fancy math. 

Deeper Learning

How AI could supercharge battery research

We need better batteries if electric vehicles are going to achieve their potential of nudging fossil-fuel-powered cars off the roads. The problem is that there are a million different potential materials, and combinations of materials, we could use to make these batteries. It’s very labor-intensive and expensive to do rounds and rounds of trial and error. 

Enter AI: Startup Aionics is using AI tools to help researchers find better battery chemistries faster. It uses machine learning to sort through the wide range of material options and suggest combinations. Generative AI can also help researchers design new materials more quickly. Read more from Casey Crownhart in her weekly newsletter, The Spark, on the tech that could solve the climate crisis.

Bits and Bytes

Big Tech struggles to turn AI hype into profits
Microsoft has reportedly lost money on one of its first generative AI products. And it’s not alone: the other tech giants are equally struggling to find a way to capitalize on their massive investment in generative AI, which is eye-wateringly expensive to train and run. (The Wall Street Journal) 

How AI reduces the world to stereotypes
Rest of World analyzed 3,000 AI-generated images of different countries and cultures, and found they portray the world in a deeply stereotypical way. No surprises there, but this visual piece neatly shows just how deeply ingrained biases are in AI systems. (Rest of World) 

Even Google insiders are questioning the usefulness of the Bard chatbot
Glad to know it’s not just me! In leaked messages from an official invite-only Discord chat, Google product managers and designers share their skepticism about the utility of the company’s AI chatbot Bard, considering that the system makes things up. Google insiders seem to think it is best for creative uses, brainstorming, or coding—and even then, it needs lots of supervision. (Bloomberg)

The US is mulling escalating its AI tech blockade on China
Anxious about the prospect of China gaining AI supremacy, the UA has been limiting its access to the computer chips needed to power AI. The US is now considering escalating its blockade and restricting China’s access to a broad category of general-purpose AI programs, not just physical parts. (The Atlantic) 

How a billionaire-backed network of AI advisors took over Washington
The little-known Horizon Institute for Public Service, a nonprofit created in 2022, is funding salaries of people working in key Senate offices, agencies, and think tanks. The group is pushing to put the existential risk posed by AI at the top of Washington’s agenda, which could benefit AI companies with ties to the network. 
(Politico)

Google offers to pay its customers’ legal feel in generative AI lawsuits
Google has joined Microsoft and Getty Images in promising to cough up legal fees if its customers get sued over the outputs of its generative AI models or the training data they use. This is a smart move from Big Tech, as it could help persuade organizations that are hesitating to adopt these companies’ AI tools until there is more legal clarity over copyright and AI. (Google)

England fly out to Madrid today and they have a good team, especially the front six, but there’s always some baggage with them. The current issue is who is the English Pau Cubarsi? Where is the calm, commanding ball-playing centre-back with a winning mindset and record possessed by the Barcelona and Spain defender? Reads the game, anticipates danger, times the tackle, resists the press, distributes well. And is still developing - at 19. 

Cubarsi was named Best Young Player at the World Cup and runner-up to Lamine Yamal in the Kopa award for best young player at the Ballon d’Or. In the overall Ballon d’Or won by Harry Kane, the defender marking him this weekend came 12th. Aged 19. I voted Cubarsi sixth because of his individual performances, trophies and talent.

At St George’s Park, the FA is looking to develop similar defenders of that supreme calibre. Peak John Stones was close. But where is the next Rio Ferdinand, who was world class at his peak (2002 World Cup)? Marc Guehi has lost his confidence for now (but will surely regain his old poise). 

Ezri Konsa is a decade older than Cubarsi. Jarell Quansah develops by the year but still has a mistake in him. Levi Colwill could train on. Big Dan Burn is 34. Jarrad Branthwaite is promising but five years older than Cubarsi and seemingly still has to convince Thomas Tuchel. James Hill was scouted by Barcelona at 19, during a League 1 game for Fleetwood at Burton, moved to Bournemouth and has just been drafted into the England squad. Like Branthwaite, Hill’s five years older than Cubarsi. From the Under-21s, Max Alleyne, Stephen Mfuni and Josh Acheampong offer hope.

None are in Cubarsi’s league. Centre-back is the most significant concern for England. Given the work of the academies and FA coaching and development staff, England are well stocked in many other positions. In goal with the Trafford/Pickford succession slowly taking place (but Pickford deserves to remain No 1 for now). Right-back: James, Alexander-Arnold, White, Livramento. text:
Advances in artificial intelligence are coming to your freezer, in the form of robot-assembled prepared meals. 

Chef Robotics, a San Francisco–based startup, has launched a system of AI-powered robotic arms that can be quickly programmed with a recipe to dole out accurate portions of everything from tikka masala to pesto tortellini. After experiments with leading brands, including Amy’s Kitchen, the company says its robots have proved their worth and are being rolled out at scale to more production facilities. They are also being offered to new customers in the US and Canada. 

You might think the meals that end up in the grocery store’s frozen aisle, at Starbucks, or on airplanes are robot-packed already, but that’s rarely the case. Workers are often much more flexible than robots and can handle production lines that frequently rotate recipes. Not only that, but certain ingredients, like rice or shredded cheese, are hard to portion out with robotic arms. That means the vast majority of meals from recognizable brands are still typically hand-packed. 

However, advancements from AI have changed the calculus, making robots more useful on production lines, says David Griego, senior director of engineering at Amy’s.

“Before Silicon Valley got involved, the industry was much more about ‘Okay, we’re gonna program—a robot is gonna do this and do this only,’” he says. For a brand with so many different meals, that wasn’t very helpful. But the robots Griego is now able to add to the production line can learn how scooping a portion of peas is different from scooping cauliflower, and they can improve their accuracy for next time. “It’s astounding just how they can adapt to all the different types of ingredients that we use,” he says. Meal-packing robots suddenly make much more financial sense. 

Rather than selling the machines outright, Chef uses a service model, where customers pay a yearly fee that covers maintenance and training. Amy’s currently uses eight systems (each with two robotic arms) spread across two of its plants. One of these systems can now do the work of two to four workers depending on which ingredients are being packed, Griego says. The robots also reduce waste, since they can pack more consistent portions than their human counterparts. One-arm systems typically cost less than $135,000 per year, according to Chef CEO Rajat Bhageria.

With these advantages in mind, Griego imagines the robots handling more and more of the meal assembly process. “I have a vision,” he says, “where the only thing people would do is run the systems.” They’d make sure the hoppers of ingredients and packaging materials were full, for example, and the robots would do the rest. 

Robot chefs have been getting more skilled in recent years thanks to AI, and some companies have promised that burger-flipping and nugget-frying robots can provide cost savings to restaurants. But much of this technology has seen little adoption in the restaurant industry so far, says Bhageria. That’s because fast-casual restaurants often only need one cook running the grill, and if a robot cannot fully replace that person because it still needs supervision, it makes little sense to use it. Packaged meal companies, however, have a larger source of labor costs that they want to bring down: plating and assembly.

“That’s going to be the highest bang for our buck for our customers,” Bhageria says. 

The notion that more flexible robots could mean broader adoption in new industries is no surprise, says Lerrel Pinto, who leads the General-Purpose Robotics and AI Lab at New York University and is not involved with Chef or Amy’s Kitchen. 

“A lot of robots deployed in the real world are used in a very repetitive way, where they’re supposed to do the same thing over and over again,” he says. Deep learning has caused a paradigm shift over the past few years, sparking the idea that more generally capable robots might be not only possible but necessary for more widespread adoption. If Chef’s robots can perform without frequent stops for repair or training, they could deliver material savings to food companies and shift how they use human labor, Pinto says: “In the next few years, we will probably see a lot more companies trying to actually deploy these types of learning-based robots in the real world.”

One new challenge the robots have created for Amy’s, Griego says, is maintaining the look of a hand-packed meal when it was assembled by a robot. The company’s cheese enchilada dish in particular was causing trouble: it’s finished with a hand-distributed sprinkling of cheddar on top, but Amy’s panel of examiners said the cheese on the robot-packed dish looked too machine-spread, sending Griego back to the drawing board.

“The first few tests went pretty well,” he says. After a couple of changes, the robots are ready to take over. Amy’s plans to bring them to more of its facilities and train them on a growing list of ingredients, meaning your frozen meals are increasingly likely to be packed by a robot.

Update: This story has been amended to include updating pricing information from Chef.

My first marriage lasted less than five years. I raised my daughter on my own. When she moved out, I bought a tiny rice cooker and made breakfast in it for a week straight because I liked that it could make just enough for me.

On our second date, my new husband noticed that I’d stopped eating because my food was too spicy. He offered to switch plates. I remember how good it felt to have someone notice.

Living together, I started noticing things too. The way he shut a cupboard. How long he took to answer. One Sunday we’d planned to go to a diner. I put on my coat and asked if he was ready.

“If you’re in such a hurry, go by yourself.”

I took my coat off. I was already thinking about what the house would feel like when I came back.

My daughter reminded me of the last time she’d visited. My husband had gone to bed. She made a joke and I shushed her.

“At your old place, I could show up at eleven and you’d put a pot on.”

text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

In the late autumn of 1862 Abraham Lincoln had run out of patience. The Army of the Potomac had bled heavily at Antietam and then sat still while McClellan rebuilt and hesitated. Lincoln removed him and handed command to Ambrose Burnside. Burnside did not want the job. He told the president so. He was a solid corps commander, popular with the men, but he doubted his own fitness for independent army command. Ordered to take it, he offered a plan that promised speed: march southeast, cross the Rappahannock at Fredericksburg, seize the town, and push on Richmond before Lee could concentrate.

Lincoln approved. For once the Army of the Potomac moved quickly. Burnside’s columns reached the river while Lee’s forces were still scattered. A prompt crossing might have put the Union army between the Confederate capital and its defenders. Then the pontoon bridges, requisitioned from the Washington depot, failed to arrive. Rain fell. Roads turned to mud. Day after day the army waited on the north bank while the chance slipped away.

Lee used the time. Longstreet’s corps filed into position on the heights behind the town and strengthened the stone wall and sunken road at Marye’s Heights. Jackson’s corps came up and anchored the Confederate right along the wooded ridge. When the bridges finally appeared and Union engineers began laying them under fire, the defensive line was already strong.

On December 13 the Army of the Potomac attacked. In the streets of Fredericksburg the fighting was close and savage. On the open slope in front of Marye’s Heights it became a series of frontal assaults into prepared fire. Brigade after brigade went forward. The Irish Brigade advanced under its green flags and was shattered. New York, Pennsylvania, and New England regiments followed and met the same wall of musketry and canister. Men fell in ranks. Survivors crawled back or lay among the dead. By the end of the day the Union army had lost more than 12,600 men killed, wounded, and missing. Confederate casualties were under 5,400. The drive on Richmond was never launched.

The defeat was complete. Burnside’s army remained on the field through a bitter night, listening to the wounded between the lines. A later attempt to maneuver around the Confederate flank dissolved in winter mud. Lincoln soon replaced him. For the North it was a hard winter. The men who had charged the stone wall had done what was asked of them. The failure belonged to timing, logistics, and the decision to attack fortified ground after the advantage had been lost. Fredericksburg stands as one of the clearest examples in the war of what courage alone cannot overcome when the ground and the moment both favor the defender.

Since 2011, the census in England and Wales has asked three separate questions:

The Russian Embassy's response to the @FT article on @wesstreeting's call for a backchannel with Moscow.

The Curious Business of Diplomacy - When London Wants to Talk to Moscow Again

There is something rather wonderfully British about closing a door with considerable indignation, only to return some time later and express surprise that nobody is answering the bell.

Such, it seems, is the latest chapter in Anglo-Russian relations.

Responding to a Financial Times article concerning Defence Secretary @wesstreeting's desire to restore military communication channels with Moscow, the Russian Embassy in London @RussianEmbassy offered a pointed reminder:

"Just a reminder: military communication channels were cut at Britain's initiative in 2024, when London chose to expel Russia's Defence Attaché on a flimsy pretext."

The British Government, it should be remembered, had accused the diplomat of being an undeclared military intelligence officer - an allegation Moscow rejected.

And therein lies the curious contradiction of modern diplomacy.

For there is a time to disagree, a time to protest, and sometimes even a time to expel diplomats. But there is surely never a sensible time for two nuclear powers to abandon the means of speaking directly to one another.

Wars have begun through miscalculation, misunderstandings and the dangerous assumption that the other fellow knows precisely what one intends.

Diplomacy, after all, is not the art of speaking only to one's friends. Its greatest value often lies in keeping a telephone line open to one's adversaries.

And perhaps the most remarkable thing about this little exchange is that Moscow now says it is perfectly willing to answer the telephone.

The question, one supposes, is whether London is prepared to make the call.

The Embassy's statement is genuine and was published in connection with Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova's remarks on 11 November 2026. Britain's stated justification for the 2024 expulsion remains disputed by Moscow.
